Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat az-Zumar

It is a Meccan surah according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca."

An-Nahhas narrated in his book on abrogation (Nasikh) from him that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca, except for three verses which were revealed in Medina concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–55], the three verses."

Others said: "Up to seven verses, from His saying: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–59], to the end of the seven."

An-Nasa'i narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fast until we said he would not break his fast, and he would break it until we said he would not fast. And he used to recite in every night Bani Isra'il and az-Zumar."

At-Tirmidhi narrated it from her with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-1274) would not sleep until he had recited az-Zumar and Bani Isra'il."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject which is a demonstrative pronoun, meaning: "This is the revelation."

Abu Hayyan said: the omitted subject is the pronoun "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87], as if it was said: "And what is this reminder?" So it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book." It was also said that it is in the nominative case as a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase following it, meaning: "A revelation from Allah." This is the view of az-Zajjaj and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: It may also be nominative in the sense of "This is a revelation." Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative, as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "Follow" or "recite the revelation of the Book."

Al-Farra' said: It may be accusative as an incitement (al-igra'), meaning: "Adhere to." "The Book" is the Qur'an. His saying ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, according to the first reading, is either a complement of "revelation," or a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or related to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) governed by the omitted demonstrative.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The "ba'" (with) is causal (sababiyyah), connected to "sending down," meaning: "We sent it down because of the truth." It may also be connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause of the agent, meaning: "while you are bearing the truth," or of the object, meaning: "while it bears the truth." The intended meaning is everything in it of affirming monotheism, prophethood, the Return, and the various kinds of obligations.

Muqatil said: It means: "We did not send it down in vain, for no purpose."

﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His﴾. The "fa'" indicates the consequence of what follows from what precedes. "Sincerely" (mukhlisan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "worship." Sincerity (ikhlas) is that the servant intends by his deed the Face of Allah, glory be to Him. "Religion" (din) means worship and obedience, and its foundation is the oneness of Allah and that He has no partner.

The majority read "ad-din" in the accusative as the object of "mukhlisan." Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the nominative, treating "mukhlisan" as predicated of "ad-din" in a metaphorical manner.

It was said: He should have read "mukhlisa" with a fatha on the lam (i.e., the accusative form of the participle agreeing with the pronoun).

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of intention and for purifying it from impurities, because sincerity is among the matters of the heart, which can only be achieved through the actions of the heart. The authentic Sunnah has also established that the basis of matters in statements and actions is intention, as in the hadith "Actions are only by intentions," and the hadith "There is no statement and no action except with intention."

The sentence ﴿Certainly, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾ is a resumptive clause affirming what precedes of the command to sincerity: that the pure religion, free from the taints of polytheism and other things, belongs to Allah, and that whatever else of religions is not the pure religion of Allah which He commanded.

Qatadah said: "The pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. When He, glory be to Him, commanded worship in the manner of sincerity, and that the pure religion is for Him alone and not for another, He made clear the falsehood of polytheism, which contradicts sincerity. The relative pronoun refers to the polytheists, and its position is nominative as the subject; its predicate is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾. The clause ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause with an implied "saying," and the exception is a restricted exception from the most general of causes. The meaning: "And those who did not make worship sincerely for Allah, but mixed it with the worship of others, saying: 'We do not worship them for anything of things except that they bring us near to Allah in nearness.'" The pronoun in "worship them" refers to the things they worshipped, namely the angels, Jesus and the idols, and these are the ones meant by "protectors." What is meant by their saying ﴿only that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ is intercession, as al-Wahidi related from the exegetes.

Qatadah said: When it was said to them, "Who is your Lord and your Creator? Who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky?" they said, "Allah." Then it was said to them, "What is the meaning of your worship of idols?" They said, "That they may bring us near to Allah in position and intercede for us with Him."

Al-Kalbi said: The answer to this statement is His saying in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿Why then did those they had taken as gods besides Allah for [perceived] nearness [to Him] not help them?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. "Zulfa" is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, as if He had said: "only that they bring us near to Allah in nearness."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid: "They said, 'We do not worship them.'" The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ is: between the people of the religions on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense each according to what it deserves. It was also said: between those who were sincere in religion and those who were not sincere; the first is omitted because the situation indicates it. The meaning of ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ is: concerning what they differed about in religion, of monotheism and polytheism, for every group claims that the truth is with it. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾: that is, He does not guide to His religion, nor grants success in being guided to the truth, one who is a liar in his claim that the idols bring him near to Allah, and who disbelieves by taking them as gods and making them partners with Allah. "Kuffar" is an intensive form indicating that the disbelief of these people has reached its extreme.

Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "kadhdhab" (liar) in the intensive form like "kuffar," and this reading is reported from Anas.

﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen [from what He creates] whatever He willed﴾. This establishes what preceded of the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the angels are daughters of Allah, since it implies the impossibility of a son for Him, glory be to Him, absolutely. So if He had intended to take a son, the taking of a son in reality would have been impossible, and this could only have been achieved by choosing from what He creates whatever He wills, that is, selecting from among His creation whatever He wishes to choose, since there is no existent apart from Him except that it is created by Him. And it is not valid that the created be a son of the Creator, because there is no homogeneity between them. So nothing remains but that He chooses it as a servant, as the expression "chooses" (yasta fi) in place of "takes" (yattakhidh) indicates. (p-1275) The meaning of the verse is: Had He intended to take a son, there would have occurred something which is not the taking of a son, but rather a choosing of some of His creatures. For this reason He, glory be to Him, declared Himself exempt from taking a son absolutely, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning: exalted above that. The sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ clarifies His transcendence with respect to attributes, after His transcendence with respect to essence; that is, He is the one who possesses all the attributes of perfection, uniquely one in His essence, so there is no like unto Him; the Subduer over all His creatures. Whoever is characterized by these attributes, the existence of a son in relation to Him is impossible, because a son resembles his father, and there is nothing like Him, glory be to Him. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Had We intended to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17].

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned His being exempt from having a son by His being the one God, the Subduer, He mentioned what indicates that from His attributes, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He did not create them in vain, for no purpose. Whoever has created this great creation is impossible to have a partner, a consort, or a son.

Then He explained the manner of His disposal over the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. "Takwir" in the language means throwing one thing upon another; it is said: "kawwara al-mata'" when one places some of the goods upon others, and from it "kawwara al-'imamah" (he wound the turban). So the meaning of the wrapping of the night over the day is its covering it until its light goes away, and the meaning of the wrapping of the day over the night is its covering it until its darkness goes away. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He covers the night with the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Thus said Qatadah and others.

Al-Dahhak said: That is, He throws this upon this and this upon this, and this is close to the first statement.

It was also said: The meaning of the verse is that what decreases from the night enters into the day, and what decreases from the day enters into the night, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13; al-Hadid: 6]. It was also said: The meaning is that this recurs upon this and this recurs upon this in successive recurrence.

Al-Raghib said: "Takwir" of a thing is its turning around and gathering some of it onto some other, like "kawwara al-'imamah." Ended.

The indication by this "takwir" mentioned in the verse is to the sun's movement through its risings, and to the decrease and increase of night and day.

Al-Razi said: Light and darkness are two great armies; each day one overcomes the other and the other overcomes it. Then he mentioned His subjugation of the authority of the day and the authority of the night, which are the sun and the moon, saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: He made them submissive to His command in rising and setting for the benefits of the servants. Then He explained the manner of this subjugation, saying: ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each runs in its orbit until the world ends, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of the specified term for their running has already been fully covered in Surat Ya-Sin. ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving﴾. "Ala" is a particle of alerting; the meaning: "Take heed, O servants; Allah is the Dominant, the One who covers the sins of His creatures by forgiveness."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His power and marvelous creation, saying: ﴿He created you from one soul﴾, which is the soul of Adam, ﴿then made from it its mate﴾. The "thumma" (then) was used to indicate the sequence of the creation of Eve after the creation of Adam, and its delay from him, because she was created from him. The conjunction is either upon an omitted element that is a qualifier of "soul," as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said, the meaning being: "He created you from a soul He created as one, then made from it its mate."

It is also possible that the conjunction is upon the meaning of "one" (wahidah), meaning: from a soul that stood alone, then He made from it, etc. The expression "made" (ja'ala) rather than "created" (khalaqa), together with the conjunction by "thumma," indicates that the creation of Eve from Adam's rib was counted among what is a marvelous sign, indicating the perfection of power, because the creation of Adam is by Allah's constant habit in His creation, whereas creating a female in the said manner was not a habitual practice, since He, glory be to Him, did not create any female from a man's rib other than her. The explanation of this verse has already been fully covered in Surat al-A'raf.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous power, saying: ﴿And He sent down for you from the livestock eight pairs﴾. This is conjoined to "created you," and He expressed it with "sent down" because it is reported that He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; so the sending down would be literal. It is also possible that it is figurative, because they did not live except by vegetation, and vegetation only lives by water, and water is sent down from the sky; so the livestock were as if they were sent down, since the cause of their cause is sent down, just as the term was applied to the cause in the poet's words:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

Al-Shawkani said: It was also said that (أَنْزَلَ, *anzala*, "sent down") here means "created" (أَنْشَأ) and "made" (جَعَلَ), or means "gave" (أَعْطَى). It was also said that the creation was made a "sending down," because creation only occurs by a command that descends from the heavens. The "eight pairs" are those mentioned in His words: ﴿Two pairs of sheep and two of goats﴾ [al-An'am: 143] ﴿and two pairs of camels and two of cattle﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. By "the two" in the four places, He means the male and the female. The tafsir of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear another kind of His wondrous power, saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. The sentence is a new (*isti'nafiyyah*) clause, explaining what it contains of the different stages of their creation. (خَلْقًا, *khalqan*, "creation") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing the verb mentioned, and (مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ, "after creation") is a qualifier of it, meaning: a creation occurring after a creation.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bone (*'izam*), then flesh (*lahm*).

Ibn Zayd said: He created you a creation in the wombs of your mothers after your creation in the loins of Adam. His words ﴿in three darknesses﴾ are connected to His words "He creates you." These three darknesses are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (*mashimah*), as said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the night. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darkness of the man's loins, the darkness of the woman's belly, and the darkness of the womb.

The reference in His words ﴿That is Allah﴾ is to Him, glorified is He, in view of His previous acts. The noble name (*Allah*) is the subject of the predicate ﴿your Lord﴾, which is another predicate of it. ﴿To Him belongs true sovereignty in this world and the Hereafter; no partner shares in it﴾ is a third predicate. His words ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ are a fourth predicate. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Him and turn from it to the worship of others?

Hamzah read (إِمَّهَاتِكُمْ, *immahatikum*, "your mothers") with a kasrah on the hamzah and the meem. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem. The rest read with a dammah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking remembrance (*dhikr*); will we have a reward for that?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, we only give seeking reward and remembrance; will we have a reward?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts only what is done sincerely for Him," and then he recited this verse: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs sincere devotion (*al-din al-khalis*)﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿He wraps the night﴾ that he said: "He carries the night."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿creation after creation﴾ that he said: "a clot, then a lump, then bones," ﴿in three darknesses﴾: "the belly, the womb, and the placenta."

Then He explained the manner of this subjugation, saying: ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each runs in its orbit until the world ends, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of the specified term for their running has already been fully covered in Surat Ya-Sin. ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving﴾. "Ala" is a particle of alerting; the meaning: "Take heed, O servants; Allah is the Dominant, the One who covers the sins of His creatures by forgiveness."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His power and marvelous creation, saying: ﴿He created you from one soul﴾, which is the soul of Adam, ﴿then made from it its mate﴾. The "thumma" (then) was used to indicate the sequence of the creation of Eve after the creation of Adam, and its delay from him, because she was created from him. The conjunction is either upon an omitted element that is a qualifier of "soul," as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said, the meaning being: "He created you from a soul He created as one, then made from it its mate."

It is also possible that the conjunction is upon the meaning of "one" (wahidah), meaning: from a soul that stood alone, then He made from it, etc. The expression "made" (ja'ala) rather than "created" (khalaqa), together with the conjunction by "thumma," indicates that the creation of Eve from Adam's rib was counted among what is a marvelous sign, indicating the perfection of power, because the creation of Adam is by Allah's constant habit in His creation, whereas creating a female in the said manner was not a habitual practice, since He, glory be to Him, did not create any female from a man's rib other than her. The explanation of this verse has already been fully covered in Surat al-A'raf.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous power, saying: ﴿And He sent down for you from the livestock eight pairs﴾. This is conjoined to "created you," and He expressed it with "sent down" because it is reported that He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; so the sending down would be literal. It is also possible that it is figurative, because they did not live except by vegetation, and vegetation only lives by water, and water is sent down from the sky; so the livestock were as if they were sent down, since the cause of their cause is sent down, just as the term was applied to the cause in the poet's words:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

Al-Shawkani said: It was also said that (أَنْزَلَ, *anzala*, "sent down") here means "created" (أَنْشَأ) and "made" (جَعَلَ), or means "gave" (أَعْطَى). It was also said that the creation was made a "sending down," because creation only occurs by a command that descends from the heavens. The "eight pairs" are those mentioned in His words: ﴿Two pairs of sheep and two of goats﴾ [al-An'am: 143] ﴿and two pairs of camels and two of cattle﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. By "the two" in the four places, He means the male and the female. The tafsir of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear another kind of His wondrous power, saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. The sentence is a new (*isti'nafiyyah*) clause, explaining what it contains of the different stages of their creation. (خَلْقًا, *khalqan*, "creation") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing the verb mentioned, and (مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ, "after creation") is a qualifier of it, meaning: a creation occurring after a creation.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bone (*'izam*), then flesh (*lahm*).

Ibn Zayd said: He created you a creation in the wombs of your mothers after your creation in the loins of Adam. His words ﴿in three darknesses﴾ are connected to His words "He creates you." These three darknesses are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (*mashimah*), as said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the night. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darkness of the man's loins, the darkness of the woman's belly, and the darkness of the womb.

The reference in His words ﴿That is Allah﴾ is to Him, glorified is He, in view of His previous acts. The noble name (*Allah*) is the subject of the predicate ﴿your Lord﴾, which is another predicate of it. ﴿To Him belongs true sovereignty in this world and the Hereafter; no partner shares in it﴾ is a third predicate. His words ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ are a fourth predicate. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Him and turn from it to the worship of others?

Hamzah read (إِمَّهَاتِكُمْ, *immahatikum*, "your mothers") with a kasrah on the hamzah and the meem. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem. The rest read with a dammah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking remembrance (*dhikr*); will we have a reward for that?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, we only give seeking reward and remembrance; will we have a reward?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts only what is done sincerely for Him," and then he recited this verse: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs sincere devotion (*al-din al-khalis*)﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿He wraps the night﴾ that he said: "He carries the night."

Others said: "Up to seven verses, from His saying: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–59], to the end of the seven."

An-Nasa'i narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fast until we said he would not break his fast, and he would break it until we said he would not fast. And he used to recite in every night Bani Isra'il and az-Zumar."

At-Tirmidhi narrated it from her with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-1274) would not sleep until he had recited az-Zumar and Bani Isra'il."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject which is a demonstrative pronoun, meaning: "This is the revelation."

Abu Hayyan said: the omitted subject is the pronoun "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87], as if it was said: "And what is this reminder?" So it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book." It was also said that it is in the nominative case as a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase following it, meaning: "A revelation from Allah." This is the view of az-Zajjaj and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: It may also be nominative in the sense of "This is a revelation." Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative, as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "Follow" or "recite the revelation of the Book."

Al-Farra' said: It may be accusative as an incitement (al-igra'), meaning: "Adhere to." "The Book" is the Qur'an. His saying ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, according to the first reading, is either a complement of "revelation," or a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or related to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) governed by the omitted demonstrative.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The "ba'" (with) is causal (sababiyyah), connected to "sending down," meaning: "We sent it down because of the truth." It may also be connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause of the agent, meaning: "while you are bearing the truth," or of the object, meaning: "while it bears the truth." The intended meaning is everything in it of affirming monotheism, prophethood, the Return, and the various kinds of obligations.

Muqatil said: It means: "We did not send it down in vain, for no purpose."

﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His﴾. The "fa'" indicates the consequence of what follows from what precedes. "Sincerely" (mukhlisan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "worship." Sincerity (ikhlas) is that the servant intends by his deed the Face of Allah, glory be to Him. "Religion" (din) means worship and obedience, and its foundation is the oneness of Allah and that He has no partner.

The majority read "ad-din" in the accusative as the object of "mukhlisan." Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the nominative, treating "mukhlisan" as predicated of "ad-din" in a metaphorical manner.

It was said: He should have read "mukhlisa" with a fatha on the lam (i.e., the accusative form of the participle agreeing with the pronoun).

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of intention and for purifying it from impurities, because sincerity is among the matters of the heart, which can only be achieved through the actions of the heart. The authentic Sunnah has also established that the basis of matters in statements and actions is intention, as in the hadith "Actions are only by intentions," and the hadith "There is no statement and no action except with intention."

The sentence ﴿Certainly, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾ is a resumptive clause affirming what precedes of the command to sincerity: that the pure religion, free from the taints of polytheism and other things, belongs to Allah, and that whatever else of religions is not the pure religion of Allah which He commanded.

Qatadah said: "The pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. The relative pronoun refers to the polytheists, and its position is nominative as the subject; its predicate is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾. The clause ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause with an implied "saying," and the exception is a restricted exception from the most general of causes. The meaning: "And those who did not make worship sincerely for Allah, but mixed it with the worship of others, saying: 'We do not worship them for anything of things except that they bring us near to Allah in nearness.'" The pronoun in "worship them" refers to the things they worshipped, namely the angels, Jesus and the idols, and these are the ones meant by "protectors." What is meant by their saying ﴿only that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ is intercession, as al-Wahidi related from the exegetes.

Qatadah said: When it was said to them, "Who is your Lord and your Creator? Who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky?" they said, "Allah." Then it was said to them, "What is the meaning of your worship of idols?" They said, "That they may bring us near to Allah in position and intercede for us with Him."

"Zulfa" is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, as if He had said: "only that they bring us near to Allah in nearness."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid: "They said, 'We do not worship them.'" The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ is: between the people of the religions on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense each according to what it deserves. It was also said: between those who were sincere in religion and those who were not sincere; the first is omitted because the situation indicates it. The meaning of ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ is: concerning what they differed about in religion, of monotheism and polytheism, for every group claims that the truth is with it. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾: that is, He does not guide to His religion, nor grants success in being guided to the truth, one who is a liar in his claim that the idols bring him near to Allah, and who disbelieves by taking them as gods and making them partners with Allah. "Kuffar" is an intensive form indicating that the disbelief of these people has reached its extreme.

Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "kadhdhab" (liar) in the intensive form like "kuffar," and this reading is reported from Anas.

﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen [from what He creates] whatever He willed﴾. This establishes what preceded of the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the angels are daughters of Allah, since it implies the impossibility of a son for Him, glory be to Him, absolutely. So if He had intended to take a son, the taking of a son in reality would have been impossible, and this could only have been achieved by choosing from what He creates whatever He wills, that is, selecting from among His creation whatever He wishes to choose, since there is no existent apart from Him except that it is created by Him. And it is not valid that the created be a son of the Creator, because there is no homogeneity between them. So nothing remains but that He chooses it as a servant, as the expression "chooses" (yasta fi) in place of "takes" (yattakhidh) indicates. For this reason He, glory be to Him, declared Himself exempt from taking a son absolutely, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning: exalted above that. The sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ clarifies His transcendence with respect to attributes, after His transcendence with respect to essence; that is, He is the one who possesses all the attributes of perfection, uniquely one in His essence, so there is no like unto Him; the Subduer over all His creatures. Whoever is characterized by these attributes, the existence of a son in relation to Him is impossible, because a son resembles his father, and there is nothing like Him, glory be to Him. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Had We intended to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17].

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned His being exempt from having a son by His being the one God, the Subduer, He mentioned what indicates that from His attributes, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He did not create them in vain, for no purpose. Whoever has created this great creation is impossible to have a partner, a consort, or a son.

Then He explained the manner of His disposal over the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. "Takwir" in the language means throwing one thing upon another; it is said: "kawwara al-mata'" when one places some of the goods upon others, and from it "kawwara al-'imamah" (he wound the turban). So the meaning of the wrapping of the night over the day is its covering it until its light goes away, and the meaning of the wrapping of the day over the night is its covering it until its darkness goes away. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He covers the night with the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Thus said Qatadah and others.

Al-Dahhak said: That is, He throws this upon this and this upon this, and this is close to the first statement.

It was also said: The meaning of the verse is that what decreases from the night enters into the day, and what decreases from the day enters into the night, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13; al-Hadid: 6]. It was also said: The meaning is that this recurs upon this and this recurs upon this in successive recurrence.

Al-Raghib said: "Takwir" of a thing is its turning around and gathering some of it onto some other, like "kawwara al-'imamah." Ended.

The indication by this "takwir" mentioned in the verse is to the sun's movement through its risings, and to the decrease and increase of night and day.

Al-Razi said: Light and darkness are two great armies; each day one overcomes the other and the other overcomes it. Then he mentioned His subjugation of the authority of the day and the authority of the night, which are the sun and the moon, saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: He made them submissive to His command in rising and setting for the benefits of the servants. When He, glory be to Him, commanded worship in the manner of sincerity, and that the pure religion is for Him alone and not for another, He made clear the falsehood of polytheism, which contradicts sincerity. The relative pronoun refers to the polytheists, and its position is nominative as the subject; its predicate is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾. The clause ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause with an implied "saying," and the exception is a restricted exception from the most general of causes. The meaning: "And those who did not make worship sincerely for Allah, but mixed it with the worship of others, saying: 'We do not worship them for anything of things except that they bring us near to Allah in nearness.'" The pronoun in "worship them" refers to the things they worshipped, namely the angels, Jesus and the idols, and these are the ones meant by "protectors." What is meant by their saying ﴿only that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ is intercession, as al-Wahidi related from the exegetes.

Qatadah said: When it was said to them, "Who is your Lord and your Creator? Who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky?" they said, "Allah." Then it was said to them, "What is the meaning of your worship of idols?" They said, "That they may bring us near to Allah in position and intercede for us with Him."

Al-Kalbi said: The answer to this statement is His saying in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿Why then did those they had taken as gods besides Allah for [perceived] nearness [to Him] not help them?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. "Zulfa" is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, as if He had said: "only that they bring us near to Allah in nearness."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid: "They said, 'We do not worship them.'" The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ is: between the people of the religions on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense each according to what it deserves. It was also said: between those who were sincere in religion and those who were not sincere; the first is omitted because the situation indicates it. The meaning of ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ is: concerning what they differed about in religion, of monotheism and polytheism, for every group claims that the truth is with it. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾: that is, He does not guide to His religion, nor grants success in being guided to the truth, one who is a liar in his claim that the idols bring him near to Allah, and who disbelieves by taking them as gods and making them partners with Allah. "Kuffar" is an intensive form indicating that the disbelief of these people has reached its extreme.

Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "kadhdhab" (liar) in the intensive form like "kuffar," and this reading is reported from Anas.

﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen [from what He creates] whatever He willed﴾. This establishes what preceded of the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the angels are daughters of Allah, since it implies the impossibility of a son for Him, glory be to Him, absolutely. So if He had intended to take a son, the taking of a son in reality would have been impossible, and this could only have been achieved by choosing from what He creates whatever He wills, that is, selecting from among His creation whatever He wishes to choose, since there is no existent apart from Him except that it is created by Him. And it is not valid that the created be a son of the Creator, because there is no homogeneity between them. So nothing remains but that He chooses it as a servant, as the expression "chooses" (yasta fi) in place of "takes" (yattakhidh) indicates. (p-1275) The meaning of the verse is: Had He intended to take a son, there would have occurred something which is not the taking of a son, but rather a choosing of some of His creatures. For this reason He, glory be to Him, declared Himself exempt from taking a son absolutely, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning: exalted above that. The sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ clarifies His transcendence with respect to attributes, after His transcendence with respect to essence; that is, He is the one who possesses all the attributes of perfection, uniquely one in His essence, so there is no like unto Him; the Subduer over all His creatures. Whoever is characterized by these attributes, the existence of a son in relation to Him is impossible, because a son resembles his father, and there is nothing like Him, glory be to Him. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Had We intended to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17].

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned His being exempt from having a son by His being the one God, the Subduer, He mentioned what indicates that from His attributes, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He did not create them in vain, for no purpose. Whoever has created this great creation is impossible to have a partner, a consort, or a son.

Then He explained the manner of His disposal over the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. "Takwir" in the language means throwing one thing upon another; it is said: "kawwara al-mata'" when one places some of the goods upon others, and from it "kawwara al-'imamah" (he wound the turban). So the meaning of the wrapping of the night over the day is its covering it until its light goes away, and the meaning of the wrapping of the day over the night is its covering it until its darkness goes away. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He covers the night with the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Thus said Qatadah and others.

Al-Dahhak said: That is, He throws this upon this and this upon this, and this is close to the first statement.

It was also said: The meaning of the verse is that what decreases from the night enters into the day, and what decreases from the day enters into the night, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13; al-Hadid: 6]. It was also said: The meaning is that this recurs upon this and this recurs upon this in successive recurrence.

Al-Raghib said: "Takwir" of a thing is its turning around and gathering some of it onto some other, like "kawwara al-'imamah." Ended.

The indication by this "takwir" mentioned in the verse is to the sun's movement through its risings, and to the decrease and increase of night and day.

Al-Razi said: Light and darkness are two great armies; each day one overcomes the other and the other overcomes it. Then he mentioned His subjugation of the authority of the day and the authority of the night, which are the sun and the moon, saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: He made them submissive to His command in rising and setting for the benefits of the servants. Then He explained the manner of this subjugation, saying: ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each runs in its orbit until the world ends, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of the specified term for their running has already been fully covered in Surat Ya-Sin. ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving﴾. "Ala" is a particle of alerting; the meaning: "Take heed, O servants; Allah is the Dominant, the One who covers the sins of His creatures by forgiveness."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His power and marvelous creation, saying: ﴿He created you from one soul﴾, which is the soul of Adam, ﴿then made from it its mate﴾. The "thumma" (then) was used to indicate the sequence of the creation of Eve after the creation of Adam, and its delay from him, because she was created from him. The conjunction is either upon an omitted element that is a qualifier of "soul," as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said, the meaning being: "He created you from a soul He created as one, then made from it its mate."

It is also possible that the conjunction is upon the meaning of "one" (wahidah), meaning: from a soul that stood alone, then He made from it, etc. The expression "made" (ja'ala) rather than "created" (khalaqa), together with the conjunction by "thumma," indicates that the creation of Eve from Adam's rib was counted among what is a marvelous sign, indicating the perfection of power, because the creation of Adam is by Allah's constant habit in His creation, whereas creating a female in the said manner was not a habitual practice, since He, glory be to Him, did not create any female from a man's rib other than her. The explanation of this verse has already been fully covered in Surat al-A'raf.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous power, saying: ﴿And He sent down for you from the livestock eight pairs﴾. This is conjoined to "created you," and He expressed it with "sent down" because it is reported that He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; so the sending down would be literal. It is also possible that it is figurative, because they did not live except by vegetation, and vegetation only lives by water, and water is sent down from the sky; so the livestock were as if they were sent down, since the cause of their cause is sent down, just as the term was applied to the cause in the poet's words:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

Al-Shawkani said: It was also said that (أَنْزَلَ, *anzala*, "sent down") here means "created" (أَنْشَأ) and "made" (جَعَلَ), or means "gave" (أَعْطَى). It was also said that the creation was made a "sending down," because creation only occurs by a command that descends from the heavens. The "eight pairs" are those mentioned in His words: ﴿Two pairs of sheep and two of goats﴾ [al-An'am: 143] ﴿and two pairs of camels and two of cattle﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. By "the two" in the four places, He means the male and the female. The tafsir of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear another kind of His wondrous power, saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. The sentence is a new (*isti'nafiyyah*) clause, explaining what it contains of the different stages of their creation. (خَلْقًا, *khalqan*, "creation") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing the verb mentioned, and (مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ, "after creation") is a qualifier of it, meaning: a creation occurring after a creation.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bone (*'izam*), then flesh (*lahm*).

Ibn Zayd said: He created you a creation in the wombs of your mothers after your creation in the loins of Adam. His words ﴿in three darknesses﴾ are connected to His words "He creates you." These three darknesses are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (*mashimah*), as said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the night. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darkness of the man's loins, the darkness of the woman's belly, and the darkness of the womb.

The reference in His words ﴿That is Allah﴾ is to Him, glorified is He, in view of His previous acts. The noble name (*Allah*) is the subject of the predicate ﴿your Lord﴾, which is another predicate of it. ﴿To Him belongs true sovereignty in this world and the Hereafter; no partner shares in it﴾ is a third predicate. His words ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ are a fourth predicate. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Him and turn from it to the worship of others?

Hamzah read (إِمَّهَاتِكُمْ, *immahatikum*, "your mothers") with a kasrah on the hamzah and the meem. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem. The rest read with a dammah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking remembrance (*dhikr*); will we have a reward for that?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, we only give seeking reward and remembrance; will we have a reward?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts only what is done sincerely for Him," and then he recited this verse: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs sincere devotion (*al-din al-khalis*)﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿He wraps the night﴾ that he said: "He carries the night."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿creation after creation﴾ that he said: "a clot, then a lump, then bones," ﴿in three darknesses﴾: "the belly, the womb, and the placenta."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat az-Zumar

It is a Meccan surah according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca."

An-Nahhas narrated in his book on abrogation (Nasikh) from him that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca, except for three verses which were revealed in Medina concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–55], the three verses."

Others said: "Up to seven verses, from His saying: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–59], to the end of the seven."

An-Nasa'i narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fast until we said he would not break his fast, and he would break it until we said he would not fast. And he used to recite in every night Bani Isra'il and az-Zumar."

At-Tirmidhi narrated it from her with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-1274) would not sleep until he had recited az-Zumar and Bani Isra'il."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject which is a demonstrative pronoun, meaning: "This is the revelation."

Abu Hayyan said: the omitted subject is the pronoun "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87], as if it was said: "And what is this reminder?" So it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book." It was also said that it is in the nominative case as a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase following it, meaning: "A revelation from Allah." This is the view of az-Zajjaj and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: It may also be nominative in the sense of "This is a revelation." Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative, as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "Follow" or "recite the revelation of the Book."

Al-Farra' said: It may be accusative as an incitement (al-igra'), meaning: "Adhere to." "The Book" is the Qur'an. His saying ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, according to the first reading, is either a complement of "revelation," or a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or related to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) governed by the omitted demonstrative.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The "ba'" (with) is causal (sababiyyah), connected to "sending down," meaning: "We sent it down because of the truth." It may also be connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause of the agent, meaning: "while you are bearing the truth," or of the object, meaning: "while it bears the truth." The intended meaning is everything in it of affirming monotheism, prophethood, the Return, and the various kinds of obligations.

Muqatil said: It means: "We did not send it down in vain, for no purpose."

﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His﴾. The "fa'" indicates the consequence of what follows from what precedes. "Sincerely" (mukhlisan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "worship." Sincerity (ikhlas) is that the servant intends by his deed the Face of Allah, glory be to Him. "Religion" (din) means worship and obedience, and its foundation is the oneness of Allah and that He has no partner.

The majority read "ad-din" in the accusative as the object of "mukhlisan." Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the nominative, treating "mukhlisan" as predicated of "ad-din" in a metaphorical manner.

It was said: He should have read "mukhlisa" with a fatha on the lam (i.e., the accusative form of the participle agreeing with the pronoun).

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of intention and for purifying it from impurities, because sincerity is among the matters of the heart, which can only be achieved through the actions of the heart. The authentic Sunnah has also established that the basis of matters in statements and actions is intention, as in the hadith "Actions are only by intentions," and the hadith "There is no statement and no action except with intention."

The sentence ﴿Certainly, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾ is a resumptive clause affirming what precedes of the command to sincerity: that the pure religion, free from the taints of polytheism and other things, belongs to Allah, and that whatever else of religions is not the pure religion of Allah which He commanded.

Qatadah said: "The pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. When He, glory be to Him, commanded worship in the manner of sincerity, and that the pure religion is for Him alone and not for another, He made clear the falsehood of polytheism, which contradicts sincerity.
