The reference in His words ﴿That is Allah﴾ is to Him, glorified is He, in view of His previous acts. The noble name (*Allah*) is the subject of the predicate ﴿your Lord﴾, which is another predicate of it. ﴿To Him belongs true sovereignty in this world and the Hereafter; no partner shares in it﴾ is a third predicate. His words ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ are a fourth predicate. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Him and turn from it to the worship of others?

Hamzah read (إِمَّهَاتِكُمْ, *immahatikum*, "your mothers") with a kasrah on the hamzah and the meem. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem. The rest read with a dammah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking remembrance (*dhikr*); will we have a reward for that?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, we only give seeking reward and remembrance; will we have a reward?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts only what is done sincerely for Him," and then he recited this verse: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs sincere devotion (*al-din al-khalis*)﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿He wraps the night﴾ that he said: "He carries the night."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿creation after creation﴾ that he said: "a clot, then a lump, then bones," ﴿in three darknesses﴾: "the belly, the womb, and the placenta."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat az-Zumar

It is a Meccan surah according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Jabir ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca."

An-Nahhas narrated in his book on abrogation (Nasikh) from him that he said: "Surat az-Zumar was revealed in Mecca, except for three verses which were revealed in Medina concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–55], the three verses."

Others said: "Up to seven verses, from His saying: ﴿Say, O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [az-Zumar: 53–59], to the end of the seven."

An-Nasa'i narrated from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fast until we said he would not break his fast, and he would break it until we said he would not fast. And he used to recite in every night Bani Isra'il and az-Zumar."

At-Tirmidhi narrated it from her with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (p-1274) would not sleep until he had recited az-Zumar and Bani Isra'il."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject which is a demonstrative pronoun, meaning: "This is the revelation."

Abu Hayyan said: the omitted subject is the pronoun "huwa" (it), referring back to His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87], as if it was said: "And what is this reminder?" So it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book." It was also said that it is in the nominative case as a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase following it, meaning: "A revelation from Allah." This is the view of az-Zajjaj and al-Farra'.

Al-Farra' said: It may also be nominative in the sense of "This is a revelation." Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative, as an object of an omitted verb, meaning: "Follow" or "recite the revelation of the Book."

Al-Farra' said: It may be accusative as an incitement (al-igra'), meaning: "Adhere to." "The Book" is the Qur'an. His saying ﴿from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, according to the first reading, is either a complement of "revelation," or a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or related to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) governed by the omitted demonstrative.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The "ba'" (with) is causal (sababiyyah), connected to "sending down," meaning: "We sent it down because of the truth." It may also be connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause of the agent, meaning: "while you are bearing the truth," or of the object, meaning: "while it bears the truth." The intended meaning is everything in it of affirming monotheism, prophethood, the Return, and the various kinds of obligations.

Muqatil said: It means: "We did not send it down in vain, for no purpose."

﴿So worship Allah, making your religion sincerely His﴾. The "fa'" indicates the consequence of what follows from what precedes. "Sincerely" (mukhlisan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject of "worship." Sincerity (ikhlas) is that the servant intends by his deed the Face of Allah, glory be to Him. "Religion" (din) means worship and obedience, and its foundation is the oneness of Allah and that He has no partner.

The majority read "ad-din" in the accusative as the object of "mukhlisan." Ibn Abi Ablah read it in the nominative, treating "mukhlisan" as predicated of "ad-din" in a metaphorical manner.

It was said: He should have read "mukhlisa" with a fatha on the lam (i.e., the accusative form of the participle agreeing with the pronoun).

In the verse there is evidence for the obligation of intention and for purifying it from impurities, because sincerity is among the matters of the heart, which can only be achieved through the actions of the heart. The authentic Sunnah has also established that the basis of matters in statements and actions is intention, as in the hadith "Actions are only by intentions," and the hadith "There is no statement and no action except with intention."

The sentence ﴿Certainly, to Allah belongs the pure religion﴾ is a resumptive clause affirming what precedes of the command to sincerity: that the pure religion, free from the taints of polytheism and other things, belongs to Allah, and that whatever else of religions is not the pure religion of Allah which He commanded.

Qatadah said: "The pure religion is the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. When He, glory be to Him, commanded worship in the manner of sincerity, and that the pure religion is for Him alone and not for another, He made clear the falsehood of polytheism, which contradicts sincerity. The relative pronoun refers to the polytheists, and its position is nominative as the subject; its predicate is His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾. The clause ﴿We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause with an implied "saying," and the exception is a restricted exception from the most general of causes. The meaning: "And those who did not make worship sincerely for Allah, but mixed it with the worship of others, saying: 'We do not worship them for anything of things except that they bring us near to Allah in nearness.'" The pronoun in "worship them" refers to the things they worshipped, namely the angels, Jesus and the idols, and these are the ones meant by "protectors." What is meant by their saying ﴿only that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ is intercession, as al-Wahidi related from the exegetes.

Qatadah said: When it was said to them, "Who is your Lord and your Creator? Who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water from the sky?" they said, "Allah." Then it was said to them, "What is the meaning of your worship of idols?" They said, "That they may bring us near to Allah in position and intercede for us with Him."

Al-Kalbi said: The answer to this statement is His saying in Surat al-Ahqaf: ﴿Why then did those they had taken as gods besides Allah for [perceived] nearness [to Him] not help them?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28]. "Zulfa" is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, as if He had said: "only that they bring us near to Allah in nearness."

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid: "They said, 'We do not worship them.'" The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾ is: between the people of the religions on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense each according to what it deserves. It was also said: between those who were sincere in religion and those who were not sincere; the first is omitted because the situation indicates it. The meaning of ﴿concerning that over which they differ﴾ is: concerning what they differed about in religion, of monotheism and polytheism, for every group claims that the truth is with it. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a liar and ungrateful﴾: that is, He does not guide to His religion, nor grants success in being guided to the truth, one who is a liar in his claim that the idols bring him near to Allah, and who disbelieves by taking them as gods and making them partners with Allah. "Kuffar" is an intensive form indicating that the disbelief of these people has reached its extreme.

Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "kadhdhab" (liar) in the intensive form like "kuffar," and this reading is reported from Anas.

﴿Had Allah intended to take a son, He would have chosen [from what He creates] whatever He willed﴾. This establishes what preceded of the refutation of the claim of the polytheists that the angels are daughters of Allah, since it implies the impossibility of a son for Him, glory be to Him, absolutely. So if He had intended to take a son, the taking of a son in reality would have been impossible, and this could only have been achieved by choosing from what He creates whatever He wills, that is, selecting from among His creation whatever He wishes to choose, since there is no existent apart from Him except that it is created by Him. And it is not valid that the created be a son of the Creator, because there is no homogeneity between them. So nothing remains but that He chooses it as a servant, as the expression "chooses" (yasta fi) in place of "takes" (yattakhidh) indicates. (p-1275) The meaning of the verse is: Had He intended to take a son, there would have occurred something which is not the taking of a son, but rather a choosing of some of His creatures. For this reason He, glory be to Him, declared Himself exempt from taking a son absolutely, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾, meaning: exalted above that. The sentence ﴿He is Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ clarifies His transcendence with respect to attributes, after His transcendence with respect to essence; that is, He is the one who possesses all the attributes of perfection, uniquely one in His essence, so there is no like unto Him; the Subduer over all His creatures. Whoever is characterized by these attributes, the existence of a son in relation to Him is impossible, because a son resembles his father, and there is nothing like Him, glory be to Him. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Had We intended to take a diversion, We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 17].

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned His being exempt from having a son by His being the one God, the Subduer, He mentioned what indicates that from His attributes, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He did not create them in vain, for no purpose. Whoever has created this great creation is impossible to have a partner, a consort, or a son.

Then He explained the manner of His disposal over the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾. "Takwir" in the language means throwing one thing upon another; it is said: "kawwara al-mata'" when one places some of the goods upon others, and from it "kawwara al-'imamah" (he wound the turban). So the meaning of the wrapping of the night over the day is its covering it until its light goes away, and the meaning of the wrapping of the day over the night is its covering it until its darkness goes away. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿He covers the night with the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Thus said Qatadah and others.

Al-Dahhak said: That is, He throws this upon this and this upon this, and this is close to the first statement.

It was also said: The meaning of the verse is that what decreases from the night enters into the day, and what decreases from the day enters into the night, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13; al-Hadid: 6]. It was also said: The meaning is that this recurs upon this and this recurs upon this in successive recurrence.

Al-Raghib said: "Takwir" of a thing is its turning around and gathering some of it onto some other, like "kawwara al-'imamah." Ended.

The indication by this "takwir" mentioned in the verse is to the sun's movement through its risings, and to the decrease and increase of night and day.

Al-Razi said: Light and darkness are two great armies; each day one overcomes the other and the other overcomes it. Then he mentioned His subjugation of the authority of the day and the authority of the night, which are the sun and the moon, saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: He made them submissive to His command in rising and setting for the benefits of the servants. Then He explained the manner of this subjugation, saying: ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾, meaning: each runs in its orbit until the world ends, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The discussion of the specified term for their running has already been fully covered in Surat Ya-Sin. ﴿Unquestionably, He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving﴾. "Ala" is a particle of alerting; the meaning: "Take heed, O servants; Allah is the Dominant, the One who covers the sins of His creatures by forgiveness."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His power and marvelous creation, saying: ﴿He created you from one soul﴾, which is the soul of Adam, ﴿then made from it its mate﴾. The "thumma" (then) was used to indicate the sequence of the creation of Eve after the creation of Adam, and its delay from him, because she was created from him. The conjunction is either upon an omitted element that is a qualifier of "soul," as al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said, the meaning being: "He created you from a soul He created as one, then made from it its mate."

It is also possible that the conjunction is upon the meaning of "one" (wahidah), meaning: from a soul that stood alone, then He made from it, etc. The expression "made" (ja'ala) rather than "created" (khalaqa), together with the conjunction by "thumma," indicates that the creation of Eve from Adam's rib was counted among what is a marvelous sign, indicating the perfection of power, because the creation of Adam is by Allah's constant habit in His creation, whereas creating a female in the said manner was not a habitual practice, since He, glory be to Him, did not create any female from a man's rib other than her. The explanation of this verse has already been fully covered in Surat al-A'raf.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of His marvelous power, saying: ﴿And He sent down for you from the livestock eight pairs﴾. This is conjoined to "created you," and He expressed it with "sent down" because it is reported that He created them in Paradise and then sent them down; so the sending down would be literal. It is also possible that it is figurative, because they did not live except by vegetation, and vegetation only lives by water, and water is sent down from the sky; so the livestock were as if they were sent down, since the cause of their cause is sent down, just as the term was applied to the cause in the poet's words:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry."

Al-Shawkani said: It was also said that (أَنْزَلَ, *anzala*, "sent down") here means "created" (أَنْشَأ) and "made" (جَعَلَ), or means "gave" (أَعْطَى). It was also said that the creation was made a "sending down," because creation only occurs by a command that descends from the heavens. The "eight pairs" are those mentioned in His words: ﴿Two pairs of sheep and two of goats﴾ [al-An'am: 143] ﴿and two pairs of camels and two of cattle﴾ [al-An'am: 144]. By "the two" in the four places, He means the male and the female. The tafsir of this verse has already been explained in Surat al-An'am.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear another kind of His wondrous power, saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾. The sentence is a new (*isti'nafiyyah*) clause, explaining what it contains of the different stages of their creation. (خَلْقًا, *khalqan*, "creation") is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing the verb mentioned, and (مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ, "after creation") is a qualifier of it, meaning: a creation occurring after a creation.

Qatadah and al-Suddi said: a drop (*nutfah*), then a clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bone (*'izam*), then flesh (*lahm*).

Ibn Zayd said: He created you a creation in the wombs of your mothers after your creation in the loins of Adam. His words ﴿in three darknesses﴾ are connected to His words "He creates you." These three darknesses are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (*mashimah*), as said by Mujahid, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the darkness of the placenta, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the night. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the darkness of the man's loins, the darkness of the woman's belly, and the darkness of the womb.

The reference in His words ﴿That is Allah﴾ is to Him, glorified is He, in view of His previous acts. The noble name (*Allah*) is the subject of the predicate ﴿your Lord﴾, which is another predicate of it. ﴿To Him belongs true sovereignty in this world and the Hereafter; no partner shares in it﴾ is a third predicate. His words ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ are a fourth predicate. ﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Him and turn from it to the worship of others?

Hamzah read (إِمَّهَاتِكُمْ, *immahatikum*, "your mothers") with a kasrah on the hamzah and the meem. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasrah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem. The rest read with a dammah on the hamzah and a fathah on the meem.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking remembrance (*dhikr*); will we have a reward for that?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, we only give seeking reward and remembrance; will we have a reward?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah accepts only what is done sincerely for Him," and then he recited this verse: ﴿Surely, to Allah belongs sincere devotion (*al-din al-khalis*)﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿He wraps the night﴾ that he said: "He carries the night."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿creation after creation﴾ that he said: "a clot, then a lump, then bones," ﴿in three darknesses﴾: "the belly, the womb, and the placenta."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 7–12 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the blessings He had bestowed upon His servants, and clarified for them, from His wondrous creation and marvelous action, what obliges every rational person to believe in Him, He followed it with His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, meaning: He is not in need of you, nor of your faith, nor of your worship of Him, for He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani al-Mutlaq). "And" together with the fact that the disbelief of the disbeliever does not harm Him, just as the faith of the believer does not benefit Him, He also does not approve for His servants disbelief, meaning: He does not approve for any of His servants disbelief, nor does He love it, nor does He command it. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth altogether, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8]. Similar to it also is what is established in Sahih Muslim from His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the heart of the most wicked man among you, that would not decrease My dominion in the least."
The exegetes have differed regarding this verse: is it general, such that disbelief is not pleasing to Allah, glorified be He, in every circumstance, as is the apparent meaning, or is it specific? The meaning would then be: He does not approve for His believing servants disbelief. Ibn Abbas, the scholar of the Ummah, may Allah be pleased with him, held the view of specification, as will be explained at the end of this discussion, and Ikrimah, as-Suddi and others followed him in that. Then they differed over the verse in another respect. Some said: He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever but does not approve of it; others said: He does not will it and does not approve of it. The discussion in verifying such matters is very lengthy.
Those who argued for the specification of this verse, and those who affirm the will without approval, have relied upon what is established in many verses of the Noble Book: that He, glorified be He, leads astray whom He wills [ar-Ra'd: 27] and guides whom He wills [Yunus: 25], and ﴿You do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30; at-Takwir: 29], and similar to this, whose meaning is expressed by many verses in the Noble Book.
Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned that He does not approve for His servants disbelief, He clarified that He approves for them gratitude, so He said: ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾, meaning: He approves for you the gratitude indicated by His saying "if you are grateful," and rewards you for it. He, glorified be He, approved gratitude for them only because it is the cause of their happiness in this world and the Hereafter, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. Abu Ja'far, Abu Amr, Shaybah, and Hubayrah from Asim read "yarduhu" with the ha' sukun; Ibn Dhakwan, Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Muhaysin, and Warsh from Nafi' lengthened the damma on the ha'; and the rest read it with the vowel shortened (ikhtilas). ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: no soul carrying a burden will carry the burden of another soul. The explanation of this verse has already been given in full. ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, "so He will inform you of what you used to do" of good and evil, and in this is a severe warning. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: what hearts conceal and hide, so how much more so what they show and display.
﴿And when harm touches man﴾, meaning: harm whether from illness, poverty, or fear, ﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾, meaning: returning to Him, seeking His aid to remove what has befallen him, abandoning what he used to call upon and seek help from, whether a dead person, a living one, an idol, or other than that. ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Him﴾, meaning: He gives him and makes him possess it. It is said: "khawwalahu" means "he made him possess it," and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala used to recite:
"There, if they are asked for wealth they become miserly; if they are asked, they give; if they are in ease, they exceed."
And from it is the saying of Abu an-Najm:
"He gave and did not withhold, and did not hold back ... the chief of the summit, the lord of the possessed"
﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾, meaning: he forgets the harm for which he used to call upon Allah to remove it from him, before He bestowed upon him what He bestowed. It was also said: he forgets the supplication with which he used to humble himself, and abandons it; or he forgets his Lord whom he used to call upon and humble himself to. Then he went beyond that to association with Allah, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾, meaning: partners from idols or other things, seeking help from them and worshipping them, ﴿to mislead from His way﴾, meaning: to mislead people from the path of Allah, which is Islam and monotheism.
As-Suddi said: it means rivals from among men upon whom he relies in all his affairs.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to threaten whoever was characterized by that attribute, so He said: ﴿Say: enjoy your disbelief a little﴾, meaning: a little enjoyment or a short time, for the enjoyment of this world is little. Then He gave the reason for that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning: your destination is toward it soon, and in this is a great threat.
Az-Zajjaj said: its wording is the wording of a command, but its meaning is threat and warning. The majority read "liyudilla" with a damma on the ya'; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha.
Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned the attributes of the polytheists and their clinging to other than Allah at the time of the removal of what is disliked from them, He mentioned the attributes of the believers, so He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night﴾, and this, to its end, is part of the speech commanded to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace.
The meaning: that disbeliever is in a state and outcome that is better. Is one who is steadfast in acts of obedience to Allah in ease and hardship, during the hours of the night, persisting in that, not confining himself to calling upon Allah, glorified be He, only when harm descends upon him—
(p-1277) [Note: page marker retained as in source]
Al-Hasan, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim, and al-Kisa'i read "amman" with shadda; Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read it with takhfif. According to the first reading, "am" enters upon "man" which is relative, and the mim is assimilated into the mim, and "am" is the connecting one, and its counterpart is omitted, its estimate being: "the disbeliever is better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" It was said: it is the disconnecting one, estimated as "bal" and the hamza, meaning: "Rather, is one who is devoutly obedient like the disbeliever?" As for the second reading, it was said: the hamza is interrogative, entering upon "man," and the interrogation is for affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted, meaning: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like one who disbelieved?"
Al-Farra' said: the hamza in this reading is for calling (vocative), and "man" is a vocative, and it refers to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, who was commanded with His saying "Say: enjoy," and the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, say: such-and-such." It was said: the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, indeed you are of the companions of Paradise."
Among those who held that the hamza is vocative is al-Farra'; Abu Hayyan rejected that, and said: it is unrelated to what precedes it and to what follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi had preceded him in this rejection. Abu Hatim and al-Akhfash objected to this reading from its basis, but there is no basis for that, for when the transmission is established, reasoning (dirayah) is set aside.
The meaning of "al-qanit" here has been differed upon: it was said: the obedient; it was said: the humble in his prayer; it was said: the one standing in his prayer; it was said: the one calling upon his Lord.
An-Nahhas said: the origin of qunut is obedience, so whatever is said about it is included within obedience. The intended meaning of "hours of the night" is its periods. It was said: its middle; it was said: what is between Maghrib and Isha. The accusative of "sajidan wa qa'iman" is in the state (hal), meaning: combining prostration and standing. Prostration is placed before standing because it is more inclusive in worship. The position of "yahdharu al-akhirah" is also in the accusative as a state, meaning: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. "And hopes for the mercy of his Lord" — thus he combines hope and fear, and whoever combines them in one heart succeeds.
It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Is one like one who does none of that," as the context indicates.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them another statement by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, so He said: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, meaning: those who know that what Allah promised of resurrection, reward, and punishment is true, and those who do not know that; or those who know what Allah sent down to His messengers and those who do not know that; or the intended meaning is the scholars and the ignorant. And it is known to everyone who has intellect that there is no equality between knowledge and ignorance, nor between the knowing and the ignorant.
Az-Zajjaj said: meaning, just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, likewise the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.
It was said: the intended meaning of "those who know" is those who act upon their knowledge, for they are the ones who benefit from it, since whoever does not act is in the position of one who does not know. ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾, meaning: only those who are admonished, reflect, and think are the people of intellects, and they are the believers, not the disbelievers, for although they claim to have intellects, those are like nonexistence. This sentence is not part of the speech commanded, but is from Allah, glorified be He.
﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾. When He, glorified be He, negated equality between one who knows and one who does not know, and clarified that ﴿only those of understanding are reminded﴾, He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to command the believers among His servants to persist in His piety and faith in Him.

His saying "in this world" is connected to "did good." It was also said: it is connected to "good," as an explanation of its place, so the meaning would be: for those who did good in action, there is good in this world through health, well-being, victory, and spoils. The first is preferable.
Then, since some servants may find it difficult to perform acts of obedience and good in their homeland, Allah, glorified be He, directed whoever is in that situation to emigration, so He said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious﴾, meaning: let him emigrate to wherever he is able to obey Allah, act upon what He commanded, and abandon what He forbade. Similar to this is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [an-Nisa': 97]. The discussion of emigration has already been given in full in Surat an-Nisa'. The first is preferable.

When the intelligent person conceives this as it truly should be conceived, and understands it as it truly should be understood, he knows that the one who is patient with what has befallen him has attained this great reward and gained this weighty recompense, whereas the impatient one, the decree has descended upon him whether he wills or not, and yet he has missed a reward whose measure cannot be estimated and whose extent cannot be reached. So he has added to his calamity another calamity, and gains nothing but impatience. How excellent is the saying of one who said:

I see patience praised, though it has its avenues, * but how (is it) when there is no avenue from it?

There patience is right and patience is obligatory, * and what comes from it out of necessity is more obligatory.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to inform them of what he was commanded of tawhid (Divine unity) and sincerity, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾. Abu Ja'far, Abu Amr, Shaybah, and Hubayrah from Asim read "yarduhu" with the ha' sukun; Ibn Dhakwan, Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Muhaysin, and Warsh from Nafi' lengthened the damma on the ha'; and the rest read it with the vowel shortened (ikhtilas). ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: no soul carrying a burden will carry the burden of another soul. The explanation of this verse has already been given in full. ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, "so He will inform you of what you used to do" of good and evil, and in this is a severe warning. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: what hearts conceal and hide, so how much more so what they show and display.
﴿And when harm touches man﴾, meaning: harm whether from illness, poverty, or fear, ﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾, meaning: returning to Him, seeking His aid to remove what has befallen him, abandoning what he used to call upon and seek help from, whether a dead person, a living one, an idol, or other than that. ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Him﴾, meaning: He gives him and makes him possess it. It is said: "khawwalahu" means "he made him possess it," and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala used to recite:
"There, if they are asked for wealth they become miserly; if they are asked, they give; if they are in ease, they exceed."
And from it is the saying of Abu an-Najm:
"He gave and did not withhold, and did not hold back ... the chief of the summit, the lord of the possessed"
﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾, meaning: he forgets the harm for which he used to call upon Allah to remove it from him, before He bestowed upon him what He bestowed. It was also said: he forgets the supplication with which he used to humble himself, and abandons it; or he forgets his Lord whom he used to call upon and humble himself to. Then he went beyond that to association with Allah, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾, meaning: partners from idols or other things, seeking help from them and worshipping them, ﴿to mislead from His way﴾, meaning: to mislead people from the path of Allah, which is Islam and monotheism.
As-Suddi said: it means rivals from among men upon whom he relies in all his affairs.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to threaten whoever was characterized by that attribute, so He said: ﴿Say: enjoy your disbelief a little﴾, meaning: a little enjoyment or a short time, for the enjoyment of this world is little. Then He gave the reason for that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning: your destination is toward it soon, and in this is a great threat.
Az-Zajjaj said: its wording is the wording of a command, but its meaning is threat and warning. The majority read "liyudilla" with a damma on the ya'; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha.
Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned the attributes of the polytheists and their clinging to other than Allah at the time of the removal of what is disliked from them, He mentioned the attributes of the believers, so He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night﴾, and this, to its end, is part of the speech commanded to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace.
The meaning: that disbeliever is in a state and outcome that is better. Is one who is steadfast in acts of obedience to Allah in ease and hardship, during the hours of the night, persisting in that, not confining himself to calling upon Allah, glorified be He, only when harm descends upon him—
(p-1277) [Note: page marker retained as in source]
Al-Hasan, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim, and al-Kisa'i read "amman" with shadda; Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read it with takhfif. According to the first reading, "am" enters upon "man" which is relative, and the mim is assimilated into the mim, and "am" is the connecting one, and its counterpart is omitted, its estimate being: "the disbeliever is better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" It was said: it is the disconnecting one, estimated as "bal" and the hamza, meaning: "Rather, is one who is devoutly obedient like the disbeliever?" As for the second reading, it was said: the hamza is interrogative, entering upon "man," and the interrogation is for affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted, meaning: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like one who disbelieved?"
Al-Farra' said: the hamza in this reading is for calling (vocative), and "man" is a vocative, and it refers to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, who was commanded with His saying "Say: enjoy," and the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, say: such-and-such." It was said: the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, indeed you are of the companions of Paradise."
Among those who held that the hamza is vocative is al-Farra'; Abu Hayyan rejected that, and said: it is unrelated to what precedes it and to what follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi had preceded him in this rejection. Abu Hatim and al-Akhfash objected to this reading from its basis, but there is no basis for that, for when the transmission is established, reasoning (dirayah) is set aside.
The meaning of "al-qanit" here has been differed upon: it was said: the obedient; it was said: the humble in his prayer; it was said: the one standing in his prayer; it was said: the one calling upon his Lord.
An-Nahhas said: the origin of qunut is obedience, so whatever is said about it is included within obedience. The intended meaning of "hours of the night" is its periods. It was said: its middle; it was said: what is between Maghrib and Isha. The accusative of "sajidan wa qa'iman" is in the state (hal), meaning: combining prostration and standing. Prostration is placed before standing because it is more inclusive in worship. The position of "yahdharu al-akhirah" is also in the accusative as a state, meaning: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. "And hopes for the mercy of his Lord" — thus he combines hope and fear, and whoever combines them in one heart succeeds.
It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Is one like one who does none of that," as the context indicates.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them another statement by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, so He said: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, meaning: those who know that what Allah promised of resurrection, reward, and punishment is true, and those who do not know that; or those who know what Allah sent down to His messengers and those who do not know that; or the intended meaning is the scholars and the ignorant. And it is known to everyone who has intellect that there is no equality between knowledge and ignorance, nor between the knowing and the ignorant.
Az-Zajjaj said: meaning, just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, likewise the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.
It was said: the intended meaning of "those who know" is those who act upon their knowledge, for they are the ones who benefit from it, since whoever does not act is in the position of one who does not know. ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾, meaning: only those who are admonished, reflect, and think are the people of intellects, and they are the believers, not the disbelievers, for although they claim to have intellects, those are like nonexistence. This sentence is not part of the speech commanded, but is from Allah, glorified be He.
﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾. When He, glorified be He, negated equality between one who knows and one who does not know, and clarified that ﴿only those of understanding are reminded﴾, He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to command the believers among His servants to persist in His piety and faith in Him.
The meaning: O you who affirmed the oneness of Allah, fear your Lord by obeying Him, avoiding His disobedience, sincerely believing in Him, and negating partners from Him. And the intended meaning is: say to them this statement of mine exactly.
Then, when Allah, glorified be He, commanded the believers to piety, He clarified for them the benefits in this piety, so He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world is good﴾, meaning: for those who did good deeds in this world, sincerely, is a great good, which is Paradise. His saying "in this world" is connected to "did good." It was also said: it is connected to "good," as an explanation of its place, so the meaning would be: for those who did good in action, there is good in this world through health, well-being, victory, and spoils. The first is preferable.
Then, since some servants may find it difficult to perform acts of obedience and good in their homeland, Allah, glorified be He, directed whoever is in that situation to emigration, so He said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious﴾, meaning: let him emigrate to wherever he is able to obey Allah, act upon what He commanded, and abandon what He forbade. Similar to this is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [an-Nisa': 97]. The discussion of emigration has already been given in full in Surat an-Nisa'. It was also said: the intended meaning of "earth" here is the earth of Paradise, encouraging them toward its vastness and the vastness of its bounty, as in His saying: ﴿and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 133]. The first is preferable.
Then, when He, glorified be He, clarified what is for the good-doers when they do good, and there must be patience in performing obedience and restraining the self from desires, He pointed to the virtue of patience and its great value, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾, meaning: Allah will give them their reward in return for their patience without account, that is, in an amount that no counter can count, and no calculator can compute.
ʿAṭāʾ said: in an amount that no mind or description can grasp. Muqatil said: their reward is Paradise, and their provisions therein are without account.

The summary of the matter is that the verse indicates that the reward of those who are patient, and their recompense, has no end, because everything that falls under reckoning is finite, while whatever does not fall under reckoning is infinite. This is a great virtue and a noble reward, which requires that everyone who desires the reward of Allah and aspires to the good that is with Him should devote himself to patience, bridle his soul with its bridle, and restrain it with its restraint. For impatience does not turn back a decree that has already descended, nor bring back good that has been taken away, nor repel a harm that has already befallen. When the intelligent person conceives this as it truly should be conceived, and understands it as it truly should be understood, he knows that the one who is patient with what has befallen him has attained this great reward and gained this weighty recompense, whereas the impatient one, the decree has descended upon him whether he wills or not, and yet he has missed a reward whose measure cannot be estimated and whose extent cannot be reached. So he has added to his calamity another calamity, and gains nothing but impatience. How excellent is the saying of one who said:

I see patience praised, though it has its avenues, * but how (is it) when there is no avenue from it?

There patience is right and patience is obligatory, * and what comes from it out of necessity is more obligatory.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to inform them of what he was commanded of tawhid (Divine unity) and sincerity, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾. That is: I worship Him with worship purified from shirk (associating partners), showing-off (riya') and other than that.

Muqatil said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What drives you to what you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and your grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza, so that you would adhere to them?" So Allah revealed the verse. The explanation of the meaning of the verse has already preceded at the beginning of this surah.

﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾. That is: of this community. And thus he (ﷺ) was, for he was the first to oppose the religion of his fathers and to call to tawhid. The lam here is for causation (ta'lil), meaning: I have been commanded with what I was commanded for the sake of my being (the first). It has been said that it is extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, but the first (view) is preferable.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, that it means: the disbelievers whom Allah did not intend to purify their hearts, who say "There is no god but Allah," then He said: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, and they are His sincere servants about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], so He bound them to the testimony that there is no god but Allah and made it beloved to them.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ikrimah concerning ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ that he said: He does not approve for His Muslim servants disbelief.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that he said: By Allah, Allah has not approved for a servant misguidance, nor commanded him with it, nor called to it; rather He approved for you His obedience, commanded you with it, and forbade you from His disobedience.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Umar that he recited this verse: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter﴾, and he said: That is 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. In another wording: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan.

Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾, that he said: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon a man who was in his death throes, and he said: 'How do you find yourself?' He said: 'I hope in Allah and I fear my sins.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'These two do not gather in the heart of a servant in such a situation except that Allah gives him what he hopes for and grants him security from what he fears.'"

They related it through the route of Sayyar ibn Hatim from Ja'far ibn Sulayman from Thabit from Anas.

al-Tirmidhi said: It is gharib (strange), and some of them related it from Thabit from the Prophet (ﷺ) as mursal.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 7–12 (part 1 of 2):

"And" together with the fact that the disbelief of the disbeliever does not harm Him, just as the faith of the believer does not benefit Him, He also does not approve for His servants disbelief, meaning: He does not approve for any of His servants disbelief, nor does He love it, nor does He command it. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth altogether, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8]. Similar to it also is what is established in Sahih Muslim from His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the heart of the most wicked man among you, that would not decrease My dominion in the least."

The meaning would then be: He does not approve for His believing servants disbelief. Then they differed over the verse in another respect. Some said: He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever but does not approve of it; others said: He does not will it and does not approve of it. The discussion in verifying such matters is very lengthy.
Those who argued for the specification of this verse, and those who affirm the will without approval, have relied upon what is established in many verses of the Noble Book: that He, glorified be He, leads astray whom He wills [ar-Ra'd: 27] and guides whom He wills [Yunus: 25], and ﴿You do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30; at-Takwir: 29], and similar to this, whose meaning is expressed by many verses in the Noble Book.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 7–12 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the blessings He had bestowed upon His servants, and clarified for them, from His wondrous creation and marvelous action, what obliges every rational person to believe in Him, He followed it with His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, meaning: He is not in need of you, nor of your faith, nor of your worship of Him, for He is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani al-Mutlaq). "And" together with the fact that the disbelief of the disbeliever does not harm Him, just as the faith of the believer does not benefit Him, He also does not approve for His servants disbelief, meaning: He does not approve for any of His servants disbelief, nor does He love it, nor does He command it. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, you and everyone on earth altogether, then indeed Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾ [Ibrahim: 8]. Similar to it also is what is established in Sahih Muslim from His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humans and your jinn, were upon the heart of the most wicked man among you, that would not decrease My dominion in the least."
The exegetes have differed regarding this verse: is it general, such that disbelief is not pleasing to Allah, glorified be He, in every circumstance, as is the apparent meaning, or is it specific? The meaning would then be: He does not approve for His believing servants disbelief. Ibn Abbas, the scholar of the Ummah, may Allah be pleased with him, held the view of specification, as will be explained at the end of this discussion, and Ikrimah, as-Suddi and others followed him in that. Then they differed over the verse in another respect. Some said: He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever but does not approve of it; others said: He does not will it and does not approve of it. The discussion in verifying such matters is very lengthy.
Those who argued for the specification of this verse, and those who affirm the will without approval, have relied upon what is established in many verses of the Noble Book: that He, glorified be He, leads astray whom He wills [ar-Ra'd: 27] and guides whom He wills [Yunus: 25], and ﴿You do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30; at-Takwir: 29], and similar to this, whose meaning is expressed by many verses in the Noble Book.
Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned that He does not approve for His servants disbelief, He clarified that He approves for them gratitude, so He said: ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾, meaning: He approves for you the gratitude indicated by His saying "if you are grateful," and rewards you for it. He, glorified be He, approved gratitude for them only because it is the cause of their happiness in this world and the Hereafter, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. Abu Ja'far, Abu Amr, Shaybah, and Hubayrah from Asim read "yarduhu" with the ha' sukun; Ibn Dhakwan, Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Muhaysin, and Warsh from Nafi' lengthened the damma on the ha'; and the rest read it with the vowel shortened (ikhtilas). ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: no soul carrying a burden will carry the burden of another soul. The explanation of this verse has already been given in full. ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, "so He will inform you of what you used to do" of good and evil, and in this is a severe warning. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, meaning: what hearts conceal and hide, so how much more so what they show and display.
﴿And when harm touches man﴾, meaning: harm whether from illness, poverty, or fear, ﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning back to Him in repentance﴾, meaning: returning to Him, seeking His aid to remove what has befallen him, abandoning what he used to call upon and seek help from, whether a dead person, a living one, an idol, or other than that. ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Him﴾, meaning: He gives him and makes him possess it. It is said: "khawwalahu" means "he made him possess it," and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala used to recite:
"There, if they are asked for wealth they become miserly; if they are asked, they give; if they are in ease, they exceed."
And from it is the saying of Abu an-Najm:
"He gave and did not withhold, and did not hold back ... the chief of the summit, the lord of the possessed"
﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾, meaning: he forgets the harm for which he used to call upon Allah to remove it from him, before He bestowed upon him what He bestowed. It was also said: he forgets the supplication with which he used to humble himself, and abandons it; or he forgets his Lord whom he used to call upon and humble himself to. Then he went beyond that to association with Allah, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and sets up rivals to Allah﴾, meaning: partners from idols or other things, seeking help from them and worshipping them, ﴿to mislead from His way﴾, meaning: to mislead people from the path of Allah, which is Islam and monotheism.
As-Suddi said: it means rivals from among men upon whom he relies in all his affairs.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to threaten whoever was characterized by that attribute, so He said: ﴿Say: enjoy your disbelief a little﴾, meaning: a little enjoyment or a short time, for the enjoyment of this world is little. Then He gave the reason for that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are of the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning: your destination is toward it soon, and in this is a great threat.
Az-Zajjaj said: its wording is the wording of a command, but its meaning is threat and warning. The majority read "liyudilla" with a damma on the ya'; Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha.
Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned the attributes of the polytheists and their clinging to other than Allah at the time of the removal of what is disliked from them, He mentioned the attributes of the believers, so He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night﴾, and this, to its end, is part of the speech commanded to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace.
The meaning: that disbeliever is in a state and outcome that is better. Is one who is steadfast in acts of obedience to Allah in ease and hardship, during the hours of the night, persisting in that, not confining himself to calling upon Allah, glorified be He, only when harm descends upon him—

Al-Hasan, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim, and al-Kisa'i read "amman" with shadda; Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read it with takhfif. According to the first reading, "am" enters upon "man" which is relative, and the mim is assimilated into the mim, and "am" is the connecting one, and its counterpart is omitted, its estimate being: "the disbeliever is better, or the one who is devoutly obedient?" It was said: it is the disconnecting one, estimated as "bal" and the hamza, meaning: "Rather, is one who is devoutly obedient like the disbeliever?" As for the second reading, it was said: the hamza is interrogative, entering upon "man," and the interrogation is for affirmation, and its counterpart is omitted, meaning: "Is one who is devoutly obedient like one who disbelieved?"
Al-Farra' said: the hamza in this reading is for calling (vocative), and "man" is a vocative, and it refers to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, who was commanded with His saying "Say: enjoy," and the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, say: such-and-such." It was said: the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, indeed you are of the companions of Paradise."
Among those who held that the hamza is vocative is al-Farra'; Abu Hayyan rejected that, and said: it is unrelated to what precedes it and to what follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi had preceded him in this rejection. Abu Hatim and al-Akhfash objected to this reading from its basis, but there is no basis for that, for when the transmission is established, reasoning (dirayah) is set aside.
The meaning of "al-qanit" here has been differed upon: it was said: the obedient; it was said: the humble in his prayer; it was said: the one standing in his prayer; it was said: the one calling upon his Lord.
An-Nahhas said: the origin of qunut is obedience, so whatever is said about it is included within obedience. The intended meaning of "hours of the night" is its periods. It was said: its middle; it was said: what is between Maghrib and Isha. The accusative of "sajidan wa qa'iman" is in the state (hal), meaning: combining prostration and standing. Prostration is placed before standing because it is more inclusive in worship. The position of "yahdharu al-akhirah" is also in the accusative as a state, meaning: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. "And hopes for the mercy of his Lord" — thus he combines hope and fear, and whoever combines them in one heart succeeds.
It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Is one like one who does none of that," as the context indicates.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them another statement by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, so He said: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, meaning: those who know that what Allah promised of resurrection, reward, and punishment is true, and those who do not know that; or those who know what Allah sent down to His messengers and those who do not know that; or the intended meaning is the scholars and the ignorant. And it is known to everyone who has intellect that there is no equality between knowledge and ignorance, nor between the knowing and the ignorant.
Az-Zajjaj said: meaning, just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, likewise the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.
It was said: the intended meaning of "those who know" is those who act upon their knowledge, for they are the ones who benefit from it, since whoever does not act is in the position of one who does not know. ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾, meaning: only those who are admonished, reflect, and think are the people of intellects, and they are the believers, not the disbelievers, for although they claim to have intellects, those are like nonexistence. This sentence is not part of the speech commanded, but is from Allah, glorified be He.
﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾. When He, glorified be He, negated equality between one who knows and one who does not know, and clarified that ﴿only those of understanding are reminded﴾, He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to command the believers among His servants to persist in His piety and faith in Him.
The meaning: O you who affirmed the oneness of Allah, fear your Lord by obeying Him, avoiding His disobedience, sincerely believing in Him, and negating partners from Him. And the intended meaning is: say to them this statement of mine exactly.
Then, when Allah, glorified be He, commanded the believers to piety, He clarified for them the benefits in this piety, so He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world is good﴾, meaning: for those who did good deeds in this world, sincerely, is a great good, which is Paradise. His saying "in this world" is connected to "did good." It was also said: it is connected to "good," as an explanation of its place, so the meaning would be: for those who did good in action, there is good in this world through health, well-being, victory, and spoils. The first is preferable.
Then, since some servants may find it difficult to perform acts of obedience and good in their homeland, Allah, glorified be He, directed whoever is in that situation to emigration, so He said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious﴾, meaning: let him emigrate to wherever he is able to obey Allah, act upon what He commanded, and abandon what He forbade. Similar to this is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [an-Nisa': 97]. The discussion of emigration has already been given in full in Surat an-Nisa'. It was also said: the intended meaning of "earth" here is the earth of Paradise, encouraging them toward its vastness and the vastness of its bounty, as in His saying: ﴿and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 133]. The first is preferable.
Then, when He, glorified be He, clarified what is for the good-doers when they do good, and there must be patience in performing obedience and restraining the self from desires, He pointed to the virtue of patience and its great value, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾, meaning: Allah will give them their reward in return for their patience without account, that is, in an amount that no counter can count, and no calculator can compute.
ʿAṭāʾ said: in an amount that no mind or description can grasp. Muqatil said: their reward is Paradise, and their provisions therein are without account.

The summary of the matter is that the verse indicates that the reward of those who are patient, and their recompense, has no end, because everything that falls under reckoning is finite, while whatever does not fall under reckoning is infinite. This is a great virtue and a noble reward, which requires that everyone who desires the reward of Allah and aspires to the good that is with Him should devote himself to patience, bridle his soul with its bridle, and restrain it with its restraint. For impatience does not turn back a decree that has already descended, nor bring back good that has been taken away, nor repel a harm that has already befallen. When the intelligent person conceives this as it truly should be conceived, and understands it as it truly should be understood, he knows that the one who is patient with what has befallen him has attained this great reward and gained this weighty recompense, whereas the impatient one, the decree has descended upon him whether he wills or not, and yet he has missed a reward whose measure cannot be estimated and whose extent cannot be reached. So he has added to his calamity another calamity, and gains nothing but impatience. How excellent is the saying of one who said:

I see patience praised, though it has its avenues, * but how (is it) when there is no avenue from it?

There patience is right and patience is obligatory, * and what comes from it out of necessity is more obligatory.
