Al-Farra' said: the hamza in this reading is for calling (vocative), and "man" is a vocative, and it refers to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, who was commanded with His saying "Say: enjoy," and the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, say: such-and-such." It was said: the estimate is: "O you who are devoutly obedient, indeed you are of the companions of Paradise."
Among those who held that the hamza is vocative is al-Farra'; Abu Hayyan rejected that, and said: it is unrelated to what precedes it and to what follows it. Abu Ali al-Farisi had preceded him in this rejection. Abu Hatim and al-Akhfash objected to this reading from its basis, but there is no basis for that, for when the transmission is established, reasoning (dirayah) is set aside.
The meaning of "al-qanit" here has been differed upon: it was said: the obedient; it was said: the humble in his prayer; it was said: the one standing in his prayer; it was said: the one calling upon his Lord.
An-Nahhas said: the origin of qunut is obedience, so whatever is said about it is included within obedience. The intended meaning of "hours of the night" is its periods. It was said: its middle; it was said: what is between Maghrib and Isha. The accusative of "sajidan wa qa'iman" is in the state (hal), meaning: combining prostration and standing. Prostration is placed before standing because it is more inclusive in worship. The position of "yahdharu al-akhirah" is also in the accusative as a state, meaning: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. "And hopes for the mercy of his Lord" — thus he combines hope and fear, and whoever combines them in one heart succeeds.
It was said: in the speech there is an omission, and the estimate is: "Is one like one who does none of that," as the context indicates.
Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to say to them another statement by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, so He said: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾, meaning: those who know that what Allah promised of resurrection, reward, and punishment is true, and those who do not know that; or those who know what Allah sent down to His messengers and those who do not know that; or the intended meaning is the scholars and the ignorant. And it is known to everyone who has intellect that there is no equality between knowledge and ignorance, nor between the knowing and the ignorant.
Az-Zajjaj said: meaning, just as those who know and those who do not know are not equal, likewise the obedient and the disobedient are not equal.
It was said: the intended meaning of "those who know" is those who act upon their knowledge, for they are the ones who benefit from it, since whoever does not act is in the position of one who does not know. ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾, meaning: only those who are admonished, reflect, and think are the people of intellects, and they are the believers, not the disbelievers, for although they claim to have intellects, those are like nonexistence. This sentence is not part of the speech commanded, but is from Allah, glorified be He.
﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord﴾. When He, glorified be He, negated equality between one who knows and one who does not know, and clarified that ﴿only those of understanding are reminded﴾, He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to command the believers among His servants to persist in His piety and faith in Him.
The meaning: O you who affirmed the oneness of Allah, fear your Lord by obeying Him, avoiding His disobedience, sincerely believing in Him, and negating partners from Him. And the intended meaning is: say to them this statement of mine exactly.
Then, when Allah, glorified be He, commanded the believers to piety, He clarified for them the benefits in this piety, so He said: ﴿For those who do good in this world is good﴾, meaning: for those who did good deeds in this world, sincerely, is a great good, which is Paradise. His saying "in this world" is connected to "did good." It was also said: it is connected to "good," as an explanation of its place, so the meaning would be: for those who did good in action, there is good in this world through health, well-being, victory, and spoils. The first is preferable.
Then, since some servants may find it difficult to perform acts of obedience and good in their homeland, Allah, glorified be He, directed whoever is in that situation to emigration, so He said: ﴿And the earth of Allah is spacious﴾, meaning: let him emigrate to wherever he is able to obey Allah, act upon what He commanded, and abandon what He forbade. Similar to this is His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Was not the earth of Allah spacious so that you could emigrate therein?﴾ [an-Nisa': 97]. The discussion of emigration has already been given in full in Surat an-Nisa'. It was also said: the intended meaning of "earth" here is the earth of Paradise, encouraging them toward its vastness and the vastness of its bounty, as in His saying: ﴿and a Paradise whose width is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 133]. The first is preferable.
Then, when He, glorified be He, clarified what is for the good-doers when they do good, and there must be patience in performing obedience and restraining the self from desires, He pointed to the virtue of patience and its great value, so He said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾, meaning: Allah will give them their reward in return for their patience without account, that is, in an amount that no counter can count, and no calculator can compute.
ʿAṭāʾ said: in an amount that no mind or description can grasp. Muqatil said: their reward is Paradise, and their provisions therein are without account.

The summary of the matter is that the verse indicates that the reward of those who are patient, and their recompense, has no end, because everything that falls under reckoning is finite, while whatever does not fall under reckoning is infinite. This is a great virtue and a noble reward, which requires that everyone who desires the reward of Allah and aspires to the good that is with Him should devote himself to patience, bridle his soul with its bridle, and restrain it with its restraint. For impatience does not turn back a decree that has already descended, nor bring back good that has been taken away, nor repel a harm that has already befallen. When the intelligent person conceives this as it truly should be conceived, and understands it as it truly should be understood, he knows that the one who is patient with what has befallen him has attained this great reward and gained this weighty recompense, whereas the impatient one, the decree has descended upon him whether he wills or not, and yet he has missed a reward whose measure cannot be estimated and whose extent cannot be reached. So he has added to his calamity another calamity, and gains nothing but impatience. How excellent is the saying of one who said:

I see patience praised, though it has its avenues, * but how (is it) when there is no avenue from it?

There patience is right and patience is obligatory, * and what comes from it out of necessity is more obligatory.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to inform them of what he was commanded of tawhid (Divine unity) and sincerity, so He said: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾. That is: I worship Him with worship purified from shirk (associating partners), showing-off (riya') and other than that.

Muqatil said: The disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What drives you to what you have brought us? Do you not look at the religion of your father and your grandfather and the leaders of your people, who worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza, so that you would adhere to them?" So Allah revealed the verse. The explanation of the meaning of the verse has already preceded at the beginning of this surah.

﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims﴾. That is: of this community. And thus he (ﷺ) was, for he was the first to oppose the religion of his fathers and to call to tawhid. The lam here is for causation (ta'lil), meaning: I have been commanded with what I was commanded for the sake of my being (the first). It has been said that it is extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, but the first (view) is preferable.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾, that it means: the disbelievers whom Allah did not intend to purify their hearts, who say "There is no god but Allah," then He said: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, and they are His sincere servants about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], so He bound them to the testimony that there is no god but Allah and made it beloved to them.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ikrimah concerning ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ that he said: He does not approve for His Muslim servants disbelief.

'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah that he said: By Allah, Allah has not approved for a servant misguidance, nor commanded him with it, nor called to it; rather He approved for you His obedience, commanded you with it, and forbade you from His disobedience.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Umar that he recited this verse: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter﴾, and he said: That is 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. In another wording: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan.

Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying: ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾, that he said: he fears the punishment of the Hereafter.

al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon a man who was in his death throes, and he said: 'How do you find yourself?' He said: 'I hope in Allah and I fear my sins.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'These two do not gather in the heart of a servant in such a situation except that Allah gives him what he hopes for and grants him security from what he fears.'"

They related it through the route of Sayyar ibn Hatim from Ja'far ibn Sulayman from Thabit from Anas.

al-Tirmidhi said: It is gharib (strange), and some of them related it from Thabit from the Prophet (ﷺ) as mursal.

**Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 39 (al-Zumar), verses 13–20**

His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day﴾. That is: by abandoning sincere worship of Him and His oneness, and by calling people away from polytheism (shirk) and [exposing] the misguidance of its people. ﴿The punishment of a tremendous day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Indeed, I fear that if I disobey my Lord by responding to the polytheists in what they call me to, namely the worship of other than Allah."

Abu Hamza al-Yamani and Ibn al-Musayyib said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your previous and subsequent sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. In this verse there is evidence that the command is obligatory, because before it is ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 11], so what is meant is disobedience to this command.

﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾. The placing of "Allah" first indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas), that is: I do not worship other than Him, neither independently nor as a partner. The meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in my religion﴾ is that it is purely for Allah, unmixed with shirk, showing-off (riya') or anything else of that kind. Its verification has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah.

Al-Razi said: If it is asked, what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 11] and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an announcement that he is commanded by Allah to have faith and to worship, and the second is an announcement that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Allah.

﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾: this command is for threat, rebuke and reproach, like His saying ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. It was also said that the command is on its literal level, and that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword; but the first view is more preferable.

﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾. That is: the complete losers are these people, because whoever enters the Fire has lost himself and his family.

Al-Zajjaj said: By this he means the disbelievers, for they have lost themselves through eternal abiding in the Fire, and they have lost their families, because they did not enter the abode of the believers, who have families in Paradise. The sentence ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ is a separate statement to emphasize what precedes it. Introducing it with the particle of alertness indicates that this loss, and describing it as "manifest," shows that it is the complete instance of loss, that no loss equals it, and no punishment approaches it.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained this loss that had befallen them and the affliction descending upon them, by His saying: ﴿For them there will be canopies of Fire above them﴾. The "canopies" (zulal) refers to layers of Fire: that is, above them are layers of Fire blazing over them. ﴿And beneath them canopies﴾: that is, layers of Fire. What is beneath them is called "canopies" because it shades those beneath it of the people of the Fire, since in each layer of the Fire there is a group of the disbelievers. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and over them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41], and His saying: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. (p-1279)

The reference in His saying "That" is to what was mentioned earlier of the description of their punishment in the Fire. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying ﴿with which Allah frightens His servants﴾, that is: He warns them with what He has threatened the disbelievers with of punishment, so that they fear it and guard against it. This is the meaning of ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, that is: guard against these sins which bring about such punishment upon the disbelievers. The reason for specifying "servants" as the believers is that the usual usage in the Qur'an is applying the word "servants" to them. It was also said that it is for the disbelievers and the people of sins, and it was said that it is general to both believers and disbelievers.

﴿And those who avoid the taghut, not worshipping it, and turn back to Allah﴾: the relative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is His saying "for them is good tidings". Taghut (the rebellious idol or false object of worship) is an intensive form of the noun, like "rahamut" and "'azamut". It refers to idols and to Satan. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said it is Satan. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said it is the idols. It was said that it is the soothsayer; it was said that it is a non-Arabic name like "Talut" and "Jalut"; and it was said that it is an Arabic name derived from "tughyan" (transgression).

Al-Akhfash said: "Taghut" is a collective noun, and its singular may be feminine. The meaning of "avoid the taghut" is: they turn away from worshipping it and devote their worship to Allah, mighty and majestic. His saying "that they worship it" is in the position of an accusative, as an apposition (badal) of the taghut, a "badal al-ishtimal" (inclusive apposition), as if He said: "Avoid the worship of the taghut." The discussion of the explanation of taghut has already been treated in full in Surat al-Baqara. His saying ﴿and turn back to Allah﴾ is coordinated with "avoid," and the meaning is: they returned to Him and devoted themselves to His worship, turning away from all else. ﴿For them is good tidings﴾ of the great reward, which is Paradise. This good tidings is either through the tongues of the Messengers, or at the approach of death, or at the Resurrection.

﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾. The intended "servants" here is general, so it includes those described with avoidance and turning back to Him, entering primarily. The meaning: they listen to the true speech from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and they follow its best, that is, its muhkam (clear, definitive) portions, and they act upon it.

Al-Suddi said: they follow the best of what they are commanded, and act upon what is in it. It was said: it is the man who hears the good and the bad, so he speaks of the good and refrains from the bad, so he does not speak of it. It was said: they listen to the Qur'an and other than it, so they follow the Qur'an. It was said: they listen to the concessions (rukhas) and the strict obligations (‘aza'im), so they follow the strict obligations and leave the concessions. It was said: they take the pardon and leave punishment.

Then He, glory be to Him, praised those mentioned, saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾. That is: they are the ones whom Allah brought to the truth, and they are the possessors of sound intellects, because they are the ones who benefited from their minds, while those other than them did not benefit from their minds.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the one for whom wretchedness had preceded and who was deprived of happiness, saying: ﴿Then is one upon whom the word of punishment has come into effect [comparable to one who is saved]?﴾ The word "man" here may be a relative pronoun in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted, that is: "like one who fears" [or] "then you rescue him" or "you grieve over him." It may also be conditional, and its answer is ﴿Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾. So the fa' is the fa' of the answer, entering upon the clause of the consequence, and the interrogative hamza of denial is repeated to emphasize the meaning of denial. Sibawayh said that he repeated the interrogative because the speech is long. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "Would you then save one upon whom the word of punishment has come into effect?" By "the word of punishment" here is meant His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85], and His saying: ﴿Whoever follows you of them, I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 18]. The meaning of the verse is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he was eager for the faith of his people, so Allah informed him that whoever has had the decree preceded for him and the word of Allah has come into effect upon him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cannot save him from the Fire by making him a believer.

Ata' said: He means Abu Lahab and his son, and whoever remained behind from the Prophet's (ﷺ) clan in faith. In the verse there is a descent of the one who deserves punishment to the one who has already become of that kind, and the descent of his call to faith to the level of rescuing him from the punishment of the Fire.

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned earlier that the people of wretchedness have canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them, He made an exception from them for those who were of the people of happiness, saying: ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above which are chambers built [high]﴾. That is because Paradise has levels, some above others. The meaning of "built" (mabniyyah) is that they are built like the building of dwellings, in the solidity of their foundation and the strength of their construction, although the dwellings of this world are nothing in comparison to them. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is: beneath those chambers, and in that there is perfection of their splendor and an increase in their radiance. The accusative of ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is as an absolute object (masdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence, because His saying "for them are chambers" means "Allah has promised them with that." The sentence ﴿Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ confirms the promise, that is: Allah does not break what He has promised to both groups of good and evil.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, the verse. He said: they are the disbelievers whom Allah created for the Fire; the world has passed away from them, and Paradise has been forbidden to them.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿who have lost themselves and their families﴾, he said: "Their families" are from among the people of Paradise, who had been prepared for them had they worked in obedience to Allah, so they were cheated of them.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: Sa'id ibn Zayd, Abu Dharr and Salman used to follow the best of speech and words in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah): "There is no god but Allah." They said it, so Allah revealed to His Prophet ﴿who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a caller who called out: 'Whoever dies not associating anything with Allah will enter Paradise.' Then 'Umar met the Messenger and turned him back, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, I fear that people will rely on this and not work.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If people knew the extent of my Lord's mercy, they would rely on it; and if they knew the extent of my Lord's wrath and His punishment, they would belittle their deeds.'" This hadith has its origin in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Indeed, I fear that if I disobey my Lord by responding to the polytheists in what they call me to, namely the worship of other than Allah."

Abu Hamza al-Yamani and Ibn al-Musayyib said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your previous and subsequent sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. In this verse there is evidence that the command is obligatory, because before it is ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 11], so what is meant is disobedience to this command.

﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾. The placing of "Allah" first indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas), that is: I do not worship other than Him, neither independently nor as a partner. The meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in my religion﴾ is that it is purely for Allah, unmixed with shirk, showing-off (riya') or anything else of that kind. Its verification has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah.

Al-Razi said: If it is asked, what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 11] and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an announcement that he is commanded by Allah to have faith and to worship, and the second is an announcement that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Allah.

By "the word of punishment" here is meant His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85], and His saying: ﴿Whoever follows you of them, I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 18]. The meaning of the verse is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he was eager for the faith of his people, so Allah informed him that whoever has had the decree preceded for him and the word of Allah has come into effect upon him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cannot save him from the Fire by making him a believer.

Ata' said: He means Abu Lahab and his son, and whoever remained behind from the Prophet's (ﷺ) clan in faith. In the verse there is a descent of the one who deserves punishment to the one who has already become of that kind, and the descent of his call to faith to the level of rescuing him from the punishment of the Fire.

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned earlier that the people of wretchedness have canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them, He made an exception from them for those who were of the people of happiness, saying: ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above which are chambers built [high]﴾. That is because Paradise has levels, some above others. The meaning of "built" (mabniyyah) is that they are built like the building of dwellings, in the solidity of their foundation and the strength of their construction, although the dwellings of this world are nothing in comparison to them. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is: beneath those chambers, and in that there is perfection of their splendor and an increase in their radiance. The accusative of ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is as an absolute object (masdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence, because His saying "for them are chambers" means "Allah has promised them with that." The sentence ﴿Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ confirms the promise, that is: Allah does not break what He has promised to both groups of good and evil.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, the verse. He said: they are the disbelievers whom Allah created for the Fire; the world has passed away from them, and Paradise has been forbidden to them.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿who have lost themselves and their families﴾, he said: "Their families" are from among the people of Paradise, who had been prepared for them had they worked in obedience to Allah, so they were cheated of them.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: Sa'id ibn Zayd, Abu Dharr and Salman used to follow the best of speech and words in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah): "There is no god but Allah." They said it, so Allah revealed to His Prophet ﴿who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a caller who called out: 'Whoever dies not associating anything with Allah will enter Paradise.' Then 'Umar met the Messenger and turned him back, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, I fear that people will rely on this and not work.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If people knew the extent of my Lord's mercy, they would rely on it; and if they knew the extent of my Lord's wrath and His punishment, they would belittle their deeds.'" This hadith has its origin in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.

**Al-Shawkani's commentary (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 39 (al-Zumar), verses 13–20**

His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day﴾. That is: by abandoning sincere worship of Him and His oneness, and by calling people away from polytheism (shirk) and [exposing] the misguidance of its people. ﴿The punishment of a tremendous day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: the meaning is, "Indeed, I fear that if I disobey my Lord by responding to the polytheists in what they call me to, namely the worship of other than Allah."

Abu Hamza al-Yamani and Ibn al-Musayyib said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your previous and subsequent sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2]. In this verse there is evidence that the command is obligatory, because before it is ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 11], so what is meant is disobedience to this command.

﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾. The placing of "Allah" first indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas), that is: I do not worship other than Him, neither independently nor as a partner. The meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in my religion﴾ is that it is purely for Allah, unmixed with shirk, showing-off (riya') or anything else of that kind. Its verification has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah.

Al-Razi said: If it is asked, what is the meaning of the repetition in His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 11] and His saying ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion﴾? We say: this is not a repetition, because the first is an announcement that he is commanded by Allah to have faith and to worship, and the second is an announcement that he was commanded not to worship anyone other than Allah.

﴿So worship what you will besides Him﴾: this command is for threat, rebuke and reproach, like His saying ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. It was also said that the command is on its literal level, and that it is abrogated by the verse of the sword; but the first view is more preferable.

﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾. That is: the complete losers are these people, because whoever enters the Fire has lost himself and his family.

Al-Zajjaj said: By this he means the disbelievers, for they have lost themselves through eternal abiding in the Fire, and they have lost their families, because they did not enter the abode of the believers, who have families in Paradise. The sentence ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ is a separate statement to emphasize what precedes it. Introducing it with the particle of alertness indicates that this loss, and describing it as "manifest," shows that it is the complete instance of loss, that no loss equals it, and no punishment approaches it.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained this loss that had befallen them and the affliction descending upon them, by His saying: ﴿For them there will be canopies of Fire above them﴾. The "canopies" (zulal) refers to layers of Fire: that is, above them are layers of Fire blazing over them. ﴿And beneath them canopies﴾: that is, layers of Fire. What is beneath them is called "canopies" because it shades those beneath it of the people of the Fire, since in each layer of the Fire there is a group of the disbelievers. Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and over them are coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41], and His saying: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. (p-1279)

The reference in His saying "That" is to what was mentioned earlier of the description of their punishment in the Fire. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His saying ﴿with which Allah frightens His servants﴾, that is: He warns them with what He has threatened the disbelievers with of punishment, so that they fear it and guard against it. This is the meaning of ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, that is: guard against these sins which bring about such punishment upon the disbelievers. The reason for specifying "servants" as the believers is that the usual usage in the Qur'an is applying the word "servants" to them. It was also said that it is for the disbelievers and the people of sins, and it was said that it is general to both believers and disbelievers.

﴿And those who avoid the taghut, not worshipping it, and turn back to Allah﴾: the relative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is His saying "for them is good tidings". Taghut (the rebellious idol or false object of worship) is an intensive form of the noun, like "rahamut" and "'azamut". It refers to idols and to Satan. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said it is Satan. Al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said it is the idols. It was said that it is the soothsayer; it was said that it is a non-Arabic name like "Talut" and "Jalut"; and it was said that it is an Arabic name derived from "tughyan" (transgression).

Al-Akhfash said: "Taghut" is a collective noun, and its singular may be feminine. The meaning of "avoid the taghut" is: they turn away from worshipping it and devote their worship to Allah, mighty and majestic. His saying "that they worship it" is in the position of an accusative, as an apposition (badal) of the taghut, a "badal al-ishtimal" (inclusive apposition), as if He said: "Avoid the worship of the taghut." The discussion of the explanation of taghut has already been treated in full in Surat al-Baqara. His saying ﴿and turn back to Allah﴾ is coordinated with "avoid," and the meaning is: they returned to Him and devoted themselves to His worship, turning away from all else. ﴿For them is good tidings﴾ of the great reward, which is Paradise. This good tidings is either through the tongues of the Messengers, or at the approach of death, or at the Resurrection.

﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾. The intended "servants" here is general, so it includes those described with avoidance and turning back to Him, entering primarily. The meaning: they listen to the true speech from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and they follow its best, that is, its muhkam (clear, definitive) portions, and they act upon it.

Al-Suddi said: they follow the best of what they are commanded, and act upon what is in it. It was said: it is the man who hears the good and the bad, so he speaks of the good and refrains from the bad, so he does not speak of it. It was said: they listen to the Qur'an and other than it, so they follow the Qur'an. It was said: they listen to the concessions (rukhas) and the strict obligations (‘aza'im), so they follow the strict obligations and leave the concessions. It was said: they take the pardon and leave punishment.

Then He, glory be to Him, praised those mentioned, saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾. That is: they are the ones whom Allah brought to the truth, and they are the possessors of sound intellects, because they are the ones who benefited from their minds, while those other than them did not benefit from their minds.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the one for whom wretchedness had preceded and who was deprived of happiness, saying: ﴿Then is one upon whom the word of punishment has come into effect [comparable to one who is saved]?﴾ The word "man" here may be a relative pronoun in the nominative position as the subject, and its predicate is omitted, that is: "like one who fears" [or] "then you rescue him" or "you grieve over him." It may also be conditional, and its answer is ﴿Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾. So the fa' is the fa' of the answer, entering upon the clause of the consequence, and the interrogative hamza of denial is repeated to emphasize the meaning of denial. Sibawayh said that he repeated the interrogative because the speech is long. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "Would you then save one upon whom the word of punishment has come into effect?" By "the word of punishment" here is meant His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85], and His saying: ﴿Whoever follows you of them, I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 18]. The meaning of the verse is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he was eager for the faith of his people, so Allah informed him that whoever has had the decree preceded for him and the word of Allah has come into effect upon him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cannot save him from the Fire by making him a believer.

Ata' said: He means Abu Lahab and his son, and whoever remained behind from the Prophet's (ﷺ) clan in faith. In the verse there is a descent of the one who deserves punishment to the one who has already become of that kind, and the descent of his call to faith to the level of rescuing him from the punishment of the Fire.

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned earlier that the people of wretchedness have canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them, He made an exception from them for those who were of the people of happiness, saying: ﴿But those who feared their Lord will have chambers above which are chambers built [high]﴾. That is because Paradise has levels, some above others. The meaning of "built" (mabniyyah) is that they are built like the building of dwellings, in the solidity of their foundation and the strength of their construction, although the dwellings of this world are nothing in comparison to them. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is: beneath those chambers, and in that there is perfection of their splendor and an increase in their radiance. The accusative of ﴿the promise of Allah﴾ is as an absolute object (masdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence, because His saying "for them are chambers" means "Allah has promised them with that." The sentence ﴿Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ confirms the promise, that is: Allah does not break what He has promised to both groups of good and evil.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves﴾, the verse. He said: they are the disbelievers whom Allah created for the Fire; the world has passed away from them, and Paradise has been forbidden to them.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His saying: ﴿who have lost themselves and their families﴾, he said: "Their families" are from among the people of Paradise, who had been prepared for them had they worked in obedience to Allah, so they were cheated of them.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: Sa'id ibn Zayd, Abu Dharr and Salman used to follow the best of speech and words in the time of ignorance (jahiliyyah): "There is no god but Allah." They said it, so Allah revealed to His Prophet ﴿who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a caller who called out: 'Whoever dies not associating anything with Allah will enter Paradise.' Then 'Umar met the Messenger and turned him back, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, I fear that people will rely on this and not work.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If people knew the extent of my Lord's mercy, they would rely on it; and if they knew the extent of my Lord's wrath and His punishment, they would belittle their deeds.'" This hadith has its origin in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 21–26 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1280) When He, glorified is He, mentioned the Hereafter and described it with a description that necessitates desire for it and longing for it, He followed it with mention of the world (dunya) and described it with a description that necessitates turning away from it and aversion to it. He cited as an example of it the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its vanishing, together with what that contains of mention of one of the kinds of His overwhelming power and His wondrous craftsmanship. So He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: rain from the clouds. ﴿Then He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾, meaning: He causes it to enter and settle in the earth. Yanabi' (springs) is the plural of yanbu', from nabaa al-ma' yanbu' (the water gushed forth). The yanbu' is the spring of water and the places from which water gushes forth. The meaning is: He caused the water descending from the sky to enter the earth and made it there as flowing streams; or He placed it in yanabi', that is, in places from which water gushes forth. Then, on the second reading, it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-naz' al-khāfiḍ).

Muqatil said: So He made it into springs and wells in the earth. ﴿Then He brings forth by it crops of varying colours﴾, meaning: He brings forth by that water from the earth crops of varying colours, of yellow, green, white and red, or of wheat, barley and others, if by "colours" is meant "kinds". ﴿Then it dries up﴾: it is said, hāja al-nabt yahīju haījan, when its dryness is complete.

al-Jawhari said: It is said: hāja al-nabt hiyājan, when it dries out, and arḍ hā'ija is a land whose herbage has dried or yellowed, and the wind (ahājat al-rīḥ al-nabt) dried it out. al-Mubarrad said: al-Asma'i said: It is said: hājat al-arḍ tahīju, when its vegetation has turned back and departed. He said: Likewise hāja al-nabt. ﴿So you see it yellowed﴾, meaning: you see it after its greenness, freshness and fine lustre, yellowed, its greenness and freshness gone. ﴿Then He makes it into debris (ḥuṭāman)﴾, meaning: crumbled and broken, from taḥaṭṭama al-‘ūd, when a stick crumbles from dryness. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: in what has been mentioned there is a reminder for people of sound minds, for they are those who comprehend things as they truly are, so they reflect, take heed and know that the life of this world is in its state like the state of this crop in swiftness of passing and nearness of ending, and the going of its splendour and the vanishing of its brightness and freshness. When reflection and taking heed yield for them knowledge of this, there does not arise in them deception by it, or inclination to it, or preference of it over the abode of lasting bliss, the enduring life and pure pleasure. And there remains with them no doubt that Allah is able to resurrect and gather, for whoever is able to do this is able to do that.

It is also said: this is a parable which Allah struck for the Qur'an and for the breasts of those on the earth. The meaning: He sent down from the sky the Qur'an, and made it enter the hearts of the believers, then He brings forth by it a religion, some of which is better than some. As for the believer, he increases in faith and certainty; and as for one in whose heart is sickness, he becomes dried up just as the crop dries up. This is closer to being an interpretation (taghyir) than an exegesis (tafsir).

al-Jumhur read thumma yaj'aluhu with the nominative, coordinated with what precedes it. Abu Bishr read it with the accusative, by implicit an (anna). There is no basis for this.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that in that is a reminder for people of understanding, He mentioned the expansion of the breast for Islam, since complete benefit is not attained except by it. So He said: ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾, meaning: He widened it to accept the truth and opened it to be guided to the path of good.

al-Suddi said: His breast was expanded for Islam through joy in it and tranquillity toward it. The discussion of the hamza and the fa' is as previously mentioned in ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted. What indicates this omitted predicate is His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾. The meaning: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast for Islam, so he accepts it and is guided by its guidance, so he is by reason of that expansion ﴿upon a light from his Lord﴾ which overflows upon him, like one whose heart has hardened through the evil of his choice, so he is in the darknesses of misguidance and the afflictions of ignorance.

Qatadah said: The light is the Book of Allah; by it one takes, and to it one returns. al-Zajjaj said: The estimated meaning of the verse: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast like one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart, so he is not guided because of his hardness? ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hard against the remembrance of Allah﴾. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: That is, "from" the remembrance of Allah, as you say: I have become sated from food that I ate, and from food that I ate. The meaning: his heart became coarse and turned away from accepting the remembrance of Allah. It is said: qasā al-qalb when it hardens, and qalb qāsin: hard, that does not soften nor become gentle. It was also said: the meaning of (min dhikr Allah) is: because of His remembrance, which by right should cause breasts to expand and hearts to be at rest through it. The meaning: when Allah is remembered, they recoil. The first is preferable, and it is supported by the reading of those who read: "‘an dhikr Allah". The indication in His saying ﴿Those﴾ is to those whose hearts are hardened; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿in manifest error﴾, meaning: clear and evident.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the attributes of His Mighty Book, so He said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and He named it a statement (ḥadīth) because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to relate it to his people and inform them of what was revealed to him of it.

In it is an explanation that the best speech previously mentioned is the Qur'an. The accusative of ﴿a Book﴾ is in apposition to ﴿the best statement﴾, and it is possible that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from it. ﴿Consistent (mutashābihan)﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: its parts resemble one another in excellence and firmness, soundness of meanings, strength of structure, and its reaching the highest degrees of eloquence. Qatadah said: its parts resemble one another in verses and letters. It was said: it resembles the Books of Allah sent down upon His prophets. ﴿Repeated (mathani)﴾ is another attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: stories are repeated in it, and admonitions and rulings recur in it.

It was also said: it is recited repeatedly, so its hearer does not tire and its reciter does not become weary.

al-Jumhur read mathani with a fatha on the ya'. Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Bishr read it with sukun, for lightness, disliking its vowelling, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is mathani. al-Razi, in explaining mathani, said that most of the things mentioned in the Qur'an recur in pairs, such as command and prohibition, general and specific, summary and detailed, the conditions of the heavens and the earth, Paradise and Hell, light and darkness, the Preserved Tablet and the Pen, the angels and the devils, the Throne and the Footstool, promise and threat, hope and fear. The purpose of that is to show that everything other than the Truth is a pair, and that the One, the Unique, the Truth is Allah. Nothing is hidden in his speech (p-1281) of this excess and distance from the intended purpose of the revelation.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾. This clause may be an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, or a circumstantial state from it, since although it is indefinite it has become specified by the attribute; or it may be a new clause explaining what occurs in its hearers of impression. Al-iqsha'rar is contraction: it is said, iqsha'arra jiluduhu, when his skin contracts and gathers from fear. The meaning: a shudder seizes them from it.

al-Zajjaj said: When verses of punishment are mentioned, the skins of those who fear Allah shiver. ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften﴾ when verses of mercy are mentioned.

al-Wahidi said: This is the saying of all the exegetes. Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*So I spent the night struggling with the night of completeness, while the heart, from fear, is shivering.*

It was also said: the meaning is that the Qur'an, being at the utmost of eloquence and excellence, whenever they saw their inability to oppose it, their skins shivered at it in magnification of it and wonder at its beauty and eloquence. ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften towards the remembrance of Allah﴾: "talin" is construed with "ila" by implicit meaning of a verb that takes it, as if it were said: they became calm and reassured toward the remembrance of Allah, soft, not contracted. The object of "dhikr Allah" is omitted, and the estimate is: toward the remembrance of Allah, His mercy, His reward and His Garden; and it is omitted for knowledge of it.

Qatadah said: This is the description of the friends of Allah; He described them as having their skins shiver and their hearts at rest toward the remembrance of Allah, and He did not describe them as losing their minds or swooning; that is only in the people of innovation, and it is from Satan. The reference in ﴿That﴾ is to the Book described with those attributes, and it is the subject, and ﴿the guidance of Allah﴾ is its predicate, meaning: that Book is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. It was also said: the reference in ﴿That﴾ is to what Allah bestowed upon these people of fear of His punishment and hope for His reward. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: He makes his heart hard, dark, not receptive to the truth, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ who guides him to the truth and rescues him from misguidance.

al-Jumhur read min hadin without a ya'. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a ya'.

Then, when He had judged those whose hearts are hardened with a judgment in this world, which is misguidance, He judged them with another judgment in the Hereafter, which is punishment, so He said: ﴿Is then one who will shield with his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...﴾ The interrogative is for denial, and the discussion of it and of this fa' entering on "man" in His saying ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] has previously been given. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted due to the context indicating it. The meaning: Is one whose condition is to protect himself with his face, which is the noblest of his limbs, from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, because his hand has become shackled to his neck, like one who is safe, nothing of that befalls him, and he has no need to protect himself?

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment like one who enters Paradise? 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: He is thrown into the Fire bound, so the first thing the Fire touches of him is his face. Mujahid said: He is dragged on his face in the Fire. al-Akhfash said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment better, or one who is blessed? Like His saying: ﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Fussilat: 40].

Then He, glorified is He, informed of what the guardians (khazana) say to the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn﴾. It is coordinated with "yattaqi", meaning: and it will be said to them. It came in the past form to indicate certainty.

'Ata' said: that is, the recompense of what you used to do. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. The discussion of the meaning of dhawq (tasting) has previously been given in more than one place.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the condition of those disbelievers before them, so He said: ﴿Those before them denied﴾, meaning: those before the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning: they denied their messengers, ﴿so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, meaning: from a direction they did not expect the punishment to come from, and that is at their security and heedlessness of Allah's punishment for their denial.

﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾, meaning: humiliation and abasement in the worldly life through transformation, sinking into the earth, killing, captivity and other things. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾ because of its utmost severity together with its permanence, ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were among those who know things, reflect upon them and act according to the requirement of their knowledge.

al-Mubarrad said: It is said of whatever reaches a limb of something: it has tasted it, meaning it arrives at it just as sweetness and bitterness reach the one tasting them. He said: And khizy is what is disliked.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ the verse, he said: There is no water in the earth but that it descended from the sky, but veins in the earth change it; that is His saying ﴿and makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾. Whoever wishes that salt would return sweet, let him raise it up.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning His saying ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ that he said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verses 21–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam⁠—﴾ We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the expansion of his breast?' He said: 'When the light enters the heart, it expands and widens.' We said: 'What is the sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, as a marfu' mursal report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) but with a missing companion in the chain).

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated in Nawadir al-Usul from Ibn Umar that a man said: "O Prophet of Allah, which of the believers is the most astute (akyas)?" He said: "The one who remembers death most often and prepares for it best. When the light enters the heart, it expands and grows wide." They said: "What is the sign of that, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes."

He also narrated it from Abu Ja'far Abdullah ibn al-Miswar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with similar wording, and he added in it: "Then he recited: ﴿Is one whom Allah has opened his breast to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾"

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib fi al-Dhikr, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of Allah, for excessive speech without the remembrance of Allah hardens the heart, and the people furthest from Allah are those with hard hearts."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us," and so there was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech⁠—﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning His words "mathani" (oft-repeated): "The entire Qur'an is mathani."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Qur'an resembles its parts one another, and its parts are referred back to one another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Book of Allah is mathani; the command is repeated in it many times."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abdullah ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I said to my grandmother Asma', "How did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) behave when they recited the Qur'an?" She said: "They were as Allah described them: their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver." I said: "But some people here, when they hear that, are overtaken by a swoon." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment...﴾ He said: He will be dragged to the Fire bound, then cast into it, and the Fire will not touch his face.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 21–26 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1280) When He, glorified is He, mentioned the Hereafter and described it with a description that necessitates desire for it and longing for it, He followed it with mention of the world (dunya) and described it with a description that necessitates turning away from it and aversion to it. He cited as an example of it the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its vanishing, together with what that contains of mention of one of the kinds of His overwhelming power and His wondrous craftsmanship. So He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: rain from the clouds. ﴿Then He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾, meaning: He causes it to enter and settle in the earth. Yanabi' (springs) is the plural of yanbu', from nabaa al-ma' yanbu' (the water gushed forth). The yanbu' is the spring of water and the places from which water gushes forth. The meaning is: He caused the water descending from the sky to enter the earth and made it there as flowing streams; or He placed it in yanabi', that is, in places from which water gushes forth. Then, on the second reading, it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-naz' al-khāfiḍ).

Muqatil said: So He made it into springs and wells in the earth. ﴿Then He brings forth by it crops of varying colours﴾, meaning: He brings forth by that water from the earth crops of varying colours, of yellow, green, white and red, or of wheat, barley and others, if by "colours" is meant "kinds". ﴿Then it dries up﴾: it is said, hāja al-nabt yahīju haījan, when its dryness is complete.

al-Jawhari said: It is said: hāja al-nabt hiyājan, when it dries out, and arḍ hā'ija is a land whose herbage has dried or yellowed, and the wind (ahājat al-rīḥ al-nabt) dried it out. al-Mubarrad said: al-Asma'i said: It is said: hājat al-arḍ tahīju, when its vegetation has turned back and departed. He said: Likewise hāja al-nabt. ﴿So you see it yellowed﴾, meaning: you see it after its greenness, freshness and fine lustre, yellowed, its greenness and freshness gone. ﴿Then He makes it into debris (ḥuṭāman)﴾, meaning: crumbled and broken, from taḥaṭṭama al-‘ūd, when a stick crumbles from dryness. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: in what has been mentioned there is a reminder for people of sound minds, for they are those who comprehend things as they truly are, so they reflect, take heed and know that the life of this world is in its state like the state of this crop in swiftness of passing and nearness of ending, and the going of its splendour and the vanishing of its brightness and freshness. When reflection and taking heed yield for them knowledge of this, there does not arise in them deception by it, or inclination to it, or preference of it over the abode of lasting bliss, the enduring life and pure pleasure. And there remains with them no doubt that Allah is able to resurrect and gather, for whoever is able to do this is able to do that.

It is also said: this is a parable which Allah struck for the Qur'an and for the breasts of those on the earth. The meaning: He sent down from the sky the Qur'an, and made it enter the hearts of the believers, then He brings forth by it a religion, some of which is better than some. As for the believer, he increases in faith and certainty; and as for one in whose heart is sickness, he becomes dried up just as the crop dries up. This is closer to being an interpretation (taghyir) than an exegesis (tafsir).

al-Jumhur read thumma yaj'aluhu with the nominative, coordinated with what precedes it. Abu Bishr read it with the accusative, by implicit an (anna). There is no basis for this.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that in that is a reminder for people of understanding, He mentioned the expansion of the breast for Islam, since complete benefit is not attained except by it. So He said: ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾, meaning: He widened it to accept the truth and opened it to be guided to the path of good.

al-Suddi said: His breast was expanded for Islam through joy in it and tranquillity toward it. The discussion of the hamza and the fa' is as previously mentioned in ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted. What indicates this omitted predicate is His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾. The meaning: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast for Islam, so he accepts it and is guided by its guidance, so he is by reason of that expansion ﴿upon a light from his Lord﴾ which overflows upon him, like one whose heart has hardened through the evil of his choice, so he is in the darknesses of misguidance and the afflictions of ignorance.

Qatadah said: The light is the Book of Allah; by it one takes, and to it one returns. al-Zajjaj said: The estimated meaning of the verse: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast like one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart, so he is not guided because of his hardness? ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hard against the remembrance of Allah﴾. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: That is, "from" the remembrance of Allah, as you say: I have become sated from food that I ate, and from food that I ate. The meaning: his heart became coarse and turned away from accepting the remembrance of Allah. It is said: qasā al-qalb when it hardens, and qalb qāsin: hard, that does not soften nor become gentle. It was also said: the meaning of (min dhikr Allah) is: because of His remembrance, which by right should cause breasts to expand and hearts to be at rest through it. The meaning: when Allah is remembered, they recoil. The first is preferable, and it is supported by the reading of those who read: "‘an dhikr Allah". The indication in His saying ﴿Those﴾ is to those whose hearts are hardened; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿in manifest error﴾, meaning: clear and evident.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the attributes of His Mighty Book, so He said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and He named it a statement (ḥadīth) because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to relate it to his people and inform them of what was revealed to him of it.

In it is an explanation that the best speech previously mentioned is the Qur'an. The accusative of ﴿a Book﴾ is in apposition to ﴿the best statement﴾, and it is possible that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from it. ﴿Consistent (mutashābihan)﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: its parts resemble one another in excellence and firmness, soundness of meanings, strength of structure, and its reaching the highest degrees of eloquence. Qatadah said: its parts resemble one another in verses and letters. It was said: it resembles the Books of Allah sent down upon His prophets. ﴿Repeated (mathani)﴾ is another attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: stories are repeated in it, and admonitions and rulings recur in it.

It was also said: it is recited repeatedly, so its hearer does not tire and its reciter does not become weary.

al-Jumhur read mathani with a fatha on the ya'. Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Bishr read it with sukun, for lightness, disliking its vowelling, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is mathani. al-Razi, in explaining mathani, said that most of the things mentioned in the Qur'an recur in pairs, such as command and prohibition, general and specific, summary and detailed, the conditions of the heavens and the earth, Paradise and Hell, light and darkness, the Preserved Tablet and the Pen, the angels and the devils, the Throne and the Footstool, promise and threat, hope and fear. The purpose of that is to show that everything other than the Truth is a pair, and that the One, the Unique, the Truth is Allah. Nothing is hidden in his speech (p-1281) of this excess and distance from the intended purpose of the revelation.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾. This clause may be an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, or a circumstantial state from it, since although it is indefinite it has become specified by the attribute; or it may be a new clause explaining what occurs in its hearers of impression. Al-iqsha'rar is contraction: it is said, iqsha'arra jiluduhu, when his skin contracts and gathers from fear. The meaning: a shudder seizes them from it.

al-Zajjaj said: When verses of punishment are mentioned, the skins of those who fear Allah shiver. ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften﴾ when verses of mercy are mentioned.

al-Wahidi said: This is the saying of all the exegetes. Among this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*So I spent the night struggling with the night of completeness, while the heart, from fear, is shivering.*

It was also said: the meaning is that the Qur'an, being at the utmost of eloquence and excellence, whenever they saw their inability to oppose it, their skins shivered at it in magnification of it and wonder at its beauty and eloquence. ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften towards the remembrance of Allah﴾: "talin" is construed with "ila" by implicit meaning of a verb that takes it, as if it were said: they became calm and reassured toward the remembrance of Allah, soft, not contracted. The object of "dhikr Allah" is omitted, and the estimate is: toward the remembrance of Allah, His mercy, His reward and His Garden; and it is omitted for knowledge of it.

Qatadah said: This is the description of the friends of Allah; He described them as having their skins shiver and their hearts at rest toward the remembrance of Allah, and He did not describe them as losing their minds or swooning; that is only in the people of innovation, and it is from Satan. The reference in ﴿That﴾ is to the Book described with those attributes, and it is the subject, and ﴿the guidance of Allah﴾ is its predicate, meaning: that Book is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. It was also said: the reference in ﴿That﴾ is to what Allah bestowed upon these people of fear of His punishment and hope for His reward. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: He makes his heart hard, dark, not receptive to the truth, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ who guides him to the truth and rescues him from misguidance.

al-Jumhur read min hadin without a ya'. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a ya'.

Then, when He had judged those whose hearts are hardened with a judgment in this world, which is misguidance, He judged them with another judgment in the Hereafter, which is punishment, so He said: ﴿Is then one who will shield with his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...﴾ The interrogative is for denial, and the discussion of it and of this fa' entering on "man" in His saying ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] has previously been given. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted due to the context indicating it. The meaning: Is one whose condition is to protect himself with his face, which is the noblest of his limbs, from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, because his hand has become shackled to his neck, like one who is safe, nothing of that befalls him, and he has no need to protect himself?

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment like one who enters Paradise? 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: He is thrown into the Fire bound, so the first thing the Fire touches of him is his face. Mujahid said: He is dragged on his face in the Fire. al-Akhfash said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment better, or one who is blessed? Like His saying: ﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Fussilat: 40].

Then He, glorified is He, informed of what the guardians (khazana) say to the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn﴾. It is coordinated with "yattaqi", meaning: and it will be said to them. It came in the past form to indicate certainty.

'Ata' said: that is, the recompense of what you used to do. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. The discussion of the meaning of dhawq (tasting) has previously been given in more than one place.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the condition of those disbelievers before them, so He said: ﴿Those before them denied﴾, meaning: those before the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning: they denied their messengers, ﴿so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, meaning: from a direction they did not expect the punishment to come from, and that is at their security and heedlessness of Allah's punishment for their denial.

﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾, meaning: humiliation and abasement in the worldly life through transformation, sinking into the earth, killing, captivity and other things. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾ because of its utmost severity together with its permanence, ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were among those who know things, reflect upon them and act according to the requirement of their knowledge.

al-Mubarrad said: It is said of whatever reaches a limb of something: it has tasted it, meaning it arrives at it just as sweetness and bitterness reach the one tasting them. He said: And khizy is what is disliked.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ the verse, he said: There is no water in the earth but that it descended from the sky, but veins in the earth change it; that is His saying ﴿and makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾. Whoever wishes that salt would return sweet, let him raise it up.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning His saying ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ that he said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.
