It was also said: the meaning is that the Qur'an, being at the utmost of eloquence and excellence, whenever they saw their inability to oppose it, their skins shivered at it in magnification of it and wonder at its beauty and eloquence. ﴿Then their skins and hearts soften towards the remembrance of Allah﴾: "talin" is construed with "ila" by implicit meaning of a verb that takes it, as if it were said: they became calm and reassured toward the remembrance of Allah, soft, not contracted. The object of "dhikr Allah" is omitted, and the estimate is: toward the remembrance of Allah, His mercy, His reward and His Garden; and it is omitted for knowledge of it.

Qatadah said: This is the description of the friends of Allah; He described them as having their skins shiver and their hearts at rest toward the remembrance of Allah, and He did not describe them as losing their minds or swooning; that is only in the people of innovation, and it is from Satan. The reference in ﴿That﴾ is to the Book described with those attributes, and it is the subject, and ﴿the guidance of Allah﴾ is its predicate, meaning: that Book is the guidance of Allah, by which He guides whom He wills of His servants. It was also said: the reference in ﴿That﴾ is to what Allah bestowed upon these people of fear of His punishment and hope for His reward. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray﴾, meaning: He makes his heart hard, dark, not receptive to the truth, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ who guides him to the truth and rescues him from misguidance.

al-Jumhur read min hadin without a ya'. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a ya'.

Then, when He had judged those whose hearts are hardened with a judgment in this world, which is misguidance, He judged them with another judgment in the Hereafter, which is punishment, so He said: ﴿Is then one who will shield with his face from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection...﴾ The interrogative is for denial, and the discussion of it and of this fa' entering on "man" in His saying ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] has previously been given. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted due to the context indicating it. The meaning: Is one whose condition is to protect himself with his face, which is the noblest of his limbs, from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, because his hand has become shackled to his neck, like one who is safe, nothing of that befalls him, and he has no need to protect himself?

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment like one who enters Paradise? 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: He is thrown into the Fire bound, so the first thing the Fire touches of him is his face. Mujahid said: He is dragged on his face in the Fire. al-Akhfash said: The meaning: Is one who protects himself with his face from the evil of punishment better, or one who is blessed? Like His saying: ﴿Is one who is thrown into the Fire better, or one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Fussilat: 40].

Then He, glorified is He, informed of what the guardians (khazana) say to the disbelievers, so He said: ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn﴾. It is coordinated with "yattaqi", meaning: and it will be said to them. It came in the past form to indicate certainty.

'Ata' said: that is, the recompense of what you used to do. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35]. The discussion of the meaning of dhawq (tasting) has previously been given in more than one place.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the condition of those disbelievers before them, so He said: ﴿Those before them denied﴾, meaning: those before the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning: they denied their messengers, ﴿so the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, meaning: from a direction they did not expect the punishment to come from, and that is at their security and heedlessness of Allah's punishment for their denial.

﴿So Allah made them taste disgrace﴾, meaning: humiliation and abasement in the worldly life through transformation, sinking into the earth, killing, captivity and other things. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾ because of its utmost severity together with its permanence, ﴿if they only knew﴾, meaning: if they were among those who know things, reflect upon them and act according to the requirement of their knowledge.

al-Mubarrad said: It is said of whatever reaches a limb of something: it has tasted it, meaning it arrives at it just as sweetness and bitterness reach the one tasting them. He said: And khizy is what is disliked.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾ the verse, he said: There is no water in the earth but that it descended from the sky, but veins in the earth change it; that is His saying ﴿and makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾. Whoever wishes that salt would return sweet, let him raise it up.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning His saying ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ that he said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verses 21–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam⁠—﴾ We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the expansion of his breast?' He said: 'When the light enters the heart, it expands and widens.' We said: 'What is the sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, as a marfu' mursal report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) but with a missing companion in the chain).

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated in Nawadir al-Usul from Ibn Umar that a man said: "O Prophet of Allah, which of the believers is the most astute (akyas)?" He said: "The one who remembers death most often and prepares for it best. When the light enters the heart, it expands and grows wide." They said: "What is the sign of that, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes."

He also narrated it from Abu Ja'far Abdullah ibn al-Miswar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with similar wording, and he added in it: "Then he recited: ﴿Is one whom Allah has opened his breast to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾"

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib fi al-Dhikr, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of Allah, for excessive speech without the remembrance of Allah hardens the heart, and the people furthest from Allah are those with hard hearts."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us," and so there was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech⁠—﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning His words "mathani" (oft-repeated): "The entire Qur'an is mathani."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Qur'an resembles its parts one another, and its parts are referred back to one another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Book of Allah is mathani; the command is repeated in it many times."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abdullah ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I said to my grandmother Asma', "How did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) behave when they recited the Qur'an?" She said: "They were as Allah described them: their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver." I said: "But some people here, when they hear that, are overtaken by a swoon." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment...﴾ He said: He will be dragged to the Fire bound, then cast into it, and the Fire will not touch his face.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 21–26 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1280) When He, glorified is He, mentioned the Hereafter and described it with a description that necessitates desire for it and longing for it, He followed it with mention of the world (dunya) and described it with a description that necessitates turning away from it and aversion to it. He cited as an example of it the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its vanishing, together with what that contains of mention of one of the kinds of His overwhelming power and His wondrous craftsmanship. So He said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: rain from the clouds. ﴿Then He makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾, meaning: He causes it to enter and settle in the earth. Yanabi' (springs) is the plural of yanbu', from nabaa al-ma' yanbu' (the water gushed forth). The yanbu' is the spring of water and the places from which water gushes forth. The meaning is: He caused the water descending from the sky to enter the earth and made it there as flowing streams; or He placed it in yanabi', that is, in places from which water gushes forth. Then, on the second reading, it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-naz' al-khāfiḍ).

Muqatil said: So He made it into springs and wells in the earth. ﴿Then He brings forth by it crops of varying colours﴾, meaning: He brings forth by that water from the earth crops of varying colours, of yellow, green, white and red, or of wheat, barley and others, if by "colours" is meant "kinds". ﴿Then it dries up﴾: it is said, hāja al-nabt yahīju haījan, when its dryness is complete.

al-Jawhari said: It is said: hāja al-nabt hiyājan, when it dries out, and arḍ hā'ija is a land whose herbage has dried or yellowed, and the wind (ahājat al-rīḥ al-nabt) dried it out. al-Mubarrad said: al-Asma'i said: It is said: hājat al-arḍ tahīju, when its vegetation has turned back and departed. He said: Likewise hāja al-nabt. ﴿So you see it yellowed﴾, meaning: you see it after its greenness, freshness and fine lustre, yellowed, its greenness and freshness gone. ﴿Then He makes it into debris (ḥuṭāman)﴾, meaning: crumbled and broken, from taḥaṭṭama al-‘ūd, when a stick crumbles from dryness. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: in what has been mentioned there is a reminder for people of sound minds, for they are those who comprehend things as they truly are, so they reflect, take heed and know that the life of this world is in its state like the state of this crop in swiftness of passing and nearness of ending, and the going of its splendour and the vanishing of its brightness and freshness. When reflection and taking heed yield for them knowledge of this, there does not arise in them deception by it, or inclination to it, or preference of it over the abode of lasting bliss, the enduring life and pure pleasure. And there remains with them no doubt that Allah is able to resurrect and gather, for whoever is able to do this is able to do that.

It is also said: this is a parable which Allah struck for the Qur'an and for the breasts of those on the earth. The meaning: He sent down from the sky the Qur'an, and made it enter the hearts of the believers, then He brings forth by it a religion, some of which is better than some. As for the believer, he increases in faith and certainty; and as for one in whose heart is sickness, he becomes dried up just as the crop dries up. This is closer to being an interpretation (taghyir) than an exegesis (tafsir).

al-Jumhur read thumma yaj'aluhu with the nominative, coordinated with what precedes it. Abu Bishr read it with the accusative, by implicit an (anna). There is no basis for this.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that in that is a reminder for people of understanding, He mentioned the expansion of the breast for Islam, since complete benefit is not attained except by it. So He said: ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾, meaning: He widened it to accept the truth and opened it to be guided to the path of good.

al-Suddi said: His breast was expanded for Islam through joy in it and tranquillity toward it. The discussion of the hamza and the fa' is as previously mentioned in ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted. What indicates this omitted predicate is His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾. The meaning: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast for Islam, so he accepts it and is guided by its guidance, so he is by reason of that expansion ﴿upon a light from his Lord﴾ which overflows upon him, like one whose heart has hardened through the evil of his choice, so he is in the darknesses of misguidance and the afflictions of ignorance.

Qatadah said: The light is the Book of Allah; by it one takes, and to it one returns. al-Zajjaj said: The estimated meaning of the verse: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast like one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart, so he is not guided because of his hardness? ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hard against the remembrance of Allah﴾. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: That is, "from" the remembrance of Allah, as you say: I have become sated from food that I ate, and from food that I ate. The meaning: his heart became coarse and turned away from accepting the remembrance of Allah. It is said: qasā al-qalb when it hardens, and qalb qāsin: hard, that does not soften nor become gentle. It was also said: the meaning of (min dhikr Allah) is: because of His remembrance, which by right should cause breasts to expand and hearts to be at rest through it. The meaning: when Allah is remembered, they recoil. The first is preferable, and it is supported by the reading of those who read: "‘an dhikr Allah". The indication in His saying ﴿Those﴾ is to those whose hearts are hardened; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿in manifest error﴾, meaning: clear and evident.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the attributes of His Mighty Book, so He said: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement﴾, meaning the Qur'an, and He named it a statement (ḥadīth) because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to relate it to his people and inform them of what was revealed to him of it.

In it is an explanation that the best speech previously mentioned is the Qur'an. The accusative of ﴿a Book﴾ is in apposition to ﴿the best statement﴾, and it is possible that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from it. ﴿Consistent (mutashābihan)﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: its parts resemble one another in excellence and firmness, soundness of meanings, strength of structure, and its reaching the highest degrees of eloquence. Qatadah said: its parts resemble one another in verses and letters. It was said: it resembles the Books of Allah sent down upon His prophets. ﴿Repeated (mathani)﴾ is another attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, meaning: stories are repeated in it, and admonitions and rulings recur in it.

It was also said: it is recited repeatedly, so its hearer does not tire and its reciter does not become weary.

al-Jumhur read mathani with a fatha on the ya'. Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Bishr read it with sukun, for lightness, disliking its vowelling, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is mathani. al-Razi, in explaining mathani, said that most of the things mentioned in the Qur'an recur in pairs, such as command and prohibition, general and specific, summary and detailed, the conditions of the heavens and the earth, Paradise and Hell, light and darkness, the Preserved Tablet and the Pen, the angels and the devils, the Throne and the Footstool, promise and threat, hope and fear. The purpose of that is to show that everything other than the Truth is a pair, and that the One, the Unique, the Truth is Allah. Nothing is hidden in his speech (p-1281) of this excess and distance from the intended purpose of the revelation.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it﴾. This clause may be an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, or a circumstantial state from it, since although it is indefinite it has become specified by the attribute; or it may be a new clause explaining what occurs in its hearers of impression. Al-iqsha'rar is contraction: it is said, iqsha'arra jiluduhu, when his skin contracts and gathers from fear. The meaning: a shudder seizes them from it.

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned that in that is a reminder for people of understanding, He mentioned the expansion of the breast for Islam, since complete benefit is not attained except by it. The discussion of the hamza and the fa' is as previously mentioned in ﴿Then is one against whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19]. "Man" is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted. What indicates this omitted predicate is His saying: ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hardened﴾. The meaning: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast for Islam, so he accepts it and is guided by its guidance, so he is by reason of that expansion ﴿upon a light from his Lord﴾ which overflows upon him, like one whose heart has hardened through the evil of his choice, so he is in the darknesses of misguidance and the afflictions of ignorance.

Qatadah said: The light is the Book of Allah; by it one takes, and to it one returns. al-Zajjaj said: The estimated meaning of the verse: Is one whom Allah has expanded his breast like one whom Allah has sealed upon his heart, so he is not guided because of his hardness? ﴿So woe to those whose hearts are hard against the remembrance of Allah﴾. al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: That is, "from" the remembrance of Allah, as you say: I have become sated from food that I ate, and from food that I ate. al-Mubarrad said: It is said of whatever reaches a limb of something: it has tasted it, meaning it arrives at it just as sweetness and bitterness reach the one tasting them. He said: And khizy is what is disliked.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning His saying ﴿Then is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam﴾ that he said: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verses 21–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam⁠—﴾ We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the expansion of his breast?' He said: 'Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes.'"

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, as a marfu' mursal report (traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) but with a missing companion in the chain).

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated in Nawadir al-Usul from Ibn Umar that a man said: "O Prophet of Allah, which of the believers is the most astute (akyas)?" He said: "The one who remembers death most often and prepares for it best. When the light enters the heart, it expands and grows wide." They said: "What is the sign of that, O Prophet of Allah?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before death comes."

He also narrated it from Abu Ja'far Abdullah ibn al-Miswar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with similar wording, and he added in it: "Then he recited: ﴿Is one whom Allah has opened his breast to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?﴾"

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib fi al-Dhikr, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of Allah, for excessive speech without the remembrance of Allah hardens the heart, and the people furthest from Allah are those with hard hearts."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us," and so there was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech⁠—﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning His words "mathani" (oft-repeated): "The entire Qur'an is mathani."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Qur'an resembles its parts one another, and its parts are referred back to one another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Book of Allah is mathani; the command is repeated in it many times."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abdullah ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I said to my grandmother Asma', "How did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) behave when they recited the Qur'an?" She said: "They were as Allah described them: their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver." I said: "But some people here, when they hear that, are overtaken by a swoon." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment...﴾ He said: He will be dragged to the Fire bound, then cast into it, and the Fire will not touch his face.

He cited as an example of it the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its vanishing, together with what that contains of mention of one of the kinds of His overwhelming power and His wondrous craftsmanship. The meaning is: He caused the water descending from the sky to enter the earth and made it there as flowing streams; or He placed it in yanabi', that is, in places from which water gushes forth. Then, on the second reading, it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-naz' al-khāfiḍ).

Muqatil said: So He made it into springs and wells in the earth. ﴿Then He brings forth by it crops of varying colours﴾, meaning: He brings forth by that water from the earth crops of varying colours, of yellow, green, white and red, or of wheat, barley and others, if by "colours" is meant "kinds". ﴿Then it dries up﴾: it is said, hāja al-nabt yahīju haījan, when its dryness is complete.

He said: Likewise hāja al-nabt. ﴿So you see it yellowed﴾, meaning: you see it after its greenness, freshness and fine lustre, yellowed, its greenness and freshness gone. ﴿Then He makes it into debris (ḥuṭāman)﴾, meaning: crumbled and broken, from taḥaṭṭama al-‘ūd, when a stick crumbles from dryness. ﴿Indeed in that is a reminder for those of understanding﴾, meaning: in what has been mentioned there is a reminder for people of sound minds, for they are those who comprehend things as they truly are, so they reflect, take heed and know that the life of this world is in its state like the state of this crop in swiftness of passing and nearness of ending, and the going of its splendour and the vanishing of its brightness and freshness. When reflection and taking heed yield for them knowledge of this, there does not arise in them deception by it, or inclination to it, or preference of it over the abode of lasting bliss, the enduring life and pure pleasure. It is also said: this is a parable which Allah struck for the Qur'an and for the breasts of those on the earth. The meaning: He sent down from the sky the Qur'an, and made it enter the hearts of the believers, then He brings forth by it a religion, some of which is better than some. Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib fi al-Dhikr, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of Allah, for excessive speech without the remembrance of Allah hardens the heart, and the people furthest from Allah are those with hard hearts."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would relate to us," and so there was revealed: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech⁠—﴾ the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning His words "mathani" (oft-repeated): "The entire Qur'an is mathani."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Qur'an resembles its parts one another, and its parts are referred back to one another."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "The Book of Allah is mathani; the command is repeated in it many times."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abdullah ibn Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I said to my grandmother Asma', "How did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) behave when they recited the Qur'an?" She said: "They were as Allah described them: their eyes would shed tears and their skins would shiver." I said: "But some people here, when they hear that, are overtaken by a swoon." She said: "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the evil of the punishment...﴾ He said: He will be dragged to the Fire bound, then cast into it, and the Fire will not touch his face.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 27–35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly set forth for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾. We have already discussed the reality of the mathal (parable, example) and the manner of its being set forth in more than one place. The meaning of ﴿every kind of example﴾ is what they need, and it is not intended to be more general than that. Here it is like His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], meaning: nothing they need in matters of their religion. It has also been said that the meaning is: what We have mentioned of the destruction of the earlier nations is an example for these people ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may take admonition and learn a lesson.

The accusative of ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "this", and it is a confirming hal; this is called a preparatory hal (hal muwatti'ah), because the actual hal is ʿarabiyyan, and qur'anan is a preparation for it, like: "Zayd came to me a righteous man." This is what al-Akhfash said. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by way of praise.

al-Zajjaj said: ʿarabiyyan is accusative as a hal, and qur'anan is an emphasis. The meaning of ﴿without any crookedness﴾ is: without disagreement in any respect whatsoever. al-Dahhak said: that is, not varying.

al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about its meaning is the saying of al-Dahhak. It has also been said: not contradictory.

It has also been said: without ambiguity (labs). It has been said: without error in grammar (lahn). It has been said: without doubt, as the poet said:

*"There has come to you an oath without crookedness from God, and a word that is not false."*

﴿So that they may be mindful of God﴾ is a second cause after the first cause.
The first is ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may avoid disbelief and lying.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned an example from the Qur'anic parables for reminding and awakening, saying: ﴿God sets forth an example﴾, that is, the depiction of a strange situation through another like it.

Then He explained the example, saying: ﴿a man in whom are partners at odds with one another﴾. al-Kisa'i said: He put "a man" in the accusative because it is an explanation of "example". It has also been said that it is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, God sets forth an example with a man. It has also been said that "a man" is the first object and "an example" is the second object, and the first object was placed later so that it would be joined to what completes it. The reality of this has already been discussed in Surah Ya Sin. The clause ﴿in whom are partners﴾ is in the place of accusative as a descriptive of "a man". Tasharraus means disagreement. al-Farra' said: that is, they differ. al-Mubarrad said: that is, they are difficult to please, from shakisa, yashkasu, shakasan, so he is shakis, like 'asira, ya'saru, 'asaran, so he is 'asir. al-Jawhari said: tasharraus is disagreement.

He said: It is said: "a man, shaks," with the sukun, that is, difficult in character. This is like one who associates others with God and worships many gods.

Then He said: ﴿and a man wholly devoted to one man﴾, that is, pure for him. This is like one who worships God alone.

The majority read salaman with a fatha on the sin and the lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah read it with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read "saliman" with an alif and a kasra on the lam, as an active participle from salima lahu, so he is salim. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying: because the salim (sound, pure) is the opposite of the mushtarak (shared), and silm is the opposite of war, and there is no place for war here.

It has been answered that when a letter has two meanings it is not to be taken except in its more apparent sense. Silm, although it is the opposite of war, has another meaning equivalent to salim, from salima lahu kadha: when it becomes pure for him.

Also, salim has the same objection, because one says "a salim thing," meaning without defect. Abu Hatim chose the first reading.

The conclusion is that the reading of the majority is either the description by a verbal noun for emphasis, or by the omission of a modifier, that is, dhu silm (possessing peace/devotion). The reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and those with him is similar to it.

Then He, glorified is He, came with what indicates the difference between the two men, saying: ﴿Are the two equal in likeness?﴾ This interrogation is for denial and remoteness. The meaning is: Is this one who serves a group of partners whose characters differ and whose intentions are varied, each of whom employs him, so that he is exhausted and toiled, while each of them is not content with his service, equal to one who serves a single person, with no one else contending with him, so that if he obeys him, he is pleased with him, and if he disobeys him, he pardons him?

Between these two there is such a clear and evident difference that no intelligent person can utter their equality, for one of them is in the highest of ranks and the other in the lowest. The accusative of "in likeness" is a specification transferred from the subject, because the original is "Would their likeness be equal?" He used the singular for the specification and did not make it dual, because the original form of the specification is the singular, being an indicator of the genus.

The clause ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ confirms what precedes it, the negation of equality, and to inform the monotheists of the great blessing in their monotheism, which deserves the singling out of praise to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, turned away from the negation of equality implied by the denying interrogation to the explanation that most people do not know, saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. They are the polytheists, for they do not know this even though it is manifest and clear.

al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi said: by "most" is meant "all", but the apparent sense is contrary to what they both said, for the believers in God know what there is in monotheism of exaltation of its status and loftiness of its station, and that polytheism does not resemble it in any respect, and does not equal it in any attribute, and they know that God, glorified is He, deserves praise for this blessing, and that praise is exclusively His.

Then He, glorified is He, informed His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that death will reach him and reach them without doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾. The majority read mayyit and mayyitun with shaddah. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Yamani read "mai'tun and mai'tun," and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read with it.

Some exegetes have favoured this reading because his death and theirs is in the future, but there is no basis for this favouring, for the reading of the majority conveys this meaning.

al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: mayyit with shaddah is one who has not yet died but will die, and mayt with the lightening is one who has died and his soul has departed.

Qatadah said: his own soul was announced to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and their souls were announced to them. The reason for this choice is to inform the Companions that he will die, for some of them believed that he would not die. This is also a preparation and groundwork for what follows, where He said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾, that is, you (Muhammad) will dispute with them and argue against them, that you have conveyed to them and warned them, while they dispute with you; or the believer disputes with the disbeliever, and the wronged with the wrongdoer.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the state of each party of the disputants, saying: ﴿So who is more wrong than one who lies against God﴾, that is, none is more wrong than one who lies against God, claiming that He has a son or a partner or a consort, ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him﴾, which is what the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought of calling people to monotheism, commanding them to perform the obligations of the Law, forbidding them from its prohibitions, and informing them of the resurrection and the raising up, and what God has prepared for the obedient and the disobedient.

Then He, glorified is He, asked a question of affirmation, saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾, that is, is there not for these slanderers who deny the truth an abode? "Mathwa" means the dwelling, and it is derived from thawa bil-makan, when one stays in a place: yathwi thawaan and thuwiyyan, like mada, madaan and mudiyyan.

Abu 'Ubayd related that it is said: athwa, and he recited the verse of al-A'sha:

*"He stayed and shortened a night so that he might provision himself, and passed on, and broke the promise of Qutaylah."*

al-Asma'i denied this and said: we do not know "athwa."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group of believers who affirm, saying: ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it﴾. The relative clause is in the place of nominative as the subject, and it refers to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and those who follow him, and its predicate is ﴿they are the God-fearing﴾. It has been said: "He who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is Abu Bakr.

Mujahid said: "he who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

al-Suddi said: "he who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "he who confirms it" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: "he who brings the truth" is the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is the believers.

al-Nakha'i said: "he who brings the truth and confirms it" are the believers who will come with the Qur'an on the Day of Resurrection.

It has also been said that this is general for everyone who calls to the monotheism of God and guides to what He has prescribed for His servants. Ibn Jarir chose this, and it is what he chose among these sayings, and it is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "those who came with the truth and confirmed it."

The word alladhi, as it occurs in the reading of the majority, although singular, its meaning is plural, because it is intended as a genus, as His saying indicates: ﴿They are the God-fearing﴾, that is, those characterised by taqwa, which is the emblem of salvation.

Abu Salih read "wa-saddaqa" with the lightened form, meaning: the people confirmed it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what these truthful and confirming ones will have in the Hereafter: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, that is, they will have everything they wish of raising of ranks, averting of harms, and expiation of misdeeds. In this is a great encouragement and a profound inspiration. The reference by His saying "that" is to what was previously mentioned of their reward, and it is the subject, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿the reward of the good-doers﴾, that is, those who did good in their deeds.

It has been established in the Sahih from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that "Ihsan is that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

Then He, glorified is He, explained what the purpose is of what they have with their Lord, saying: ﴿So that God may expiate for them the worst of what they did﴾, for that is the greatest of what they hope for in averting harm from them, because if God, glorified is He, forgives them the worst of their deeds, He forgives them what is less than it by way of a fortiori. The lam is connected to "they will have" or to "the good-doers" or to something omitted.

The majority read "aswa'" as a superlative. It has been said: it is not for comparison, but means "evil (sayyi') of what they did." Ibn Kathir in one narration read "aswa'" with an alif between the hamza and the waw, on the pattern of ajmal, as the plural of su'.

﴿And He will reward them their wage according to the best of what they used to do﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned what indicates averting harms from them, He mentioned what indicates bringing the greatest benefits to them. The annexation of "the best" to what follows is not an annexation of the superior to the inferior, but an annexation of a thing to a part of it, intended for clarification without considering a comparison.

Muqatil said: He will reward them for the good of their deeds and will not reward them for the bad.

al-Ajurri and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿without crookedness﴾, that he said: "not created."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, concerning His saying ﴿God sets forth an example: a man...﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "The man who worships many gods: this is an example God set forth for the people of idols. ﴿And a man wholly devoted﴾ who worships one God: He set forth an example for Himself."

They also related from him, concerning His saying ﴿and a man wholly devoted﴾, that he said: "No one has any share in him."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We remained for a time of our lives, and we thought that this verse was revealed concerning us and the People of the Two Books before us: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ to the end of the verse, until I saw some of us striking the faces of others with the sword, and I knew that it had been revealed concerning us."

Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer than it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 27–35 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (Ibn Abbas? — see note below) also, who said: "The verse ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾ was revealed to us, and we did not know its interpretation until the fitnah (strife) occurred, and we said: 'This is what our Lord promised us, that we would dispute about it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ibn Mani', Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (p-1284) who graded it sound, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur narrated from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will what occurs between us in this world be repeated upon us along with the gravest of sins?' He said: 'Yes, it will indeed be repeated upon you, until every person with a right is given his right.' Al-Zubayr said: 'By Allah, the matter is indeed severe.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, we used to say: 'Our Lord is one, our religion is one, and our Prophet is one, so what is this dispute?' But when the Day of Siffin came, and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: 'Yes, this is it.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And the one who brings the truth﴾, meaning by it "There is no god but Allah," ﴿and confirms it﴾, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾, meaning: they guarded against shirk.

Ibn Jarir, al-Mawardi in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Usayd ibn Safwan, who had companionship (with the Prophet), from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The one who brings the truth is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the one who confirms it is Abu Bakr." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah the like of it.

This is what al-Akhfash said. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by way of praise.

al-Zajjaj said: ʿarabiyyan is accusative as a hal, and qur'anan is an emphasis. The meaning of ﴿without any crookedness﴾ is: without disagreement in any respect whatsoever. al-Dahhak said: that is, not varying.

al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about its meaning is the saying of al-Dahhak. It has also been said: not contradictory.

It has also been said: without ambiguity (labs). It has been said: without error in grammar (lahn). It has been said: without doubt, as the poet said:

*"There has come to you an oath without crookedness from God, and a word that is not false."*

﴿So that they may be mindful of God﴾ is a second cause after the first cause.
The first is ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may avoid disbelief and lying.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned an example from the Qur'anic parables for reminding and awakening, saying: ﴿God sets forth an example﴾, that is, the depiction of a strange situation through another like it.

Then He explained the example, saying: ﴿a man in whom are partners at odds with one another﴾. al-Kisa'i said: He put "a man" in the accusative because it is an explanation of "example". It has also been said that it is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, God sets forth an example with a man. It has also been said that "a man" is the first object and "an example" is the second object, and the first object was placed later so that it would be joined to what completes it. The reality of this has already been discussed in Surah Ya Sin. The clause ﴿in whom are partners﴾ is in the place of accusative as a descriptive of "a man". Tasharraus means disagreement. al-Farra' said: that is, they differ. al-Mubarrad said: that is, they are difficult to please, from shakisa, yashkasu, shakasan, so he is shakis, like 'asira, ya'saru, 'asaran, so he is 'asir. al-Jawhari said: tasharraus is disagreement.

He said: It is said: "a man, shaks," with the sukun, that is, difficult in character. This is like one who associates others with God and worships many gods.

It has been answered that when a letter has two meanings it is not to be taken except in its more apparent sense. Silm, although it is the opposite of war, has another meaning equivalent to salim, from salima lahu kadha: when it becomes pure for him.

The clause ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ confirms what precedes it, the negation of equality, and to inform the monotheists of the great blessing in their monotheism, which deserves the singling out of praise to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, informed His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that death will reach him and reach them without doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾. Some exegetes have favoured this reading because his death and theirs is in the future, but there is no basis for this favouring, for the reading of the majority conveys this meaning.

Mujahid said: "he who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: "he who brings the truth" is the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is the believers.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer than it.

This is what al-Akhfash said. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by way of praise.

al-Zajjaj said: ʿarabiyyan is accusative as a hal, and qur'anan is an emphasis. The meaning of ﴿without any crookedness﴾ is: without disagreement in any respect whatsoever. al-Dahhak said: that is, not varying.

al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about its meaning is the saying of al-Dahhak. It has also been said: not contradictory.

It has also been said: without ambiguity (labs). It has been said: without error in grammar (lahn). It has been said: without doubt, as the poet said:

*"There has come to you an oath without crookedness from God, and a word that is not false."*

﴿So that they may be mindful of God﴾ is a second cause after the first cause.
The first is ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may avoid disbelief and lying.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned an example from the Qur'anic parables for reminding and awakening, saying: ﴿God sets forth an example﴾, that is, the depiction of a strange situation through another like it.

It has also been said that it is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, God sets forth an example with a man. It has also been said that "a man" is the first object and "an example" is the second object, and the first object was placed later so that it would be joined to what completes it. The reality of this has already been discussed in Surah Ya Sin. The clause ﴿in whom are partners﴾ is in the place of accusative as a descriptive of "a man". Tasharraus means disagreement. al-Farra' said: that is, they differ. al-Mubarrad said: that is, they are difficult to please, from shakisa, yashkasu, shakasan, so he is shakis, like 'asira, ya'saru, 'asaran, so he is 'asir. al-Jawhari said: tasharraus is disagreement.

He said: It is said: "a man, shaks," with the sukun, that is, difficult in character. This is like one who associates others with God and worships many gods.

Then He said: ﴿and a man wholly devoted to one man﴾, that is, pure for him. This is like one who worships God alone.

The majority read salaman with a fatha on the sin and the lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah read it with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read "saliman" with an alif and a kasra on the lam, as an active participle from salima lahu, so he is salim. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying: because the salim (sound, pure) is the opposite of the mushtarak (shared), and silm is the opposite of war, and there is no place for war here.

It has been answered that when a letter has two meanings it is not to be taken except in its more apparent sense. Silm, although it is the opposite of war, has another meaning equivalent to salim, from salima lahu kadha: when it becomes pure for him.

Also, salim has the same objection, because one says "a salim thing," meaning without defect. Abu Hatim chose the first reading.

The first is ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may avoid disbelief and lying.

He said: It is said: "a man, shaks," with the sukun, that is, difficult in character. This is like one who associates others with God and worships many gods.

Then He said: ﴿and a man wholly devoted to one man﴾, that is, pure for him. This is like one who worships God alone.

Then He, glorified is He, came with what indicates the difference between the two men, saying: ﴿Are the two equal in likeness?﴾ This interrogation is for denial and remoteness. The meaning is: Is this one who serves a group of partners whose characters differ and whose intentions are varied, each of whom employs him, so that he is exhausted and toiled, while each of them is not content with his service, equal to one who serves a single person, with no one else contending with him, so that if he obeys him, he is pleased with him, and if he disobeys him, he pardons him?

Between these two there is such a clear and evident difference that no intelligent person can utter their equality, for one of them is in the highest of ranks and the other in the lowest. He used the singular for the specification and did not make it dual, because the original form of the specification is the singular, being an indicator of the genus.

The clause ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ confirms what precedes it, the negation of equality, and to inform the monotheists of the great blessing in their monotheism, which deserves the singling out of praise to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, turned away from the negation of equality implied by the denying interrogation to the explanation that most people do not know, saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. They are the polytheists, for they do not know this even though it is manifest and clear.

Then He, glorified is He, informed His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that death will reach him and reach them without doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾. Some exegetes have favoured this reading because his death and theirs is in the future, but there is no basis for this favouring, for the reading of the majority conveys this meaning.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the state of each party of the disputants, saying: ﴿So who is more wrong than one who lies against God﴾, that is, none is more wrong than one who lies against God, claiming that He has a son or a partner or a consort, ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him﴾, which is what the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought of calling people to monotheism, commanding them to perform the obligations of the Law, forbidding them from its prohibitions, and informing them of the resurrection and the raising up, and what God has prepared for the obedient and the disobedient.

*"He stayed and shortened a night so that he might provision himself, and passed on, and broke the promise of Qutaylah."*

al-Asma'i denied this and said: we do not know "athwa."

It has been said: "He who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is Abu Bakr.

Mujahid said: "he who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

al-Suddi said: "he who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "he who confirms it" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: "he who brings the truth" is the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is the believers.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer than it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 27–35 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (Ibn Abbas? — see note below) also, who said: "The verse ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾ was revealed to us, and we did not know its interpretation until the fitnah (strife) occurred, and we said: 'This is what our Lord promised us, that we would dispute about it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ibn Mani', Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (p-1284) who graded it sound, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur narrated from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will what occurs between us in this world be repeated upon us along with the gravest of sins?' He said: 'Yes, it will indeed be repeated upon you, until every person with a right is given his right.' Al-Zubayr said: 'By Allah, the matter is indeed severe.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, we used to say: 'Our Lord is one, our religion is one, and our Prophet is one, so what is this dispute?' But when the Day of Siffin came, and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: 'Yes, this is it.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And the one who brings the truth﴾, meaning by it "There is no god but Allah," ﴿and confirms it﴾, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾, meaning: they guarded against shirk.

Ibn Jarir, al-Mawardi in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Usayd ibn Safwan, who had companionship (with the Prophet), from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The one who brings the truth is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the one who confirms it is Abu Bakr." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah the like of it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 27–35 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly set forth for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example﴾. We have already discussed the reality of the mathal (parable, example) and the manner of its being set forth in more than one place. The meaning of ﴿every kind of example﴾ is what they need, and it is not intended to be more general than that. Here it is like His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An'am: 38], meaning: nothing they need in matters of their religion. It has also been said that the meaning is: what We have mentioned of the destruction of the earlier nations is an example for these people ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may take admonition and learn a lesson.

The accusative of ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "this", and it is a confirming hal; this is called a preparatory hal (hal muwatti'ah), because the actual hal is ʿarabiyyan, and qur'anan is a preparation for it, like: "Zayd came to me a righteous man." This is what al-Akhfash said. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by way of praise.

al-Zajjaj said: ʿarabiyyan is accusative as a hal, and qur'anan is an emphasis. The meaning of ﴿without any crookedness﴾ is: without disagreement in any respect whatsoever. al-Dahhak said: that is, not varying.

al-Nahhas said: the best of what has been said about its meaning is the saying of al-Dahhak. It has also been said: not contradictory.

It has also been said: without ambiguity (labs). It has been said: without error in grammar (lahn). It has been said: without doubt, as the poet said:

*"There has come to you an oath without crookedness from God, and a word that is not false."*

﴿So that they may be mindful of God﴾ is a second cause after the first cause.
The first is ﴿so that they may remember﴾, that is, so that they may avoid disbelief and lying.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned an example from the Qur'anic parables for reminding and awakening, saying: ﴿God sets forth an example﴾, that is, the depiction of a strange situation through another like it.

Then He explained the example, saying: ﴿a man in whom are partners at odds with one another﴾. al-Kisa'i said: He put "a man" in the accusative because it is an explanation of "example". It has also been said that it is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, God sets forth an example with a man. It has also been said that "a man" is the first object and "an example" is the second object, and the first object was placed later so that it would be joined to what completes it. The reality of this has already been discussed in Surah Ya Sin. The clause ﴿in whom are partners﴾ is in the place of accusative as a descriptive of "a man". Tasharraus means disagreement. al-Farra' said: that is, they differ. al-Mubarrad said: that is, they are difficult to please, from shakisa, yashkasu, shakasan, so he is shakis, like 'asira, ya'saru, 'asaran, so he is 'asir. al-Jawhari said: tasharraus is disagreement.

He said: It is said: "a man, shaks," with the sukun, that is, difficult in character. This is like one who associates others with God and worships many gods.

Then He said: ﴿and a man wholly devoted to one man﴾, that is, pure for him. This is like one who worships God alone.

The majority read salaman with a fatha on the sin and the lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah read it with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read "saliman" with an alif and a kasra on the lam, as an active participle from salima lahu, so he is salim. Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading, saying: because the salim (sound, pure) is the opposite of the mushtarak (shared), and silm is the opposite of war, and there is no place for war here.

It has been answered that when a letter has two meanings it is not to be taken except in its more apparent sense. Silm, although it is the opposite of war, has another meaning equivalent to salim, from salima lahu kadha: when it becomes pure for him.

Also, salim has the same objection, because one says "a salim thing," meaning without defect. Abu Hatim chose the first reading.

The conclusion is that the reading of the majority is either the description by a verbal noun for emphasis, or by the omission of a modifier, that is, dhu silm (possessing peace/devotion). The reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and those with him is similar to it.

Then He, glorified is He, came with what indicates the difference between the two men, saying: ﴿Are the two equal in likeness?﴾ This interrogation is for denial and remoteness. The meaning is: Is this one who serves a group of partners whose characters differ and whose intentions are varied, each of whom employs him, so that he is exhausted and toiled, while each of them is not content with his service, equal to one who serves a single person, with no one else contending with him, so that if he obeys him, he is pleased with him, and if he disobeys him, he pardons him?

Between these two there is such a clear and evident difference that no intelligent person can utter their equality, for one of them is in the highest of ranks and the other in the lowest. The accusative of "in likeness" is a specification transferred from the subject, because the original is "Would their likeness be equal?" He used the singular for the specification and did not make it dual, because the original form of the specification is the singular, being an indicator of the genus.

The clause ﴿All praise is due to God﴾ confirms what precedes it, the negation of equality, and to inform the monotheists of the great blessing in their monotheism, which deserves the singling out of praise to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, turned away from the negation of equality implied by the denying interrogation to the explanation that most people do not know, saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. They are the polytheists, for they do not know this even though it is manifest and clear.

al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi said: by "most" is meant "all", but the apparent sense is contrary to what they both said, for the believers in God know what there is in monotheism of exaltation of its status and loftiness of its station, and that polytheism does not resemble it in any respect, and does not equal it in any attribute, and they know that God, glorified is He, deserves praise for this blessing, and that praise is exclusively His.

Then He, glorified is He, informed His Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that death will reach him and reach them without doubt, saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾. The majority read mayyit and mayyitun with shaddah. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Yamani read "mai'tun and mai'tun," and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read with it.

Some exegetes have favoured this reading because his death and theirs is in the future, but there is no basis for this favouring, for the reading of the majority conveys this meaning.

al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said: mayyit with shaddah is one who has not yet died but will die, and mayt with the lightening is one who has died and his soul has departed.

Qatadah said: his own soul was announced to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and their souls were announced to them. The reason for this choice is to inform the Companions that he will die, for some of them believed that he would not die. This is also a preparation and groundwork for what follows, where He said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾, that is, you (Muhammad) will dispute with them and argue against them, that you have conveyed to them and warned them, while they dispute with you; or the believer disputes with the disbeliever, and the wronged with the wrongdoer.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the state of each party of the disputants, saying: ﴿So who is more wrong than one who lies against God﴾, that is, none is more wrong than one who lies against God, claiming that He has a son or a partner or a consort, ﴿and denies the truth when it has come to him﴾, which is what the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, brought of calling people to monotheism, commanding them to perform the obligations of the Law, forbidding them from its prohibitions, and informing them of the resurrection and the raising up, and what God has prepared for the obedient and the disobedient.

Then He, glorified is He, asked a question of affirmation, saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾, that is, is there not for these slanderers who deny the truth an abode? "Mathwa" means the dwelling, and it is derived from thawa bil-makan, when one stays in a place: yathwi thawaan and thuwiyyan, like mada, madaan and mudiyyan.

Abu 'Ubayd related that it is said: athwa, and he recited the verse of al-A'sha:

*"He stayed and shortened a night so that he might provision himself, and passed on, and broke the promise of Qutaylah."*

al-Asma'i denied this and said: we do not know "athwa."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the group of believers who affirm, saying: ﴿And he who brings the truth and confirms it﴾. The relative clause is in the place of nominative as the subject, and it refers to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and those who follow him, and its predicate is ﴿they are the God-fearing﴾. It has been said: "He who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is Abu Bakr.

Mujahid said: "he who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

al-Suddi said: "he who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "he who confirms it" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: "he who brings the truth" is the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is the believers.

al-Nakha'i said: "he who brings the truth and confirms it" are the believers who will come with the Qur'an on the Day of Resurrection.

It has also been said that this is general for everyone who calls to the monotheism of God and guides to what He has prescribed for His servants. Ibn Jarir chose this, and it is what he chose among these sayings, and it is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "those who came with the truth and confirmed it."

The word alladhi, as it occurs in the reading of the majority, although singular, its meaning is plural, because it is intended as a genus, as His saying indicates: ﴿They are the God-fearing﴾, that is, those characterised by taqwa, which is the emblem of salvation.

Abu Salih read "wa-saddaqa" with the lightened form, meaning: the people confirmed it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what these truthful and confirming ones will have in the Hereafter: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, that is, they will have everything they wish of raising of ranks, averting of harms, and expiation of misdeeds. In this is a great encouragement and a profound inspiration. The reference by His saying "that" is to what was previously mentioned of their reward, and it is the subject, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿the reward of the good-doers﴾, that is, those who did good in their deeds.

It has been established in the Sahih from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that "Ihsan is that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

Then He, glorified is He, explained what the purpose is of what they have with their Lord, saying: ﴿So that God may expiate for them the worst of what they did﴾, for that is the greatest of what they hope for in averting harm from them, because if God, glorified is He, forgives them the worst of their deeds, He forgives them what is less than it by way of a fortiori. The lam is connected to "they will have" or to "the good-doers" or to something omitted.

The majority read "aswa'" as a superlative. It has been said: it is not for comparison, but means "evil (sayyi') of what they did." Ibn Kathir in one narration read "aswa'" with an alif between the hamza and the waw, on the pattern of ajmal, as the plural of su'.

﴿And He will reward them their wage according to the best of what they used to do﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned what indicates averting harms from them, He mentioned what indicates bringing the greatest benefits to them. The annexation of "the best" to what follows is not an annexation of the superior to the inferior, but an annexation of a thing to a part of it, intended for clarification without considering a comparison.

Muqatil said: He will reward them for the good of their deeds and will not reward them for the bad.
