The relative clause is in the place of nominative as the subject, and it refers to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and those who follow him, and its predicate is ﴿they are the God-fearing﴾. It has been said: "He who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is Abu Bakr.

Mujahid said: "he who brings the truth" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

al-Suddi said: "he who brings the truth" is Jibril, and "he who confirms it" is the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace.

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd said: "he who brings the truth" is the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, and "he who confirms it" is the believers.

al-Nakha'i said: "he who brings the truth and confirms it" are the believers who will come with the Qur'an on the Day of Resurrection.

It has also been said that this is general for everyone who calls to the monotheism of God and guides to what He has prescribed for His servants. Ibn Jarir chose this, and it is what he chose among these sayings, and it is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "those who came with the truth and confirmed it."

The word alladhi, as it occurs in the reading of the majority, although singular, its meaning is plural, because it is intended as a genus, as His saying indicates: ﴿They are the God-fearing﴾, that is, those characterised by taqwa, which is the emblem of salvation.

Abu Salih read "wa-saddaqa" with the lightened form, meaning: the people confirmed it.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what these truthful and confirming ones will have in the Hereafter: ﴿They will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, that is, they will have everything they wish of raising of ranks, averting of harms, and expiation of misdeeds. In this is a great encouragement and a profound inspiration. The reference by His saying "that" is to what was previously mentioned of their reward, and it is the subject, and its predicate is His saying: ﴿the reward of the good-doers﴾, that is, those who did good in their deeds.

It has been established in the Sahih from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, that "Ihsan is that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."

Then He, glorified is He, explained what the purpose is of what they have with their Lord, saying: ﴿So that God may expiate for them the worst of what they did﴾, for that is the greatest of what they hope for in averting harm from them, because if God, glorified is He, forgives them the worst of their deeds, He forgives them what is less than it by way of a fortiori. The lam is connected to "they will have" or to "the good-doers" or to something omitted.

The majority read "aswa'" as a superlative. It has been said: it is not for comparison, but means "evil (sayyi') of what they did." Ibn Kathir in one narration read "aswa'" with an alif between the hamza and the waw, on the pattern of ajmal, as the plural of su'.

﴿And He will reward them their wage according to the best of what they used to do﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned what indicates averting harms from them, He mentioned what indicates bringing the greatest benefits to them. The annexation of "the best" to what follows is not an annexation of the superior to the inferior, but an annexation of a thing to a part of it, intended for clarification without considering a comparison.

Muqatil said: He will reward them for the good of their deeds and will not reward them for the bad.

al-Ajurri and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿without crookedness﴾, that he said: "not created."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, concerning His saying ﴿God sets forth an example: a man...﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "The man who worships many gods: this is an example God set forth for the people of idols. ﴿And a man wholly devoted﴾ who worships one God: He set forth an example for Himself."

They also related from him, concerning His saying ﴿and a man wholly devoted﴾, that he said: "No one has any share in him."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We remained for a time of our lives, and we thought that this verse was revealed concerning us and the People of the Two Books before us: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ to the end of the verse, until I saw some of us striking the faces of others with the sword, and I knew that it had been revealed concerning us."

Nu'aym ibn Hammad in al-Fitan, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him something similar, but longer than it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verse 27–35 (part 2 of 2):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him (Ibn Abbas? — see note below) also, who said: "The verse ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾ was revealed to us, and we did not know its interpretation until the fitnah (strife) occurred, and we said: 'This is what our Lord promised us, that we would dispute about it.'"

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ibn Mani', Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (p-1284) who graded it sound, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who graded it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa'l-Nushur narrated from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die. Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will what occurs between us in this world be repeated upon us along with the gravest of sins?' He said: 'Yes, it will indeed be repeated upon you, until every person with a right is given his right.' Al-Zubayr said: 'By Allah, the matter is indeed severe.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "When there was revealed ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, we used to say: 'Our Lord is one, our religion is one, and our Prophet is one, so what is this dispute?' But when the Day of Siffin came, and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: 'Yes, this is it.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And the one who brings the truth﴾, meaning by it "There is no god but Allah," ﴿and confirms it﴾, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿those are the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾, meaning: they guarded against shirk.

Ibn Jarir, al-Mawardi in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba, and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Usayd ibn Safwan, who had companionship (with the Prophet), from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The one who brings the truth is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the one who confirms it is Abu Bakr." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah the like of it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 39, verses 36–42:**

His saying: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ʿabdahu in the singular. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ʿibādahu in the plural. According to the first reading, the intended one is the Prophet (ﷺ) or the category (of servants), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is included in it first and foremost. According to the other reading, the intended ones are the prophets, or the believers, or all of them. Abū ʿUbayd preferred the reading of the majority because of His saying after it: ﴿And they frighten you﴾. The interrogative is for denial, because He, glory be to Him, is not sufficient in the most eloquent manner, as though it were so clear that no one could deny it.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "servant" and "servants" is that which includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

Al-Jurjānī said: Indeed Allah is sufficient for His believing servant and for His disbelieving servant; this one (is sufficient) with reward, and that one with punishment.

It was also read as *bi-kāfin ʿibādihi* (with the genitive construction), and it was read as *yukāfī* (in the present tense form). His saying: ﴿And they frighten you with those besides Him﴾ may be in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), since the meaning is: "Is He not sufficient for you at the time they frighten you?" It may also be a new (independent) sentence. ﴿Those besides Him﴾ is an expression for the objects of worship that they worship. ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, meaning: whoever Allah has decreed to be led astray, for him there is no guide who would guide him to right conduct and bring him out of error.

﴿And whomever Allah guides, for him there is no misleader﴾: He brings him out of guidance and casts him into error. ﴿Is not Allah Almighty﴾, meaning: Overpowering over everything, subduing to Him ﴿Owner of retribution﴾: He takes vengeance upon His disobedient ones by what He pours upon them of His punishment and what He sends down upon them of the lash of His chastisement.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ He, glory be to Him, mentions their acknowledgment, when they are asked about the Creator, that Allah, glory be to Him, is the one who prevented their worship of idols and their taking of deities besides Allah. In this is the greatest proof that they were in extreme heedlessness and great ignorance, because if they knew that the Creator of them and of what they worship besides Allah is Allah, glory be to Him, then how did their minds consider it good to worship other than the Creator of all, and to associate a created being with its Creator in worship? They were described as having sound intellects, perfect perception and complete shrewdness, but when they imitated their predecessors and thought well of them, they abandoned what reason requires and acted upon what is pure ignorance.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to rebuke them after this acknowledgment and to reprove them, so He said: ﴿Say, "Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intended for me some harm, could they remove His harm?"﴾ meaning: Inform me about these deities of yours: are they able to remove what Allah has intended for me of harm? Harm is hardship or something worse. ﴿Or if He intended for me mercy, could they withhold His mercy?﴾ from me, such that it would not reach me. Mercy is blessing and ease.

al-Jumhur read *mumsikāt* and *kāshifāt* in both places with the genitive construction, and Abū ʿAmr read them with tanwīn (nunation).

Muqātil said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them, and they remained silent. Others said: They said, "It does not repel anything of Allah's decree, but it intercedes." So He revealed: ﴿Say, "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ in all my affairs, in bringing benefit and repelling harm. ﴿Upon Him rely those who rely﴾, meaning: upon Him alone, not upon other than Him do those who depend (rely) depend. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the reading of Abū ʿAmr,

because *kāshifāt* is an active participle with the meaning of the future, and whatever is like that, its tanwīn is better. It was recited thus by al-Ḥasan and ʿĀṣim.

Then Allah commanded him to threaten them and warn them, so He said: ﴿Say, "O my people, work according to your position﴾, meaning: according to your state in which you are and in which you are established ﴿indeed I am working﴾, meaning: according to my state in which I am and in which I am established. That (object) is omitted because it is known from what preceded.

﴿Then you will know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him﴾, meaning: will humiliate him and debase him in this world, so it will become evident at that time that he is the falsifier and his opponent is the one upon the truth. The punishment intended here is the punishment of this world, and what befell them of killing, captivity, subjugation and humiliation.

Then He mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And there descends upon him a lasting punishment﴾, meaning: enduring, continuous in the Hereafter, and this is the punishment of the Fire.

Then, since their persistence in disbelief was grievous to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He informed him that he was not charged except with conveying, not with guiding those who had gone astray. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for the people﴾, meaning: for their sake and to make clear what they were charged with. ﴿In truth﴾ is a circumstantial clause, either of the subject or of the object, meaning: as those who are upon truth, or as one clothed with the truth. ﴿Whoever is guided﴾ to the path of truth and follows it, ﴿then it is for his own self; and whoever goes astray﴾ from it, ﴿then he only goes astray against it﴾, meaning: against his own self, so the harm of that falls upon him and does not extend to others. ﴿And you are not over them a manager﴾, meaning: you are not charged with guiding them, nor addressed with it. Rather, upon you is only the conveying, and you have done it.

These verses are abrogated (*mansūkhah*, subject to naskh) by the verse of the sword. Allah commanded His Messenger after this to fight them until they say "There is no god but Allah" and act upon the rulings of Islam.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a kind of His far-reaching power and His wondrous craftsmanship, so He said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, meaning: He seizes them when their term approaches and removes them from the bodies. ﴿And those that have not died during their sleep﴾, meaning: and He takes the souls that have not died, i.e., whose term has not arrived, during their sleep.

This has been disputed. It was said: He seizes them from acting, while the spirit remains in the body. Al-Farrāʾ said: The meaning is: He seizes those that have not died when their term has ended. He said: Their taking (tawaffī) may be their sleep, so the estimation according to this is: "and those that have not died, their taking is their sleep."

Al-Zajjāj said: Every person has two souls: one is the soul of discernment, which departs from him when he sleeps so that he does not understand; and the other is the soul of life, which when it ceases, the breath ceases with it, and the sleeper breathes.

Al-Qushayrī said: In this there is remoteness, since what is understood from the verse is that the soul that is taken in both states is one thing. For this reason He said: ﴿So He keeps those upon whom He has decreed death and sends the others﴾, meaning: the sleeping one, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the appointed time for his death. Ibn al-Anbārī said the same as the saying of al-Zajjāj.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: Allah seizes the spirits of the dead when they die, and the spirits of the living when they sleep, so they meet as Allah wills that they meet. ﴿So He keeps those upon whom He has decreed death and sends the others﴾, meaning: He returns them. The preferable view is to say: the taking of souls during sleep is by the removal of sensation and the occurrence of a defect in the locus of sensation. So He keeps the one upon whom He has decreed death and does not return it to the body in which it was, and He sends the other, by restoring its sensation to it.

It was said: The meaning of ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ is by omitting a modifier, meaning: at the death of their bodies.

The scholars have differed concerning the soul and the spirit: are they one thing or two? The discussion of that is very lengthy, and it is known in the books written for this matter.

al-Jumhur read *qaḍā* (decreed) in the active voice, meaning: Allah decreed death upon it. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read it in the passive voice. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the first reading because it agrees with His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls﴾. The indication in His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ refers to what preceded of taking, withholding and releasing of souls; ﴿signs﴾, meaning: wondrous, marvelous signs indicating overwhelming power. But the fact that these are signs is not something everyone understands, rather it is for ﴿a people who reflect﴾ upon it, contemplate it, and derive evidence from it for the oneness of Allah and the perfection of His power. Indeed in this taking, withholding and releasing is admonition for those who take heed and a reminder for those who remember.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "A soul and a spirit, between them is like the ray of the sun. Allah takes the soul during its sleep and leaves the spirit within its body, moving about and living. If it appears to Him to seize it, He seizes the spirit and it dies. And if He delays its term, He returns the soul to its place within the body."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Abū al-Shaykh in al-ʿAẓamah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ḍiyāʾ in al-Mukhtārah transmitted from him concerning the verse, that he said: "The spirits of the living and the spirits of the dead meet in sleep, and they ask one another what Allah wills. Then Allah withholds the spirits of the dead and releases the spirits of the living into their bodies, ﴿until a specified term﴾, without error in anything of them. That is His saying: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd also transmitted from him, concerning the verse, that he said: "Every soul has a cause in which it runs. When death is decreed upon it, it sleeps until the cause ends. And the one that has not died in its sleep is left (to continue)."

al-Bukhārī and Muslim transmitted from the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When one of you goes to his bed, let him shake it with the inside of his waist-wrapper, for he does not know what may have fallen upon it. Then let him say: 'In Your name, my Lord, I have laid down my side, and in Your name I raise it. If You take my soul, then have mercy upon it, and if You release it, then protect it with that with which You protect Your righteous servants.'"

He emphasized *al-shafa'ah* (الشَّفاعَةُ, intercession) with the emphatic form used for two or more, because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that applies to one, two, or a group. Then He described Him with the vastness of dominion, saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning He owns them, owns what is in them, and disposes of that as He wills and does what He desires. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾, not to anyone else, and that will be after resurrection.

﴿When Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink in aversion.﴾ The accusative of *waḥdahu* (وحْدَهُ, "alone") is a circumstantial qualifier according to Yunus, and a verbal noun according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh. *Ishmi'zaz* (الِاشْمِئْزازُ, "shrinking in aversion") in the lexicon means revulsion (al-nufur). Abu 'Ubaydah said: *ishma'azzat* means "recoiled." Al-Mubarrad said: "contracted." Qatada followed the first interpretation, and Mujahid the second, and the meanings are close. Al-Mu'arrij said: "denied." Abu Zayd said: "The man *ishma'azza* means he was frightened by fear." What fits the context is interpreting *ishma'azzat* as "contracted," and in origin it means turning away. When the polytheists were told, "There is no god but Allah," they would contract, as Allah reported about them in His saying: ﴿When you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their backs in aversion﴾ [al-Isra': 46]. Then He (glorified is He) mentioned their delight at the mention of their idols, saying: ﴿But when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice﴾, meaning they are glad at that and rejoice in it. The governing element for *idhā* (إذا, "when") in ﴿When Allah is mentioned﴾ is the verb following it, *ishma'azzat*. The governing element for *idhā* in ﴿When those besides Him are mentioned﴾ is the verb that governs the sudden *idhā* (إذا الفُجائِيَّةِ, "sudden-when"), and the estimated sense is: "they suddenly rejoiced at the time of the mention of those besides Him."

When the rebellious disbelievers did not accept what the Messenger (ﷺ) had brought them of calling to goodness, and they persisted in their disbelief, Allah (glorified is He) commanded him to return the matter, saying: ﴿Say: O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ.﴾ The explanation of ﴿Originator of the heavens﴾ has already passed, as has the explanation of ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. Both are in the accusative as vocatives (al-nida'). The meaning of ﴿You will judge between Your servants﴾ is that You will reward the good-doer for his goodness and punish the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing, for by that He makes clear who is the one in the right and who is the one in the wrong, and their disagreement and the quarrel of the disputants are removed in His judgment.

Then, when He had related what He related about the disbelievers' contraction at the mention of Allah and their delight at the mention of the idols, He mentioned what indicates the severity of their punishment and the magnitude of their retribution, saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it﴾, meaning all that is in this world of wealth and treasures, ﴿they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning from the evil of the punishment of that Day. The explanation of this has already passed in Al 'Imran. ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting on﴾, meaning there will become apparent to them from the punishments of Allah, His wrath, and the severity of His punishment what had not been in their reckoning. In this is a great warning and a far-reaching threat. Mujahid said: "They did deeds they thought were good deeds, but then they turned out to be evil deeds." Al-Suddi said likewise.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Woe to the people of showing-off (riya'), woe to the people of showing-off, woe to the people of showing-off. This is their verse and their story."

'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar said: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir became extremely distressed at his death, and he was asked, "What is this distress?" He said: "I fear a verse of the Book of Allah: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not been counting on﴾, so I fear that there will appear to me what I had not been counting on."

﴿And there will appear to them the evil of what they earned﴾, meaning the bad deeds of their works, from polytheism and the wronging of the friends of Allah. *Ma* (ما) may be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning "the evils of their earning," or a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), meaning "the evils of what they earned." ﴿And what they used to mock encompassed them﴾, meaning there surrounded them and descended upon them what they used to mock, namely the warning with which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to warn them.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿When Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts shrink﴾ and the verse: he said, "The hearts of these four became hard and recoiled: ﴿those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ — Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, Safwan, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf — ﴿And when those besides Him are mentioned﴾ — al-Lat and al-'Uzza — ﴿behold, they rejoice.﴾"

Muslim, Abu Dawud, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* reported from 'A'ishah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would rise at night, he would open his prayer with: 'O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ. Guide me to the truth concerning what has been disputed, by Your permission, for indeed You guide whom You will to a straight path.'"

[p. 1287] His saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾. By "man" here is meant the species, taken with regard to some or most of its individuals. It was said that it refers only to the disbelievers, but the first view is preferable. Restricting it to the species does not conflict with the specific occasion of its revelation, because what counts is the generality of the wording. Taking it generally does justice to the Qur'anic text and fulfils its meaning. The sense is that it is the habit of most of mankind that when harm touches them, whether sickness, poverty or something else, they call upon God and humble themselves before Him to remove it and ward it off. ﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us﴾: that is, We give him a blessing that comes from Us. ﴿He says, "I have only been given it because of knowledge"﴾: that is, knowledge from me of the ways of gaining wealth, or because of some good in me, or because of knowledge from God regarding my merit.

Al-Hasan said: "Because of knowledge which God taught me." It was also said: "I knew that if I was given this in this world, I would have a station with God." The pronoun in ﴿ʾūtītuhu﴾ ("I have been given it") is masculine, although it refers back to "favour" (niʿmah), because the word is equivalent in meaning to "bestowal" (ināʿm).

It was also said that the pronoun refers back to "mā" (that which), which is a relative pronoun, but the first view is preferable. ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: this is a rejection of what he said. That is, that which We have given you is not what you claim. Rather, it is a test for you and an examination of your condition: will you give thanks or will you disbelieve? Al-Farra' said: "He made the pronoun in His words ﴿hiya﴾ ('it') feminine because of the feminine gender of 'trial'. Had He said ﴿huwa fitnah﴾ ('it is a trial', masculine), it would have been permissible." Al-Nahhas said: "Rather, His gift is a trial." It was also said that the feminine pronoun is taken according to the wording of "trial", while the masculine in the first case, ﴿ūtītuhu﴾, is taken according to its meaning. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: that this is a respite granted to them by God and a testing of what they have of gratitude or disbelief.

﴿Those before them had already said it﴾: that is, those who went before said this same word which they said, namely "I have only been given it because of knowledge", as Qarun did. For Qarun said: ﴿"I have only been given it because of knowledge that is with me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. ﴿So what they earned did not avail them﴾: the word "mā" here may be a negation, meaning that what they gained of the goods of this world did not avail them at all. It may also be interrogative, meaning: what did that avail them?

﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them﴾: that is, the recompense for the evil of their earning, or evil consequences which are the recompense for their earning. The recompense is called "evil" because it falls in return for their evil deeds, and this is an instance of al-mushākalah (matching of expression), like His words: ﴿"And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it"﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Then He, glory be to Him, threatened the disbelievers of his own time, saying: ﴿As for those who did wrong among these﴾, the present disbelievers, ﴿the evil consequences of what they earned will befall them﴾, just as it befell those before them. It has indeed befallen them in this world, in the form of famine, killing, captivity and subjugation. ﴿And they cannot escape﴾: that is, they cannot outrun God, but their return is to Him, and He will do with them whatever punishment He wills.

﴿Do they not know that God expands provision for whom He wills﴾: that is, He widens provision for whom He wills to widen it for, and He restricts it, that is, withholds it, from whom He wills to withhold it and constrict it upon him. Muqatil said: "God admonished them so that they would take heed regarding His oneness. This was when they were given rain after seven years of drought, and He said: ﴿Do they not know that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills﴾." ﴿Surely in that are signs﴾: that is, in what has been mentioned there are great proofs and sublime indications. ﴿For a people who believe﴾. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from the signs and reflect upon them.

Then, after mentioning the threat He had stated, He followed it with mention of the vastness of His mercy and the greatness of His forgiveness.

He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give them this glad tidings, and He said: ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God"﴾. By "transgression" (israf) is meant excess in sins and great abundance of them.

The meaning of ﴿do not despair (taqnaṭū)﴾ is: do not lose hope, ﴿of the mercy of God﴾, of His forgiveness.

Then, after forbidding them to despair, He informed them of what removes that and lifts it, and makes hope take the place of despair. He said: ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾.

Know that this verse is the most hope-giving verse in the Book of God, glory be to Him, because it includes the greatest good tidings. For first He attributed the servants to Himself, to honour them and to increase their joy. Then He described them as having transgressed in sins and having committed many of them. Then He followed this with a prohibition against despair of mercy, addressed to these who had multiplied their sins. So the prohibition of despair for sinners who are not excessive is by way of a fortiori reasoning (min bāb al-awlā) and by the implication of the address (bi-fahwā al-khiṭāb). Then He came with something that leaves no doubt after it and in which no suspicion stirs in the heart upon hearing it. He said: ﴿Indeed God forgives sins﴾. The definite article has turned the plural to which it is attached into a generic noun which implies the totality of its instances, so it is in effect: "Indeed God forgives every sin, whatever it may be," except what the Qur'anic text has excluded, which is shirk (associating partners with God): ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48, 116].

Then He did not suffice with what He had informed His servants of regarding the forgiveness of every sin, but He emphasised it by His words: ﴿all﴾. How wonderful a glad tiding this is, which the hearts of the believers who think well of their Lord rejoice in, the truthful in hoping for Him, those who cast off the garments of despair and reject bad thoughts about the One for whom no sin is too great, who does not withhold His forgiveness and mercy from His servants who turn to Him seeking pardon and take refuge in Him for the forgiveness of their sins. How excellent is the reason which God, glory be to Him, gave for this statement when He said: ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

That is: abundant in forgiveness and mercy, great in both, profound in them and vast in them. Whoever refuses this great grace and this immense bounty, and thinks that causing God's servants to despair and to lose hope of His mercy is better for them than what God has given them as glad tidings, has indeed committed the greatest excess and made the most hideous error. For the glad tidings and the absence of despair which came in God's promises in His Mighty Book, and the path which His Messenger (ﷺ) took, as is authentically reported from him in his saying: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not drive people away."

Once this is established for you, know that the reconciliation between this verse and His words: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116, 48] is that every sin, whatever it may be, apart from associating partners with God, is forgiven for whom God wills to forgive. Moreover, it may be said: His informing us that He forgives all sins indicates that He wills to forgive them all, and this entails that He wills forgiveness for all sinful Muslims. Thus no contradiction remains between the two verses from this standpoint.

As for what a group of exegetes claim, restricting this verse to repentance, saying that it forgives only the sins of those who repent, and they claim that they said this to reconcile the verses, then it is a combining of the lizard and the fish, and of the sailor and the one who sings to the camels, and "Barāqish has brought harm upon herself" [a proverb]. For if this great glad tiding were restricted to repentance, it would have little effect. For repentance from a polytheist, by which God forgives him the shirk he committed, is agreed upon by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Muslims, and yet He said: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116, 48]. [p. 1288] If repentance were a condition for forgiveness, there would be no benefit in explicitly mentioning shirk. And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]. Al-Wahidi said: "All the exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning a people who feared that if they embraced Islam, God would not forgive them the great sins they had committed, such as shirk, killing a soul, and enmity towards the Prophet (ﷺ)."

I say: Suppose it was about those people; so what? For the consideration is with what the verse contains of generality, not with the specificity of the occasion, as is agreed upon among the scholars. Had the Qur'anic verses and the prophetic traditions been restricted to their occasions and not extended beyond them, most obligations would have been lifted from the community, if not all of them, and the consequent is false by consensus, so the antecedent is likewise false.

In the purified Sunnah there are authentic traditions in the two Sahihs and others on this subject which, if one who has examined them knows them as they should be known and appreciates them as they should be appreciated, he will know the soundness of what we have mentioned and recognise the truth of what we have set forth.

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿yā ʿibādī﴾ ("O My servants") with the yā (ي) affirmed both in continuous recitation and at pause. Abu Bakr narrated from ʿAsim that he pauses without the yā. Al-Jumhur recited ﴿taqnaṭū﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn, while Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasrah.

﴿And turn back to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, then you will not be helped﴾: that is, return to Him in obedience. When He gave them glad tidings that He forgives all sins, He commanded them to return to Him by doing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. There is nothing in this that indicates restricting the first verse to repentance, neither by direct correspondence, nor by implication, nor by necessary inference. Rather, the most that is in it is that He gave them that great glad tiding, then called them to good and warned them against evil. Moreover, it may be said that this sentence is a new discourse addressed to the disbelievers who had not embraced Islam, as shown by His words: ﴿and submit to Him﴾. It came to warn the disbelievers and admonish them after encouraging the Muslims with the first verse and giving them glad tidings. Although this is remote, it may be upheld. The meaning, according to the apparent sense, is that God combined for His servants the great glad tiding, the command to turn to Him, to devote themselves sincerely to Him, to submit to His command and to humble themselves before His judgment. His words ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ mean the punishment of this world, as His words ﴿before it comes upon you﴾ indicate. There is nothing in that which indicates what those who make claims have claimed, and which those who despair and cause others to despair have clung to. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾: meaning the Qur'an. It says: make lawful what it makes lawful and make unlawful what it makes unlawful; the entire Qur'an is good. Al-Hasan said: "Commit yourselves to His obedience and avoid His disobediences." Al-Suddi said: "The best is what God has commanded in His Book."

Ibn Zayd said: "It means the definite verses (muḥkamāt), and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous verses (mutashābihāt) to the One who knows them."

It was said: the abrogating (nāsikh) rather than the abrogated (mansūkh). It was said: pardon rather than retaliation where retaliation is due. It was said: the best of what has been sent down to you concerns the reports of past nations. ﴿Before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾: that is, before the punishment ambushes you while you are heedless of it and do not sense it. It was also said that He meant that they would die suddenly and thus fall into punishment.

The first view is preferable, because what comes upon them suddenly is the punishment of this world, by killing, captivity, subjugation, fear and drought, not the punishment of the Hereafter nor death, since He did not attribute the coming to death.

﴿Lest a soul say, "Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning God's side"﴾. The Basrians said: that is, out of fear that one should say. The Kufans said: "so that one should not say." Al-Mubarrad said: "Hasten, for fear that one should say, or out of caution that a soul should say." Al-Zajjaj said: "For fear that you should come to a state in which you say: 'Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning God's side.'" It was said: by "soul" here is meant the disbelieving soul. It was also said: it means multiplicity, as in His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has brought forward﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿yā ḥasratā﴾ with an alif replacing the yā' of the possessive suffix, the original being yā ḥasratī. Ibn Kathir recited "yā ḥasratāh" with the hā' of pause at a pause. Abu Ja'far recited "yā ḥasratī" with the yā' according to the original form.

Al-ḥasrah means regret. The meaning of ﴿for what I neglected concerning God's side﴾ is: for what I neglected in obedience to God, as said by al-Hasan.

Al-Dahhak said: "for what I neglected concerning the remembrance of God," meaning the Qur'an and acting upon it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: ﴿concerning God's side﴾ means: concerning God's reward.

Al-Farra' said: *al-janb* means nearness and proximity (القُرْبُ والجِوارُ), that is, in the nearness of Allah and His neighbourhood. From this is His saying: ﴿and the companion by your side﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. According to this view, the meaning is: "for what I neglected in seeking *janb* Allah," that is, in seeking His neighbourhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Ibn al-A'rabi also held this view.

Al-Zajjaj said: it means that I neglected the path which is the way of Allah, namely His Tawhid and affirming the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). On this view, *al-janb* has the meaning of *al-jani'b* (the side), that is, I fell short in the side that leads to the pleasure of Allah. From this is the words of the poet:

*"For the people there is a side, and for the commander a side."*

That is: the people are on one side and the commander is on another side.

﴿And indeed I was among those who mocked﴾, that is: I was only among those who ridiculed the religion of Allah in the world. The clause's position (*mahall*) is in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject).

Qatadah said: "It was not enough for him that he wasted obedience to Allah, until he mocked its people."

﴿Or [lest] he say: "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous"﴾, that is: if only Allah had guided me to His religion, I would have been among those who guard against shirk and sins. This is among the false arguments which the polytheists use, and the baseless excuses they offer, as in His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him"﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. So it is a word of truth, by which they intend falsehood.

Then He—glorified is He—mentioned another of their statements, saying: ﴿Or [lest] he say when he sees the punishment: "If only I had a return [to the world], so that I might be among the doers of good"﴾, that is: a return to the world, ﴿so that I might be among the doers of good﴾, the believers in Allah, those who single Him out, who do good in their deeds. The accusative of *akun* (I would be) is either because it is in apposition to *karrah* (return), since it is a verbal noun, and *akun* is in the sense of a verbal noun, as in the poet's words:

*"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye / are dearer to me than the wearing of fine garments."*

Al-Farra' cited this as an example:

*"Of her you have nothing but remembrance and dread, / and you ask about her riders, where they headed."*

Or it is because it is the answer to the wish implied in His saying: ﴿If only I had a return﴾.

Then He—glorified is He—mentioned His answer to these souls that wish and make excuses without a reason, saying: ﴿Yes! My signs had come to you, but you denied them, and you were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers﴾.

The "signs" here are the revealed signs, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of denying them is his saying that they are not from Allah, and arrogance toward belief in them. Along with that denial and arrogance, he was among the disbelievers in Allah.

He—glorified is He—used the masculine form in His words: *jā'atka* (came to you), *kadhdhabta* (you denied), *istakbarta* (you were arrogant), and *kunta* (you were), because the word *nafs* (soul) applies to both masculine and feminine.

Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs say *nafsun wahid*, that is, one person. The Jumhur (majority of readers) read these places with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. Al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read them with a *kasra* on it throughout. This is the reading of Abu Bakr, his daughter Aisha, and Umm Salamah, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah, their faces blackened﴾, that is: you will see those who lied about Allah by claiming He has partners, a consort, and a son, with their faces blackened because of the punishment that surrounded them and what they witnessed of Allah's wrath and vengeance. The clause ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Al-Akhfash said: *tara* (you see) is not governing ﴿their faces blackened﴾; rather it is a subject and predicate. The preferred view is that if *tara* is from sight (visual seeing), then the clause ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is circumstantial; and if it is from the heart (knowing), then it is in the accusative position as the second object of *tara*. The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ is for affirmation, that is: there is no place in it for those who were arrogant toward obeying Allah. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people, as is established in the sound hadith.

﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared [Him]﴾, that is: those who feared shirk and the disobedience of Allah. The preposition *bi* in ﴿with their success﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, that is: "they being entangled with their success."

The Jumhur read ﴿bi-mafāzatihim﴾ in the singular, as a *mīmī* verbal noun. *Al-fawz* is attaining good and being saved from evil.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-mafāzah* is *mafʿalah* from *al-fawz*, which is happiness. If it is pluralized, it is fine, as in your saying: *al-sa'adah* and *al-sa'adat* (happiness and happinesses).

The meaning: Allah will deliver them through their success, that is, through their deliverance from the Fire and their success in attaining Paradise.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr read *bi-mafāzātihim* in the plural, the plural of *mafāzah*. Its pluralization, even though it is a verbal noun, is because of the difference in types. ﴿Evil will not touch them﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, and likewise ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is: He negates evil and grief from them. It is also permissible that the *bā'* in *bi-mafāzatihim* is causal, that is: because of their success, along with the absence of any touch of evil on them and the non-arrival of grief in their hearts, because they were content with the reward of Allah and felt secure from His punishment.

Ibn Abi Hatim—al-Suyuti said with a sound chain—and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The verse ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "We used to say, 'There is no repentance for one who has been tempted (into apostasy), and Allah will not accept anything from him.' They had known Allah and believed in Him and affirmed His Messenger, then they turned back from that because of a trial that befell them, and they used to say this to themselves. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verses." Ibn Umar said: "So I wrote them with my own hand, then sent them to Hisham ibn al-'As."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id that he said: "When Wahshi embraced Islam, Allah revealed: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. Wahshi and his companions said: 'We have committed all of this.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to a group of his companions while they were laughing and talking. He said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.' Then he left, and it made the people weep. Allah revealed to him: 'O Muhammad, why do you make My servants despair?' So the Prophet (ﷺ) returned and said: 'Rejoice, be steadfast, and draw near (to right conduct).'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that it was revealed concerning those who were tempted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca when they said: "Allah will not forgive them what they have committed of shirk, the killing of souls, and other things."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Thawban: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'I would not love to have the world and what is in it in exchange for this verse: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ to the end of the verse.' A man said: 'And what about one who associates partners (with Allah)?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent. He said: 'Beware! And one who associates partners (with Allah)'—three times."

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Asma' bint Yazid: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite: 'O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Husn al-Zann billah*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he passed by a judge who was admonishing the people, so he said: "O admonisher of the people, do not make the people despair!" Then he recited: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Sirin that he said: Ali said: "Which verse is the broadest in scope?" So they began to mention verses from the Qur'an, such as ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], the verse, and similar. Ali said: "There is nothing in the Qur'an broader in scope than: O My servants..."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse, that he said: "Allah has called to His forgiveness whoever claimed that the Messiah is the son of Allah, whoever claimed that Uzayr is the son of Allah, whoever claimed that Allah is poor, whoever claimed that the hand of Allah is shackled, and whoever claimed that Allah is the third of three. He says to these: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 74]. Then He called to repentance one greater in speech than these, who said ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24], and said ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]." Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever despairs of the servants' repentance after this has denied the Book of Allah. However, the servant cannot repent until Allah repents upon him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Lest a soul say﴾ that he said: "Allah informed what the servants would say before they say it, and taught them before they knew."

[p. 1287] His saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾. By "man" here is meant the species, taken with regard to some or most of its individuals. It was said that it refers only to the disbelievers, but the first view is preferable. Restricting it to the species does not conflict with the specific occasion of its revelation, because what counts is the generality of the wording. Taking it generally does justice to the Qur'anic text and fulfils its meaning. The sense is that it is the habit of most of mankind that when harm touches them, whether sickness, poverty or something else, they call upon God and humble themselves before Him to remove it and ward it off. ﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us﴾: that is, We give him a blessing that comes from Us. ﴿He says, "I have only been given it because of knowledge"﴾: that is, knowledge from me of the ways of gaining wealth, or because of some good in me, or because of knowledge from God regarding my merit.

Al-Hasan said: "Because of knowledge which God taught me." It was also said: "I knew that if I was given this in this world, I would have a station with God." The pronoun in ﴿ʾūtītuhu﴾ ("I have been given it") is masculine, although it refers back to "favour" (niʿmah), because the word is equivalent in meaning to "bestowal" (ināʿm).

It was also said that the pronoun refers back to "mā" (that which), which is a relative pronoun, but the first view is preferable. ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: this is a rejection of what he said. That is, that which We have given you is not what you claim. Rather, it is a test for you and an examination of your condition: will you give thanks or will you disbelieve? Al-Farra' said: "He made the pronoun in His words ﴿hiya﴾ ('it') feminine because of the feminine gender of 'trial'. Had He said ﴿huwa fitnah﴾ ('it is a trial', masculine), it would have been permissible." Al-Nahhas said: "Rather, His gift is a trial." It was also said that the feminine pronoun is taken according to the wording of "trial", while the masculine in the first case, ﴿ūtītuhu﴾, is taken according to its meaning. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: that this is a respite granted to them by God and a testing of what they have of gratitude or disbelief.

﴿Those before them had already said it﴾: that is, those who went before said this same word which they said, namely "I have only been given it because of knowledge", as Qarun did. For Qarun said: ﴿"I have only been given it because of knowledge that is with me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. ﴿So what they earned did not avail them﴾: the word "mā" here may be a negation, meaning that what they gained of the goods of this world did not avail them at all. It may also be interrogative, meaning: what did that avail them?

﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them﴾: that is, the recompense for the evil of their earning, or evil consequences which are the recompense for their earning. The recompense is called "evil" because it falls in return for their evil deeds, and this is an instance of al-mushākalah (matching of expression), like His words: ﴿"And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it"﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Then He, glory be to Him, threatened the disbelievers of his own time, saying: ﴿As for those who did wrong among these﴾, the present disbelievers, ﴿the evil consequences of what they earned will befall them﴾, just as it befell those before them. It has indeed befallen them in this world, in the form of famine, killing, captivity and subjugation. ﴿And they cannot escape﴾: that is, they cannot outrun God, but their return is to Him, and He will do with them whatever punishment He wills.

﴿Do they not know that God expands provision for whom He wills﴾: that is, He widens provision for whom He wills to widen it for, and He restricts it, that is, withholds it, from whom He wills to withhold it and constrict it upon him. Muqatil said: "God admonished them so that they would take heed regarding His oneness. This was when they were given rain after seven years of drought, and He said: ﴿Do they not know that God expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills﴾." ﴿Surely in that are signs﴾: that is, in what has been mentioned there are great proofs and sublime indications. ﴿For a people who believe﴾. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from the signs and reflect upon them.

Then, after mentioning the threat He had stated, He followed it with mention of the vastness of His mercy and the greatness of His forgiveness.

He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to give them this glad tidings, and He said: ﴿Say: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God"﴾. By "transgression" (israf) is meant excess in sins and great abundance of them.

The meaning of ﴿do not despair (taqnaṭū)﴾ is: do not lose hope, ﴿of the mercy of God﴾, of His forgiveness.

Then, after forbidding them to despair, He informed them of what removes that and lifts it, and makes hope take the place of despair. He said: ﴿Indeed God forgives all sins﴾.

Know that this verse is the most hope-giving verse in the Book of God, glory be to Him, because it includes the greatest good tidings. For first He attributed the servants to Himself, to honour them and to increase their joy. Then He described them as having transgressed in sins and having committed many of them. Then He followed this with a prohibition against despair of mercy, addressed to these who had multiplied their sins. So the prohibition of despair for sinners who are not excessive is by way of a fortiori reasoning (min bāb al-awlā) and by the implication of the address (bi-fahwā al-khiṭāb). Then He came with something that leaves no doubt after it and in which no suspicion stirs in the heart upon hearing it. He said: ﴿Indeed God forgives sins﴾. The definite article has turned the plural to which it is attached into a generic noun which implies the totality of its instances, so it is in effect: "Indeed God forgives every sin, whatever it may be," except what the Qur'anic text has excluded, which is shirk (associating partners with God): ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48, 116].

Then He did not suffice with what He had informed His servants of regarding the forgiveness of every sin, but He emphasised it by His words: ﴿all﴾. How wonderful a glad tiding this is, which the hearts of the believers who think well of their Lord rejoice in, the truthful in hoping for Him, those who cast off the garments of despair and reject bad thoughts about the One for whom no sin is too great, who does not withhold His forgiveness and mercy from His servants who turn to Him seeking pardon and take refuge in Him for the forgiveness of their sins. How excellent is the reason which God, glory be to Him, gave for this statement when He said: ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

That is: abundant in forgiveness and mercy, great in both, profound in them and vast in them. Whoever refuses this great grace and this immense bounty, and thinks that causing God's servants to despair and to lose hope of His mercy is better for them than what God has given them as glad tidings, has indeed committed the greatest excess and made the most hideous error. For the glad tidings and the absence of despair which came in God's promises in His Mighty Book, and the path which His Messenger (ﷺ) took, as is authentically reported from him in his saying: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not drive people away."

Once this is established for you, know that the reconciliation between this verse and His words: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116, 48] is that every sin, whatever it may be, apart from associating partners with God, is forgiven for whom God wills to forgive. Moreover, it may be said: His informing us that He forgives all sins indicates that He wills to forgive them all, and this entails that He wills forgiveness for all sinful Muslims. Thus no contradiction remains between the two verses from this standpoint.

As for what a group of exegetes claim, restricting this verse to repentance, saying that it forgives only the sins of those who repent, and they claim that they said this to reconcile the verses, then it is a combining of the lizard and the fish, and of the sailor and the one who sings to the camels, and "Barāqish has brought harm upon herself" [a proverb]. For if this great glad tiding were restricted to repentance, it would have little effect. For repentance from a polytheist, by which God forgives him the shirk he committed, is agreed upon by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Muslims, and yet He said: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 116, 48]. [p. 1288] If repentance were a condition for forgiveness, there would be no benefit in explicitly mentioning shirk. And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]. Al-Wahidi said: "All the exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning a people who feared that if they embraced Islam, God would not forgive them the great sins they had committed, such as shirk, killing a soul, and enmity towards the Prophet (ﷺ)."

I say: Suppose it was about those people; so what? For the consideration is with what the verse contains of generality, not with the specificity of the occasion, as is agreed upon among the scholars. Had the Qur'anic verses and the prophetic traditions been restricted to their occasions and not extended beyond them, most obligations would have been lifted from the community, if not all of them, and the consequent is false by consensus, so the antecedent is likewise false.

In the purified Sunnah there are authentic traditions in the two Sahihs and others on this subject which, if one who has examined them knows them as they should be known and appreciates them as they should be appreciated, he will know the soundness of what we have mentioned and recognise the truth of what we have set forth.

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿yā ʿibādī﴾ ("O My servants") with the yā (ي) affirmed both in continuous recitation and at pause. Abu Bakr narrated from ʿAsim that he pauses without the yā. Al-Jumhur recited ﴿taqnaṭū﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn, while Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasrah.

﴿And turn back to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, then you will not be helped﴾: that is, return to Him in obedience. When He gave them glad tidings that He forgives all sins, He commanded them to return to Him by doing acts of obedience and avoiding acts of disobedience. There is nothing in this that indicates restricting the first verse to repentance, neither by direct correspondence, nor by implication, nor by necessary inference. Rather, the most that is in it is that He gave them that great glad tiding, then called them to good and warned them against evil. Moreover, it may be said that this sentence is a new discourse addressed to the disbelievers who had not embraced Islam, as shown by His words: ﴿and submit to Him﴾. It came to warn the disbelievers and admonish them after encouraging the Muslims with the first verse and giving them glad tidings. Although this is remote, it may be upheld. The meaning, according to the apparent sense, is that God combined for His servants the great glad tiding, the command to turn to Him, to devote themselves sincerely to Him, to submit to His command and to humble themselves before His judgment. His words ﴿before the punishment comes upon you﴾ mean the punishment of this world, as His words ﴿before it comes upon you﴾ indicate. There is nothing in that which indicates what those who make claims have claimed, and which those who despair and cause others to despair have clung to. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾: meaning the Qur'an. It says: make lawful what it makes lawful and make unlawful what it makes unlawful; the entire Qur'an is good. Al-Hasan said: "Commit yourselves to His obedience and avoid His disobediences." Al-Suddi said: "The best is what God has commanded in His Book."

Ibn Zayd said: "It means the definite verses (muḥkamāt), and leave the knowledge of the ambiguous verses (mutashābihāt) to the One who knows them."

It was said: the abrogating (nāsikh) rather than the abrogated (mansūkh). It was said: pardon rather than retaliation where retaliation is due. It was said: the best of what has been sent down to you concerns the reports of past nations. ﴿Before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾: that is, before the punishment ambushes you while you are heedless of it and do not sense it. It was also said that He meant that they would die suddenly and thus fall into punishment.

The first view is preferable, because what comes upon them suddenly is the punishment of this world, by killing, captivity, subjugation, fear and drought, not the punishment of the Hereafter nor death, since He did not attribute the coming to death.

﴿Lest a soul say, "Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning God's side"﴾. The Basrians said: that is, out of fear that one should say. The Kufans said: "so that one should not say." Al-Mubarrad said: "Hasten, for fear that one should say, or out of caution that a soul should say." Al-Zajjaj said: "For fear that you should come to a state in which you say: 'Alas for me, for what I neglected concerning God's side.'" It was said: by "soul" here is meant the disbelieving soul. It was also said: it means multiplicity, as in His words: ﴿A soul will know what it has brought forward﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

Al-Jumhur recited ﴿yā ḥasratā﴾ with an alif replacing the yā' of the possessive suffix, the original being yā ḥasratī. Ibn Kathir recited "yā ḥasratāh" with the hā' of pause at a pause. Abu Ja'far recited "yā ḥasratī" with the yā' according to the original form.

Al-ḥasrah means regret. The meaning of ﴿for what I neglected concerning God's side﴾ is: for what I neglected in obedience to God, as said by al-Hasan.

Al-Dahhak said: "for what I neglected concerning the remembrance of God," meaning the Qur'an and acting upon it.

Abu ʿUbayda said: ﴿concerning God's side﴾ means: concerning God's reward.

Al-Farra' said: *al-janb* means nearness and proximity (القُرْبُ والجِوارُ), that is, in the nearness of Allah and His neighbourhood. From this is His saying: ﴿and the companion by your side﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. According to this view, the meaning is: "for what I neglected in seeking *janb* Allah," that is, in seeking His neighbourhood and nearness, which is Paradise. Ibn al-A'rabi also held this view.

Al-Zajjaj said: it means that I neglected the path which is the way of Allah, namely His Tawhid and affirming the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). On this view, *al-janb* has the meaning of *al-jani'b* (the side), that is, I fell short in the side that leads to the pleasure of Allah. From this is the words of the poet:

*"For the people there is a side, and for the commander a side."*

That is: the people are on one side and the commander is on another side.

﴿And indeed I was among those who mocked﴾, that is: I was only among those who ridiculed the religion of Allah in the world. The clause's position (*mahall*) is in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject).

Qatadah said: "It was not enough for him that he wasted obedience to Allah, until he mocked its people."

﴿Or [lest] he say: "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous"﴾, that is: if only Allah had guided me to His religion, I would have been among those who guard against shirk and sins. This is among the false arguments which the polytheists use, and the baseless excuses they offer, as in His saying: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him"﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. So it is a word of truth, by which they intend falsehood.

Then He—glorified is He—mentioned another of their statements, saying: ﴿Or [lest] he say when he sees the punishment: "If only I had a return [to the world], so that I might be among the doers of good"﴾, that is: a return to the world, ﴿so that I might be among the doers of good﴾, the believers in Allah, those who single Him out, who do good in their deeds. The accusative of *akun* (I would be) is either because it is in apposition to *karrah* (return), since it is a verbal noun, and *akun* is in the sense of a verbal noun, as in the poet's words:

*"The wearing of a cloak and the comfort of my eye / are dearer to me than the wearing of fine garments."*

Al-Farra' cited this as an example:

*"Of her you have nothing but remembrance and dread, / and you ask about her riders, where they headed."*

Or it is because it is the answer to the wish implied in His saying: ﴿If only I had a return﴾.

Then He—glorified is He—mentioned His answer to these souls that wish and make excuses without a reason, saying: ﴿Yes! My signs had come to you, but you denied them, and you were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers﴾.

The "signs" here are the revealed signs, which is the Qur'an. The meaning of denying them is his saying that they are not from Allah, and arrogance toward belief in them. Along with that denial and arrogance, he was among the disbelievers in Allah.

He—glorified is He—used the masculine form in His words: *jā'atka* (came to you), *kadhdhabta* (you denied), *istakbarta* (you were arrogant), and *kunta* (you were), because the word *nafs* (soul) applies to both masculine and feminine.

Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs say *nafsun wahid*, that is, one person. The Jumhur (majority of readers) read these places with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. Al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read them with a *kasra* on it throughout. This is the reading of Abu Bakr, his daughter Aisha, and Umm Salamah, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah, their faces blackened﴾, that is: you will see those who lied about Allah by claiming He has partners, a consort, and a son, with their faces blackened because of the punishment that surrounded them and what they witnessed of Allah's wrath and vengeance. The clause ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Al-Akhfash said: *tara* (you see) is not governing ﴿their faces blackened﴾; rather it is a subject and predicate. The preferred view is that if *tara* is from sight (visual seeing), then the clause ﴿their faces blackened﴾ is circumstantial; and if it is from the heart (knowing), then it is in the accusative position as the second object of *tara*. The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾ is for affirmation, that is: there is no place in it for those who were arrogant toward obeying Allah. Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people, as is established in the sound hadith.

﴿And Allah will deliver those who feared [Him]﴾, that is: those who feared shirk and the disobedience of Allah. The preposition *bi* in ﴿with their success﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, that is: "they being entangled with their success."

The Jumhur read ﴿bi-mafāzatihim﴾ in the singular, as a *mīmī* verbal noun. *Al-fawz* is attaining good and being saved from evil.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-mafāzah* is *mafʿalah* from *al-fawz*, which is happiness. If it is pluralized, it is fine, as in your saying: *al-sa'adah* and *al-sa'adat* (happiness and happinesses).

The meaning: Allah will deliver them through their success, that is, through their deliverance from the Fire and their success in attaining Paradise.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr read *bi-mafāzātihim* in the plural, the plural of *mafāzah*. Its pluralization, even though it is a verbal noun, is because of the difference in types. ﴿Evil will not touch them﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun, and likewise ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is: He negates evil and grief from them. It is also permissible that the *bā'* in *bi-mafāzatihim* is causal, that is: because of their success, along with the absence of any touch of evil on them and the non-arrival of grief in their hearts, because they were content with the reward of Allah and felt secure from His punishment.

Ibn Abi Hatim—al-Suyuti said with a sound chain—and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The verse ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "We used to say, 'There is no repentance for one who has been tempted (into apostasy), and Allah will not accept anything from him.' They had known Allah and believed in Him and affirmed His Messenger, then they turned back from that because of a trial that befell them, and they used to say this to themselves. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verses." Ibn Umar said: "So I wrote them with my own hand, then sent them to Hisham ibn al-'As."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id that he said: "When Wahshi embraced Islam, Allah revealed: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. Wahshi and his companions said: 'We have committed all of this.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse."

Al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to a group of his companions while they were laughing and talking. He said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.' Then he left, and it made the people weep. Allah revealed to him: 'O Muhammad, why do you make My servants despair?' So the Prophet (ﷺ) returned and said: 'Rejoice, be steadfast, and draw near (to right conduct).'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that it was revealed concerning those who were tempted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca when they said: "Allah will not forgive them what they have committed of shirk, the killing of souls, and other things."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Thawban: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'I would not love to have the world and what is in it in exchange for this verse: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ to the end of the verse.' A man said: 'And what about one who associates partners (with Allah)?' The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent. He said: 'Beware! And one who associates partners (with Allah)'—three times."

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Asma' bint Yazid: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite: 'O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins, and He does not mind. Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Husn al-Zann billah*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he passed by a judge who was admonishing the people, so he said: "O admonisher of the people, do not make the people despair!" Then he recited: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Sirin that he said: Ali said: "Which verse is the broadest in scope?" So they began to mention verses from the Qur'an, such as ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 11], the verse, and similar. Ali said: "There is nothing in the Qur'an broader in scope than: O My servants..."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, the verse, that he said: "Allah has called to His forgiveness whoever claimed that the Messiah is the son of Allah, whoever claimed that Uzayr is the son of Allah, whoever claimed that Allah is poor, whoever claimed that the hand of Allah is shackled, and whoever claimed that Allah is the third of three. He says to these: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 74]. Then He called to repentance one greater in speech than these, who said ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24], and said ﴿I know of no god for you other than Me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]." Ibn Abbas said: "Whoever despairs of the servants' repentance after this has denied the Book of Allah. However, the servant cannot repent until Allah repents upon him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Lest a soul say﴾ that he said: "Allah informed what the servants would say before they say it, and taught them before they knew."

[p. 1287] His saying: ﴿When harm touches man﴾. By "man" here is meant the species, taken with regard to some or most of its individuals. It was said that it refers only to the disbelievers, but the first view is preferable. Restricting it to the species does not conflict with the specific occasion of its revelation, because what counts is the generality of the wording. Taking it generally does justice to the Qur'anic text and fulfils its meaning. The sense is that it is the habit of most of mankind that when harm touches them, whether sickness, poverty or something else, they call upon God and humble themselves before Him to remove it and ward it off. ﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us﴾: that is, We give him a blessing that comes from Us. ﴿He says, "I have only been given it because of knowledge"﴾: that is, knowledge from me of the ways of gaining wealth, or because of some good in me, or because of knowledge from God regarding my merit.

Al-Hasan said: "Because of knowledge which God taught me." It was also said: "I knew that if I was given this in this world, I would have a station with God." The pronoun in ﴿ʾūtītuhu﴾ ("I have been given it") is masculine, although it refers back to "favour" (niʿmah), because the word is equivalent in meaning to "bestowal" (ināʿm).

It was also said that the pronoun refers back to "mā" (that which), which is a relative pronoun, but the first view is preferable. ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾: this is a rejection of what he said. That is, that which We have given you is not what you claim. Rather, it is a test for you and an examination of your condition: will you give thanks or will you disbelieve? Al-Farra' said: "He made the pronoun in His words ﴿hiya﴾ ('it') feminine because of the feminine gender of 'trial'. Had He said ﴿huwa fitnah﴾ ('it is a trial', masculine), it would have been permissible." Al-Nahhas said: "Rather, His gift is a trial." It was also said that the feminine pronoun is taken according to the wording of "trial", while the masculine in the first case, ﴿ūtītuhu﴾, is taken according to its meaning. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾: that this is a respite granted to them by God and a testing of what they have of gratitude or disbelief.

﴿Those before them had already said it﴾: that is, those who went before said this same word which they said, namely "I have only been given it because of knowledge", as Qarun did. For Qarun said: ﴿"I have only been given it because of knowledge that is with me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 78]. ﴿So what they earned did not avail them﴾: the word "mā" here may be a negation, meaning that what they gained of the goods of this world did not avail them at all. It may also be interrogative, meaning: what did that avail them?

﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned befell them﴾: that is, the recompense for the evil of their earning, or evil consequences which are the recompense for their earning. The recompense is called "evil" because it falls in return for their evil deeds, and this is an instance of al-mushākalah (matching of expression), like His words: ﴿"And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it"﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. Then He, glory be to Him, threatened the disbelievers of his own time, saying: ﴿As for those who did wrong among these﴾, the present disbelievers, ﴿the evil consequences of what they earned will befall them﴾, just as it befell those before them. It has indeed befallen them in this world, in the form of famine, killing, captivity and subjugation. ﴿And they cannot escape﴾: that is, they cannot outrun God, but their return is to Him, and He will do with them whatever punishment He wills.
